Now lets talk about 2 major DLC's:

First is Narco Road: 
Why Narco Road is Terrible!

Repetitive, Hollow Gameplay

The DLC swaps out the tactical squad-based missions that made the base game unique for shallow, recycled side activities.

Most “missions” are copy-pasted tasks: chasing cars, blowing up convoys, or racing — none of which fit the Ghost Recon identity.

Awful Follower System, Basically Progression is kinda tied to grinding “followers” (basically social media clout), which feels more like a parody of Ubisoft’s obsession with metrics than meaningful gameplay.

It’s not satisfying — instead of rewarding tactical play, it forces players into repetitive stunt missions.

Achievements/trophies are tied to this pointless follower mechanic, making completionists suffer through content that already feels tedious.

Driving & Vehicle Handling = Worst in Class

Wildlands already had notoriously bad driving physics — Narco Road doubles down on it by centering DLC around racing and stunts.

The result? Floaty cars, stiff steering, zero grip, and controls that feel more broken than fun.
Not to mention the LSD-like Nitro System, Instead of improving driving, Ubisoft slapped on a ridiculous “nitro boost” that turns vehicles into uncontrollable, glowing missiles.

It looks and feels more like a cartoon power-up than anything grounded in the Ghost Recon world.

The Tone-Deaf Design:
The gritty cartel narrative of Wildlands is replaced with an over-the-top “extreme sports narco celebrity” vibe.
It clashes so hard with the base game’s identity that it feels like a parody DLC, not a serious expansion.

AND THE CHARACTERS WONT SHUT THE ♥♥♥♥ UP. 0/10

-----------------------------
Second is Fallen Ghosts:
Back to Tactical Roots

Unlike Narco Road, this DLC doesn’t forget what Ghost Recon is supposed to be: stealth, strategy, and squad-based infiltration.

The missions are built around sneaking, planning, and using your tools effectively — not grinding meaningless side tasks.

New Enemies Actually Add Challenge, Introduces tougher enemy types (snipers, jammers, armored heavies, cloaked assassins).

They force you to change tactics instead of steamrolling every fight with the same strategy.

Sometimes it feels a bit “Ubisoft-y” (throwing gimmick enemies instead of smarter AI), but overall it keeps you on your toes.

You’re stranded after a helicopter crash with limited resources.
That setup ALONE feels more desperate and immersive compared to the cartoonish tone of Narco Road.

Better progression: New weapons and skills feel meaningful instead of grindy. 
Sadly it's a bit short tho. 8/10

The Negatives:

Vehicle Controls:
Driving vehicles is still poop. The driving characteristic are almost all identical from small vehicles to large trucks. I read when the new updated controls were released how much praise it received and some boasting how well they are at video game driving blah blah. All liars; Cars rubberband around like you're on some kind of server (which in a sense you are because ubisoft places you online so people can join). So with the rubberbanding plus what feels like mouse acceleration (Im on pc and hate any kind of acceleration or boosts), you're bouncing forward backwards and too much to the left or right. Controllers might be different and if so, another example how this was made for console and the pc port was short sighted.

Airplanes are mostly ok (I use the setup where you pitch up and down with keybinds and mouse look around). The biggest problem with planes is that they kind of just suck so you don't use them all that often. Then you have to steal one for the rebel side missions and then they want you to land on a mountain top surrounded by trees and debris and the strip is kind of short. No this isn't a sim so you technically can do it, but what happens (especially your first attempt), you're trying to guesstimate the approach. Then theres no zoom to fine tune that approach so when you get close the throttle down doesn't work quite smoothly so you're almost forcing the plane to drop a lot of speed in a short amount of time. You risk smashing into a little bit of cliff and blowing up and failing.

In my opinion the new controls for helicopters are best (vs the other vehicle types). Its not perfect (especially trying to use in combat) but after a while of getting used to it, you can use it effectively to get around. What does bother me is there is some (mouse) acceleration built into the yaw'ing and it has a capped speed (i.e. move too fast and its still limited to a specified speed). Every once in a while trying to do a turn you might do a 180 when not intending to (usually around slow to high speeds).

Then for some reason they added sensitivity left right for everything except planes and helis. Its even there for the drone.. like 1 more copy n pasta wouldn't have hurt could it? They could've provided raw mouse options for pc players and included the left/right sensitivity slider and the controls would almost fix themselves.

AI:
The ai (enemies) go from being blind to seeing you kind of too well. Not too problematic but it causes the waves of backups to come. The normal baddies aren't too bad but the unidad guys seem to always replenish each wave, one right after the other. Its real annoying trying to escape and is about the only this game kills me.

Speaking of poor ai, your friendly ai's are helpful during a firefight. While sneaking they used to seem reliable enough to stay hidden. I accidentally found out a few times that if you don't tell them to hold somewhere, they will find their own path to meet up with you which includes sneaking across the base, no cover and getting spotted (its almost hilarious to watch but because this is the primary reason my team gets spotted which then turn into waves of fighters - its annoying). Then on the flip side, when baddies are alerted, team is like "looks like they're onto us, whats your call team leader" or something and its like shoot back. I wish there was a mode like engage automatically when fired on.

They also do this thing where when you tell them to hold, they do just that. Wish there was some logic to control if area is alerted and primary player is under fire to engage back. Otherwise, they just sit there and I forget I put the on hold (because trying to avoid them accidentally tripping up). This happened during a timed mission and while I was down, waiting for 20-30 seconds to wait for a single teammate to come over and revive. 

Missions:
In general they're pretty easy. However, due to the lack of refined controls or any way to fix things, they throw some mission at you that ups the ante and you fail and don't understand why. For instance, you go to a huge base, do your ghost stealthy gameplay. But because some random object doesn't provide actual visible cover - it alerts enemies.

Theres this mission in Barvechos. I've completed several other zones already (4). Im stuck on this mission El Pulpos Right Hand man. The 2nd attempt I got through everything no problem until I had to do the mine and I thought I could extract the contact via heli I came in but NOPE. I gotta stash him in something else... a land vehicle. All while trying to figure this out, getting attacked wave after wave of baddies. I go down several times, my ghosts go down several times its relentless.

Side Missions:
Intercepting convoys is pretty rough especially with how bad vehicle controls are in general. Trying to do a quick interception is almost not going to end well. You kind of need to take out the driver and passenger and then everyone else. I wish they had something like shooting out the tires or something. Or the houses you gotta bust into and clear a path to hack before the timer runs out - the inside varies (I think I've had 3 or 4 so far and they've all been different on the inside). Im sure it wouldn't kill the experience by having more time OR increase/lower time based on difficulty.

Weapons:
Mostly sniping. It seems to have this built in mechanic that while reloading, if you fire too soon before finishing, it still queues that shot. So what happens is when I mis time my reload, I obviously haven't shot anything and then ok I need to wait but then the shot goes when Im not ready and the target has moved. I'll start by saying that I don't know how this game managed to get a Mostly Positive review score. Between the removed features from previous installments and the same iconic Ubisoft gameplay loop, it has Ubisoft written all over it.


Stealth feels downright awful.
- Unlike previous titles, shadows and vegetation figuratively don't exist. They have no effect on AI detection. The only thing that matters is direct line of sight (only hard, static objects prevent this, like parked cars and barriers) and the distance from your attacker.
- Most of the time, it seems like enemies spot you from your third-person camera, as I have been spotted numerous times through cover from impossible angles.
- Higher difficulties increase the speed of detection and the distance you can be seen at. Playing on Advanced difficulty and above, CQC stealth is pretty much the only viable option so you can have consistent cover to hide behind.
- Unlike other stealth titles, there's no agency if you are spotted. The moment the detection meter fills, you can't even kill the enemy to prevent them screaming for help. Everyone knows instantly.
- Clothing pattern holds no effect on detection. Arctic camo has the same detection as black camo across the board.

The gameplay loop is tedious, and the guns are very inconsistent. I just finished Far Cry 4 expecting something different, not the same exact game. At least Far Cry had better gunplay.
- Many of the missions are instant fails if you are detected, which already makes 60% of this game extremely frustrating and it just ends up being a checkpoint abuse simulator since the stealth is so unpolished.
- Capture outposts, cookie-cutter side missions for resources, liberate sector by killing lieutenant after enough missions.
- 70% of the missions require you to drive over 5km between objectives. A lot of these are escort missions so you can't even fast travel, and if you fail you are respawned an extra 2km away from your previous position. Most of the playtime is driving through dirt roads.
- There's maybe 5 different types of missions based on the objective at hand. If you've played a Ubisoft game or GTA V before, you've played this game too.

I'm trying to enjoy this because it's still a milsim game, something that Ubisoft used to not be bad at, but it even falls short there. If you like these types of games, you should know that this game can't even do it better than a Call of Duty title.
- The game opens strong with a Gunsmith mode, but there's maybe 7 attachments per gun that don't really change anything unless you are looking for higher scope magnifications. It's like a diet MW2019 gunsmith if they didn't refill the soda syrup.
- Every gun has very unrealistic bullet travel, drop, and damage based on their caliber. It seems as if they made up random values for these for balance purposes for the multiplayer mode rather than as an attempt at their real-life counterparts.
- Pinged enemies have distance shown under their mark, so your range to target is pretty much always displayed. Not that it matters because the velocities and drop-rate are extremely deceptive and unbalanced.
- Using snipers as an example as they can be measured the easiest:
-- Bullet drop is virtually non-existent up to 200m, but then exponentially gets so heavy that it's impossible to gauge where the hell the bullet's going to go. Since there's no zeroing feature, shots beyond 500m just require knowing how your rifle works rather than actually being able to do the math. This hardly, if at all, varies between guns. Something that I think really undercuts how these games are generally played.
-- Bullet velocity makes no sense either. Guns have different bullet velocities mainly based on gun type, not caliber, but in the end they are all so extremely slow that they're all comparable to handgun rounds. An unmodified 5.56 rifle reaches a target at 300m at the same exact time as the starting 9mm handgun if that tells you anything.
-- Gun damage is either one/two hit kill headshot, or enemies can soak 10-15 5.56 rounds with basic body armor.


If this wasn't enough for you yet, that's only half the battle. The other half is bugs and microtransactions (in a Ubi game, wowee).
- I've been stuck in 3 separate Mission Failed loops that occur for literally no reason. Spawn in, game says I've been detected with no enemies nearby, fail mission. Load checkpoint. Rinse, wash, repeat. Game becomes literally unplayable unless I can navigate to the map quickly enough and switch missions.
- Every few encounters, enemies seemingly chosen at random will have 100% accuracy. One example: We finished a compound last night, they called for backup, a car rolls in and a guy hanging out a window dual-wielding UZIs had a 100% hitrate on all three of us. Killed us instantly.

- Animations are clunky and not fluid at all. An example is when getting revived, your character has to stand up, wipe himself off, and shake his head. The whole animation is around 2 seconds long, but you aren't invincible while this happens and your character is usually shaking off the 18 rounds he just took to the chest before he's instantly back on the ground.
- I wish I was exaggerating when I say 80% of the guns and clothing are locked behind this awful Loot Box system they implemented.

So I fly over to his compound in a fast helicopter with my boys (my team of 3 "Ghosts") and start some trouble. Sure enough, the enemy is alerted and he lieutenant begins to flee in a motor vehicle.

I tell my boys in the chopper to open fire and then attempt to [i]goomba stomp[/i] the lieutenant's car with my helicopter. This does not go great, as my helicopter is destroyed, but since I am on the ground it's no biggie. Unfortunately, the target starts to get away in his vehicle, so I summon an armored SUV with a minigun from the rebels. At this point, we've started taking fire from other Casa Blanca elements, so my gunner basically always has someone to play with.

I catch up to the lieutenant and do enough damage to his car that he exits his vehicle. Unfortunately, as I go to detain him I am engaged by Casa Blanca forces and KO'd. I wait for my boys to clear the area and revive me, but in the meantime the lieutenant finds another vehicle, which I follow onto a base controlled by Unidad (hostile government forces). Again, my boys succeed in forcing the lieutenant out of his car, but now the Unidad base is on full alert, and I am KO'd again. My boys revive me once again, and I thank the gods I maxed out the revives perk. The lieutenant attempts to drive away in another vehicle, but in a stroke of luck he is blocked and runs away on foot.

I manage to sprint over to the lieutenant and detain him from behind, and frantically look for some cover. That's when I spot it—an armored personnel carrier with a heavy mounted gun—and move toward it as fast as I can while pointing a gun at my detainee's bag. Somehow I manage to stow the lieutenant in the APC, and we proceed to [i]slowly [/i]drive away from the base and toward our objective, which is somewhere in the mountains a couple clicks away. The rest of the trip is mostly uneventful aside from a near disaster where our vehicle almost tumbles over the mountain's edge. But we make it to our safe house and deliver the lieutenant.

[h1]The Rest of Reality[/h1]
During your [i]Ghost Recon: Wildlands[/i] playthrough, I expect you will experience similar thrills as those I described above (and probably double or triple the number if you are playing with friends). But for every glorious mission completion or clearing of a large base, you are likely to get 3-5 frustrating failures. It's weird that the game exists in the same universe as Sam Fisher (of [i]Splinter Cell[/i] fame), but despite having released over a decade after Sam's first outing, it sometimes feels just as unforgiving. 

[h3]Thanks, Sam[/h3]
For example, there's (thankfully optional) mission when you get to meet up with Fisher, but as soon as you are within like 200 meters of him you cannot kill anyone, be seen, or be *detected (*the list of ways in which you can be detected is frustratingly long, but it includes things like a body getting seen or an explosion being heard). Once you get to Fisher, it triggers a "defend Fisher" sequence. 

I gave up on the mission after a couple of tries because, like a lot of missions in the game, there are [i]no checkpoints. [/i]I read that there is also a 3rd extraction phase in this mission, which made me feel better about my decision to bail.

[h3]Far Craaaaap[/h3]
Having played all of the [i]Far Cry[/i] games (also developed by Ubisoft), I was familiar with [i]GRW[/i]'s approach to taking outposts. You can go in guns blazing, knowing that enemy backup will arrive, or try to keep things quieter, taking out alarms, drone jammers, base power, and anti-air missile batteries. [i]GRW[/i] has a couple of things that make taking outposts more fun: the sync-shot, which allows you to mark up to 3 targets and have your boys take them out; and a drone, which is like god mode for scouting (if it isn't jammed), and later, blowing stuff up.

So taking a base [i]can [/i]be a lot of fun, but for me it neve equaled the thrill of taking out every enemy in an outpost in [i]Far Cry[/i] games (especially 3 and 4), where you'd see a celebratory screen showing what bonuses (if any) you got for being undetected or if you'd disabled the alarms.

Additionally, there are just [i]too damn many[/i] bases in [i]GRW[/i]. So it definitely starts to feel same-y with few rewards (weapon cases, rebel supplies).

[h3]Not another region[/h3]
This brings me to my core complaint of [i]GRW[/i]: it's too big! I feel like they should have cut 4-6 regions and spent that dev time improving the checkpointing for story missions. By the end of the game I was flying over unexplored regions and ignoring everything but story objectives.

[h3]This isn't your dad's Rainbow Six[/h3]
I remember playing the first [i]Rainbow Six[/i] game in the late 90s. If you're old enough to remember, that was the one where you had to plot a course for your counter-terrorist team, telling them when to breach a door, throw a flashbang, etc. It was quite difficult, and obviously [i]GRW [/i]is not [i]that [/i]tactical, but honestly I wish [i]GRW [/i]had strayed further from its Tom Clancy source material and taken more from its ridiculous [i]Far Cry [/i]siblings.

As my opening tale about the chaos that is possible in [i]GRW[/i] shows, the game can be a wild ride. And I [i]do [/i]recommend playing it—especially with friends and/or if you have a willingness to look things up and skip missions that aren't fun—but I can only imagine how much greater it would have been if it had slimmed down and taken itself a bit less seriously.

Oh, but leave Karen Bowman (the team's CIA handler and most badass videogame Karen ever) alone :p

Ghost Recon : Wildlands does not possess the most engaging story or the most immersive third person shooter controls but it has enough here to keep you coming back. 

In a similar vein to my thoughts on Assassin's Creed : Odyssey, I felt like this game really didn't cover my original understanding of what "Ghost Recon" entails. However, once I accepted that the game was not going to play like the game from my childhood and took the game less seriously, it became a relaxing and different experience. 

There are interesting story moments but most of it is gruff military shouting and uneducated cartel member NPCs yelling insults. This is not a masterfully crafted "Tom Clancy" story, but more of a story that invokes feelings of Clancy-isms. I did appreciate that the Ghosts do things that are morally questionable, with some of them questioning if they did the morally "right" thing in certain situations. This is doubly so for the CIA contact Karen Bowman, who crosses the line between acceptable and ethicially/morally questionable often. I felt very conflicted with her willingness to burn people for the sake of the mission, which they touch on in the "Operation Oracle" (Cole D. Walker/Jon Bernthal) quests, but I knew they wouldn't commit to this story direction well before the conclusion of that story beat.  

Unfortunately, the story of main Operation "Kingslayer" limits the Ghosts to American Heroes who did horrible things for the right reason, stopping El Sueño's Santa Blanca. I felt like the setup for the sequel Breakpoint had more potential to "say something" with their story than the war on drugs against the most psychotic Cartel caricatures conceived. 

That said, the game was designed to be a sandbox for players to tackle the varied missions with their friends and for that I can wholeheartedly say that the game ticks that box. There are missions that cover the gambit of stealth, assassinations, trailing missions, scouting, destruction, all out assaults, building clearing, helicopter thefts and car hijackings + MORE!

The story context is just enough to get your co-op team to the next mission, and sometimes that's enough. 

[b] || Buy on discount, much better with friends. DLC optional (only for completionists) || [/b]

[h2] Ubisoft confirmed the issue, but no fix is planned — the game is no longer maintained [/h2]

Ghost Recon Wildlands is still a [b] fantastic tactical open-world shooter [/b] — but if you're using a modern Intel CPU, you might face:

• [b] 15-minute hang on the splash screen [/b]  
• [b ]Game may not load at all [/b]

This isn’t a driver issue or slow SSD — the problem occurs even on high-end systems with fast NVMe storage and modern GPUs. — it’s a known problem with the game’s thread handling. The only workaround: [b] disable Hyper-Threading or E-Cores in BIOS [/b], depending on your CPU.

Ubisoft support acknowledged the issue, apologized, and stated that [b] no patch will be released [/b], as the game is no longer actively supported.

[b] This affects most modern Intel CPUs: [/b]

• 13th/14th gen (e.g. i9-13900K, i9-14900KS): [i]game hangs unless Hyper-Threading is disabled[/i]  
• Core Ultra (e.g. Ultra 9 185H, 285K): [i]game may not load at all unless E-Cores are disabled[/i]

[b] The game is still sold at full price, with no warning on the store page. [/b]

Most PC users won’t think to tweak BIOS settings just to launch a game — and many wouldn’t even know how.
But that’s not their fault — this isn’t user error. BIOS-level changes aren’t something most players are expected to deal with, especially when buying a game from a mainstream storefront.

That said, once it runs, it’s still a [b] beautiful and immersive experience [/b]. Even years after release, the graphics hold up impressively — especially at max settings. 
The open world is [b] massive and atmospheric [/b], and the tactical gameplay (even solo with AI teammates) is genuinely satisfying.

What I’ve seen so far absolutely deserves praise.

The penultimate game in the series at the moment, which really deserves special attention from fans of open-world shooters, tactical operations, co-op with friends, and grinda, which is associated with Ubisoft in early 2017, when it was still relevant and there was no in-game donation. Let's take a look at what's good about it and why I think this game is pretty good in my personal opinion.

Advantages over other games of this genre:

1. Quite an unusual setting; you won't find any other game set in Latin America, specifically Bolivia. Only in this game can you truly see all the beauty and changeability of the weather and climate of the Great Andes, Uyuni — a salt flat, huge spacious deep jungles that resemble the mighty taiga of the North, only here it is the warm South. There is a very interesting landscape, huge lakes and landmarks, as well as some of the traditions of this continent. You will see endless fields and lots of plains that you can ride across on a bike or fly over in a helicopter when it is convenient. After this game, I wanted to visit this country, even though it is not entirely peaceful there. There are also favelas where criminals hide, and you will see the ghetto with your own eyes and how it really is in reality.

2. The map is huge and filled with interesting quests that do not involve grinding for resources, which we will discuss later. You want to go there not because the task is highlighted, but because you don't know how beautiful the location's terrain is.

3. Well-designed weapon mechanics and textures. A very rich arsenal of weapons and clothing, as well as a well-designed modular weapon system. They even remembered to add a couple of tasks and give out an original skin for the Ghosts squad leader. This is also the only game in which weapon skins look truly military, designed to camouflage weapons rather than to make you pay.

4. Stealth has its place, and you can really feel how you tactically destroy the enemy and outposts without making a sound. The game lets you do this and allows you to choose how to resolve the situation.

5. The game has a well-crafted storyline that is not entirely linear. You can neutralise all of the main villain's subordinates and the founder of the cartel, and then you will get a different ending, which is really noteworthy because it means that everything was not in vain.

6. In this game, you don't need to purchase any in-game currency at all. Everything can be unlocked by completing quests, except for completely unavailable skins, which cannot be unlocked due to the lack of certain Ubisoft services, as the game is no longer new.

7. The main quests look quite original, with variations in the killings of people involved in the cartel. Characters can be found under escort, at loud parties, on military bases, in the air, on isolated lakes, in the mountains, in tunnels, and in deep jungles. There is variety everywhere, and if you play with friends, it's even better.

8. Members of your squad. As in previous games in the series, you can leave your comrades alone and go through everything in solo mode, or you can interact and take out three fighters at once as a team by choosing the right trajectory and tactics. You also get help from additional rebel squads, mortar fire on outposts, and all of this is available to you as you level up and capture enemy resources.

9. Convenient movement around the map. You can call a car or helicopter at any time, and there are also fast travel points if you have unlocked them. You won't always be able to get to a specific point by moving, so a helicopter or small plane is best.

10. Bots come in different levels of difficulty and, depending on the location, they can be armoured and very accurate. There are also elite squads close to the cartel's assistants, which will be difficult to deal with, but you are not alone, and there are also difficulties with waves and bots, which also adds to the interest and action.

11. I like that the game offers the opportunity to run with two main rifles for greater variety. Since the game is mainly about medium and long distances. 


Cons:

1. The driving mechanics are very clunky, and it is very inconvenient to move around the map with them. They are only useful in firefights.

2. The AI of the bots is very poor; they can shoot well, but their behaviour is not worthy of a 2017 game and tactical shooter. Except for the elite fighters in heavy armour, they are really worth paying attention to and can wipe out your entire squad.

3. Your squad is invincible unless you die. You can resurrect your allies endlessly without losing resources or the lives of your teammates. In my opinion, this is unfair because it diminishes the importance of any team member (I'm not talking about the cooperative part, but the single-player part).

4. The implementation of resource gathering for character and skill levelling is poorly designed. After half the game, you begin to tire of the monotony and only pursue new weapons and modules for them, with little interest in developing other aspects.

5. There are some very stupid bugs when delivering cargo to the base, and chasing criminals can be difficult at times because the bots are simply stupid and behave unpredictably and foolishly. There are missions where you have to take a criminal hostage without weapons and extract information without causing harm in order to increase the amount of resources, which is very stupid because the rebels and the squad can easily neutralise him.

6. You practically don't need additional weapons, unless you have two sniper rifles, which you can't carry. Shotguns are completely useless in this game; only a drum magazine can make you happy, but there is no way to use it because there are almost no narrow spaces in the game except for favelas and narrow train tunnels.

7. To my great surprise, the game does not allow you to choose rifle cartridges, only in the DLC ‘Fallen Ghosts’ will you be given a weapon with a special cartridge, but there are only a few of them and they are no longer needed when you have completed almost the entire game...

8. The game does not allow you to join an existing session of 2-3 players playing in cooperative mode.

9. The game died too quickly in terms of online play. Only a couple of years passed and they stopped supporting it, which was a shame. The game had potential.

Despite all the cons, I'll give the game a thumbs up, as I see more significant pros than cons in it. The quests may have been made without soul, but the level designers and people who worked on the atmosphere of the game and tactical developments, as well as the ammunition, deserve my attention. I would love to play this game in a four-player co-op someday.

Wildlands, my contender for Ubisoft's "Lightning in a Bottle" on game design. Open world, arcade-style military sandbox with pick up & play elements and lots of freedom to move around. Overall not too serious. If you like that stuff, it's a good one.

Graphical settings are standard fare, but extremely customizable. Anti-aliasing, filtering, shadows, bloom, DoF, lens flare, vegetation, draw distance, scaling, etc. Lots of things to tweak. My problem that I've always had with the game is stuttering at higher graphical settings (on exceptional hardware) that is kinda-sorta fixable, but you need to jump through hoops to even get right. Lots of trial and error. Just something to note if you get pissed off at UNOPTIMIZED games, this is one of them and I will never let this issue slide. This is my major issue with the game and it really brings the experience down if you care about consistent frame rates. Otherwise, ignore.

Keyboard controls are stupid in my opinion (personal issue), but I've rebound them to my liking. I don't believe every key is bindable, but can't say for sure as I don't test every key for functionality. Menu navigation sucks too. Really gives off the impression that little effort was made to adapt the game for PC. Straight up console port. If you've played Breakpoint and never touched Wildlands, it is evident how much better the gunplay/movement is in that game compared to Wildlands. No contest. And slight note if you play with a controller, the buttons will most likely be screwed up. Buttons will be reversed and/or have different functionality. An example would be pressing the right trigger to fire and instead of firing you'll swap weapons or couch instead. You'll need to go adjust it via Steam input (shift+tab to open Steam overlay, go to controller icon, etc.) I've gotten used to PC controls and have given up on controller, but this seems to be a solution that works. This still hasn't officially been fixed by Ubi in 2025, lol.

So, Wildlands. Based off of (Tom Clancy's) novels, as per usual. You're an Army special ops team (Ghost) of four sent into Bolivia to conduct (Recon®) and deal with a fictional cartel (Santa Blanca) that has taken over much of the country in terms of influence. Your team goes in to clean house because ♥♥♥♥ happens. Sound cool? Lots of killing, blowing stuff up, you name it. There's nothing else really to add as the game isn't that deep in terms of emotional value or depth. Some comedic moments & dialogue clash with the overall depressing atmosphere of the SB Cartel's brutality on the region. Thus, if you really want a deep story, I'm afraid Wildlands doesn't have it. Not a big deal honestly. That aside, the general atmopshere is great. Ordinary, everyday people in the game do live normal lives and will farm, carry things around, chill about, traverse alongside roadways or trails, and generally feel alive compared to some other games. In contrast to these 'peaceful' moments, civilians will also be held at gunpoint along the roadways by the cartel (you can intervene, of course), hanged, have their vehicles burned to send a message or just straight up be shot in the streets. Rebel forces you help with spawn around the map as their influence spreads. Cartel & the local military forces will sometimes clash. The game feels 'alive' and these small details help to sell the idea that this is a living and breathing open world that doesn't particularly revolve around you, but rather it revolves on its own. It doesn't exactly wait for the player.

Customization. Pick a gender, face, clothing and you're done. It's limited. Five custom outfit sets if I remember correctly if you like making outfits and swapping out at your prerogative. Everything is changeable via menu later on in game. Most clothing is unlocked at the start (aside from microtransactions/earnables). Weapon camos are the same way.

General voice acting is 'okay'. Not terrible. I loved the squad dialogue, but some might find it annoying. 

Gameplay wise, you aren't really required to do anything aside from the initial mission of rescuing an idiot. This opens up the map; you cannot ignore the mission and explore until it's over, but you can freely explore the highlighted region that the mission takes place in. When the map opens up and you're looking around in the open world, you'll sometimes find collectibles in the form of documents, recordings, and other intel . You'll also find more useful things such as weapon parts, medals/skillpoints (for perks), and perhaps the most sought after type of collectible: new weapons. It's your usual plethora of 'military' equipment with some fictional adjustments as per copyright etc. Lots of assault rifles, marksman rifles, sniper rifles, a couple shotguns, SMG/pistol caliber guns. No RPGs or anything remotely resembling a projectile aside from attachable grenade launchers. Weapons all mostly feel and work the same, so choose your favorite based on what you like. Game also has an XP system. Doesn't affect much aside from unlockable perks. You can easily play the game without perks.

How's the gunplay? Simple, but very solid. Shoot stuff, kill stuff. Enemies that are undetected will die in a shot. If detected or actively engaging you, enemies will turn into bullet sponges (to an extent), but will die to headshots. Sniping sucks. Enemy A.I is unforgiving and cruel. They almost never miss, so it's best to play it tactically. You should take cover, use all your abilities and tools to your advantage. Ghost/Tier Mode, stealth is mandatory in my opinion. You do NOT want enemies actively engaging you as you WILL die. Game is mainly played in 3rd person, but you can swap to first person aiming, but there's no gun model aside from sights (think Rainbow Six Vegas, but reverse if that helps give an idea). 

Exploring is the best way to enjoy the game. Find your own fun, yadda yadda. I first played this on console and know literally every spot on the map, but it never gets old to me. I chalk this up to the way the world is created from the ground up. It's a 'fictional' take on Bolivia, so do take note. There's no giant sprawling cities or anything, hence the game subtitle name "Wildlands". Terrain and landscapes range from vast deserts, forests/rainforests, jungles, small towns, mines, swamps, mountainous regions, and even a snowy area. Regions have lots of variety to them and have reasonable scaling. It's not like San Andreas where you cross the bridge after leaving a city and suddenly you're in the desert. In Wildlands, terrain change feels both gradual and natural imo. It's not jarring like the comparison just made. This makes it both grounded in reality and extremely scenic the further you travel. Keep this in mind if you dislike traversing long distances because you'll be doing that a lot in game. There is limited fast travel, but I've always held the opinion that fast travel worsens open world games. Do as you wish because at least you have the option in this game.

Vehicles? There's cars, planes (unarmed), trucks, APCs, boats, helis (armed and unarmed), and motorbikes. If I missed a vehicle class, they're not worth mentioning. How do they handle? Ubisoft game, vehicles suck. Bumping a car into a small rock will dent everything from the windshield to the bumper and lights. Cars will smoke faster than you can say 'Sicario with a submachine gun'. APCs can and will be destroyed quickly by small arms fire. Very ridiculous. Planes have some of the worst flying mechanics I've experienced in a modern game.

Overall, do I recommend Wildlands? Sure. It's not perfect, but I feel games like Wildlands are where Ubisoft's 'generic open world' is at its best. It doesn't 'redefine' anything (lol?) but satisfies a certain niche and does it well enough. You just wanna play a modern military style game with customization and freedom of engagement? This is it. Buy on sale to save money. I've only spent money on the base game. DLC is garbage.

"Ghost Recon Wildlands" is one of the most underrated tactical shooters out there.

From the moment I dropped into Bolivia, I was hooked. The open world is huge, diverse, and incredibly immersive—from snowy mountains to dense jungles, it feels alive and full of opportunity. You can approach missions however you want: go in stealthy, snipe from a ridge, or kick down the door guns blazing. That freedom makes every mission feel like your mission.

Playing solo with AI teammates is okay, but co-op is where the game really shines. Coordinating attacks, syncing sniper shots, and driving through enemy convoys with friends is incredibly fun and satisfying. The gun customization system (Gunsmith) is also super detailed and lets you tailor your loadout exactly how you like it.

Yes, the story is a bit generic and some voice lines can be cringey, but honestly? I didn’t come here for the plot—I came to blow up drug labs, take down cartel bosses, and fly helicopters through enemy territory. And Wildlands delivers that perfectly.

If you enjoy military shooters with freedom of choice, tactical gameplay, and a vast open world to explore, this game is absolutely worth picking up—especially on sale.

Final Verdict:
🟢 Great solo, amazing with friends
🔫 Deep weapon customization
🌍 Massive open world
🎯 Satisfying stealth and gunplay
🛠️ Minor bugs & AI quirks, but nothing game-breaking

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon® Wildlands delivers a sprawling open-world tactical shooter experience that pushes the boundaries of cooperative gameplay and strategic planning. Set in a vividly realized Bolivia, the game invites players to dismantle a powerful drug cartel through stealth, precision, and teamwork.

The sheer scale of the map is both a blessing and a challenge. With diverse biomes ranging from arid deserts to dense jungles and snowy mountains, exploration never feels monotonous. Each environment demands a different approach—whether it’s silent sniper shots from a distant ridge or high-speed chases through twisting mountain roads.

The cooperative multiplayer is the game’s heart and soul. Coordinating with friends to execute synchronized strikes or splitting up to cover more ground enhances the tactical depth. For solo players, the AI squad members do a decent job, though they sometimes falter in complex combat scenarios, slightly dulling the immersion.

Customization is robust, allowing players to tailor weapons, gear, and even their Ghost’s appearance to suit their playstyle. The mission design encourages creativity — you’re often rewarded for thinking outside the box, whether by using drones for reconnaissance or setting clever traps.

However, the game is not without flaws. Some mission structures can feel repetitive, and occasional bugs disrupt the otherwise polished experience. The narrative, while serviceable, takes a backseat to gameplay and world exploration, which might disappoint those looking for a deeper story.

Overall, Ghost Recon Wildlands stands out as an ambitious and enjoyable tactical shooter with an immense world begging to be tamed. It’s a must-play for fans of cooperative tactical gameplay and those who appreciate a sandbox where creativity and strategy reign supreme.

While the narrative is serviceable and mission structures can become repetitive over time, the freedom of approach, robust customization options, and tactical gameplay provide lasting appeal for fans of military shooters.

Verdict:
A highly customizable tactical shooter that rewards coordination and strategic thinking. Best experienced in co-op for full immersion.

This is quite possibly the most overindulgent application of unrestrained freedom in shooter game form ever.

While there is some bias toward being painstakingly methodical to win engagements as per the game's 'tactical' trappings, it (with admittedly a few needless exceptions) doesn't wrestle control from the player's hands for being pointlessly reckless.

Situation calls for strategic use of high-tech equipment to minimize risk? How about jumping from a helicopter and calling in a danger close airstrike. The story demanding for your attention for a boring mission that you supposedly have to partake in ASAP? Respond in three business days while you go do the side quests. Maintaining one's distance while using silenced, scoped rifles being the optimal way to play? I'll believe that when I get bored blasting cartel goons with my shotgun that has the effective range of a French kiss.

Okay, so occasionally you'll have to play the 'right' way. Defending delicate hostages requires restraining oneself from chucking explosives everywhere like candy, and AA batteries discourage airborne joyriding over the wrong side of the tracks. 

Those are nonetheless entirely unproblematic as they stem from organic ways of shaking up the gameplay loop in a genuinely interesting manner. On the other hand, the game commits a peculiar sin in its "stealth" missions, where the player has to avoid engaging with the squad of enemy NPCs that just sort of meander around as if they have crippling social anxiety. Nope, no other playstyle permitted -- you have to be funneled into this specific way to engage with the game or it will command you a game over screen, going against the game's rather consistent thematic presentation of not doing exactly this.

Besides that, this is somehow still the only game of its type that goes so far as to provide the wealth of sandbox options as it does. While it certainly has its shortcomings that is the player's responsibility to make peace with, nothing has ever dared to compare.

It's alright, but the Ghost Recon franchise has fallen so far.  It used to aim for realism and authenticity, not crazy superhero commando stuff with regenerating health, onscreen enemy markers, arcadey vehicles, etc.   Ubi is killing their Tom Clancy franchises in a messy attempt to milk them, and Ghost Recon has suffered almost as much as Rainbow Six.

This game has nice visuals and animations, and some other decent parts--clearly the team working on this game was talented. But the direction and decision to make this a super hero game rather than an authentic tactical shooter was downright depressing.

Going back to this after playing Breakpoint, I actually think Breakpoint is a better game. Neither are great, but the bullet velocity in this game is terrible, and I'm not as big of a fan of the open world in this one.

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Wildlands is an absolute gem for fans of tactical shooters and open-world exploration. Set in a massive, stunningly rendered version of Bolivia, the game offers incredible freedom in how you approach every mission—whether you're a stealth purist, a guns-blazing operator, or somewhere in between.

The co-op experience is where Wildlands truly shines. Working as a squad with friends to plan synchronized takedowns, drone scout compounds, or extract targets under pressure creates some of the most memorable moments you can have in gaming. The AI squadmates are also surprisingly competent if you play solo, giving the game flexibility no matter how you want to engage.

The progression system, weapon customization, and variety of vehicles—from helicopters to dirt bikes—keep things fresh, while the story, centered around dismantling a powerful drug cartel, adds just the right amount of narrative weight without being too heavy-handed.

If you're looking for a tactical shooter with a huge world, tons of replayability, and the kind of emergent gameplay that leads to "did that really just happen?" moments, Wildlands is a must-play.

Ghost Recon Wildlands is a bit of an anomaly to me compared to most Ghost Recon games. Unlike many of the other Ghost Recon games, it's very nicely polished; this one is fully open world, extremely beautiful, the characters look nice, and it has full voice acting for everything. The story lets you come at it from multiple angles, progression is enjoyable, 
 and the cut scenes are well made. Even if the plotline is over the top (typical of Tom Clancy and Tom Clancy inspired things), it's satisfying to take down all the bad guys one-by-one. 

So why the negative review? 

This is where the other side of the anomaly plays out: The actual tactical aspects of the game are flat out terrible. Nothing works like it is supposed to for a combat game: ammo is practically unlimited, you can just swap out your weapons for any other weapons mid-combat (helicopters chowed up? lucky I have this anti-material sniper rifle in my back pocket), drones and drone jamming don't work correctly (ground-based jamming works in an upwards cone, so you SHOULD get less jammer interference flying low to the ground avoiding LOS with the jammer rather than moving far above and looking down. This is NOT the case in game. Is it nit-picky? Yes, maybe - but this is a Tom Clancy game which used to pride themselves on alleged technical accuracy), armored vehicles can be killed by small arms gunfire, you can't actually maneuver around the environment and lean around corners without actually getting STUCK on/in objects in the environment, just everything tactical is BAD BAD BAD. Instead of being enjoyable, getting from point-A-to-B is downright miserable, something the devs must have realized because you can just fast travel everywhere. Ultimately, I just downloaded a cheat mod to finish out the single player storyline because, as I mentioned, the story is nice. But it's seriously underwhelming as an open world combat game. 

The Good: :)
- Extremely beautiful environment. Like... EVERYTHING is postcard-worthy. The environment is pretty, and the point of interest are... well... interesting!
- All the lore strewn around the map is actually probably my favorite part of the game. I'll spend hours just hiking & driving around just collecting bits of lore.
- The character models are lovely and look as close to lifelike as I've seen one of these games come. Animations are fluid and feel natural.
- Plenty of customization options, though to me they didn't go far enough and feel a bit like a "meet our sponsors" panel, but still you can make your character look more-or-less like you desire.
- The guns feel pretty good and it's nice you can tweak the attachments and skins and stuff.
- Did I mention it's beautiful?

Now the bad: :(
- The AI is laughably bad; I've have better battles against AI from GTA, or even the original MGS. The only challenge they manage to bring is their never ending waves of apaches if you pick a fight with the cops. They devs knew their AI was ♥♥♥♥ to the point where they only even consider the stealth of the player... so if you're stealthed the enemy and your friendly AI will walk past each other and refuse to 'see' each other. You can have a massive gun battle and then hide in a tower on the the base and after 5-10 min the enemy will just forget you were there and go back to what they were doing.
- Very poor tactical experience - I'll just say "see my review above" for fear of being redundant. 
- The vehicles drive like lead bricks on ice with rocket motors attached to them, and they crash like they're 3D printed from chinese plastics to the point you basically just become a serial car-jacker. I'm sure THAT will win over the locals. >_< The aircrafts are overly simplified to fly and feel stiff and boring.
- The UI, like many console-first games, is trash on PC. Trying to do anything in the menus from modding guns to changing outfits (arguably the worst part of the UI) is about as enjoyable as self mutilation.
- Microtransactions - enough said. 
- Multiplay experience... let's face it if you're multiplaying this with anyone but friends you probably have brain damage already. But I'm not talking about that... I'm talking about the fact this game is so poorly optimized for multiplay (THE BIGGEST THING THEY EVEN ADVERTISE... HERP DERP - PLAY WITH YOUR FRIENDS) that 90% of the time one of you will desync and leave a mission before it's complete - usually resulting in a mission fail. So... I stopped bothering going on line even.

Overall an enjoyable story where the gameplay gets in the way. You guys either need to listen to or fire your military advisor(s). I've had better more realistic and more interesting combat out of Just Cause or Mercenaries - at least they had destructible environments.

We are talking about that rare open-world shooter where the map isn't just big — it's alive. Bolivia isn't just terrain, it's a character: dusty ridges soaked in cartel blood, ghost towns echoing with radio static, neon-lit clubs rotting under drug lord rule. And you're dropped right in the middle, not as a hero, but a shadow.

The moment you land, you're not thinking about XP bars or killstreaks. You're thinking about how to get to that lieutenant in a church surrounded by sicarios. You’re planning your angles, syncing your shots with a squad that can feel frighteningly real at times. Solo or co-op, the tension is there. This game respects silence, and rewards patience.

What sets Wildlands apart isn't just the gunplay — though that's tight and satisfying — it's the slow war. You dismantle an empire piece by piece. Each boss has weight. Each intel drop feels earned. And every time you ghost your way through an outpost at 3AM with night vision flickering, it’s a movie you direct.

It’s not perfect — the dialogue stumbles, AI can derp, and some missions repeat — but none of that breaks the core feeling: you’re the hunter, deep in cartel country, carving justice into chaos.

Ghost Recon Wildlands – Tactical Chaos in a Massive Playground

So I finally jumped into Ghost Recon: Wildlands and honestly? It’s kind of a wild ride—pun totally intended. This game is like what happens when a tactical shooter and an open-world sandbox have a baby, and then hand you a squad and a whole country to mess around in.

The setup’s pretty straightforward: you’re part of a special ops team dropped into a fictional version of Bolivia that’s basically been overrun by a massive drug cartel. Your job? Systematically take it apart, one cartel lieutenant at a time. The story’s not mind-blowing, but it gives just enough context to keep you moving from target to target.

Now, the world itself is huge. Like, massive. You’ve got deserts, jungles, snowy mountains, salt flats—you name it. And you can approach missions however you want. Stealthy night op with suppressed rifles and synchronized takedowns? Go for it. Or just roll in with a chopper and RPG everything in sight. It's as tactical or chaotic as you want it to be, especially if you’ve got friends along for the ride.

Speaking of which, Wildlands is best played co-op. With a full squad of real players, it turns into this crazy blend of coordinated strikes, near-misses, and hilarious screw-ups (someone will crash a helicopter). Solo’s still fun—the AI teammates are competent enough—but it’s definitely not the same without some human chaos in the mix.

Gunplay feels solid, and there’s a ton of weapon customization, which is perfect if you love tweaking loadouts. Vehicles are a bit floaty, but they get the job done. And the drone? Absolute MVP for recon—makes you feel like a real spec-ops operator.

That said, it’s not all smooth sailing. The open world can feel a bit repetitive after a while—lots of go-here-do-this missions. Enemy AI is... let’s say, not the sharpest. And the writing leans a little too hard into macho military clichés. Also, stealth can feel inconsistent at times depending on how the game decides to react.

Comparing it to other games? If you’re into the tactical side, Wildlands is more open and flexible than something like Call of Duty. Compared to Valorant or CS2, it’s a completely different beast—way slower, more methodical, and focused on large-scale coordination instead of tight, round-based PvP. Think Metal Gear Solid V meets Far Cry, with a squad of bros and a ton of gadgets.

Final thoughts: Ghost Recon: Wildlands is a giant sandbox for tactical chaos. It’s not perfect, but if you’re into open-world shooters and like the idea of planning your own missions (or blowing them up mid-stealth because your buddy "accidentally" fired a grenade), it’s a blast—especially with friends. Just don’t expect deep story or cutting-edge AI.

Tom Clancy’s Ghost Recon: Wildland, is the last Ghost Recon game with the “Tom Clancy” name at the start of the title, so Breakpoint is waaaaay on the other side of my Steam Library and it actually makes me mad. 

You play as Nomad, the world’s sexiest man on his quest with the rest of his squad of Government sanctioned mass murderers to stop El Sueno, the leader of the Cartel and now rulers of Bolivia: Santa Blanca. Because Sicario came out two years before this game and that movie was good. 
Santa Blanca is pushing a metric ♥♥♥♥ ton of really hard drugs into the US, as well as human trafficking and all the other horrid things Cartels like to do, so the CIA, DEA, and JSOC decide that its time for some good ol’ fashion American interventionism and sends Ghost Recon into Bolivia to completely dismantle Santa Blanca and restore a “”Proper”” Bolivian government. 

But this is set five years after Advanced Warfighter and five years before Future Soldier, and neither Scott Mitchells or Joe Ramirez are willing to share their cool future tech for Nomad to use.
I mean, you can technically get some of it as cosmetics, it just doesn’t do anything for you. 

Its kind of funny to think that Predator team used the experimental gear in Future Soldier, and then the US government just went “Nah, that’s ours.” and took it back before Breakpoint. 

I like the Ghost Team from Wildlands, I think Nomad is a good successor to Mitchells, and Weaver, Holt, and Midas do a good job with the banter that it actually made me dislike the squad you can get in Breakpoint, which I know is a later edition so the dialogue probably wasn’t an option, but still.

Bolivia is also a very nice place to play the game, I actually like it more than Aurora. It might just be the colors and my weird fascination with Colonial Spanish/Latin American architecture, but its a very nice place to shoot and stab people under the cover of night. It might just be because of how open it is, only a few parts of the map are covered in big vegetation so you get a good view of the area when you’re just putzing around. 

The game lets you play with the element of surprise, you’re outnumbered and, I don’t want to say “Outgunned”, pretending to be outgunned by these losers is like pretending I eat garbage willingly. At least early game, the Sicario don’t really put up much of a fight, even on Extreme difficulty. But as the game goes on they become more organized and have deadlier weapons. There’s also Unidad, who are the Bolivian Military Police Special Operations who have an agreement with Santa Blanca. They’re funner to fight, at least I think so. 

The enemies in Wildlands never really do anything too wild, hilariously enough. They do try to advance and flank and supress, but don’t expect them to be pulling off some FEAR or Brothers in Arms tactics any time soon. Still, they keep the game interesting, and if you’re bad at firefights you can always stick to stealth, save for a few situations. 

Its an open world game, you hunt Cartel members like animals, put them in the dirt or extradite them, depending on the situation, and then you move on to new and fresher territory until everyone’s pronouns are officially changed to Were/Was. 

As the game goes on, you can gather resources for the Rebels, and in return you get points depending on what resources you find. You then use those points to level up your abilities. You can also get rebel support like vehicle drops and motar strikes. Though I never use them.
Because I forgot they existed.

Even in the first game it was just “Hello” and then everyone was dead. 

There’s other content as well. Ghost War is the game’s PVP mode, but I couldn’t get a game going. There’s also drop in Co Op and a survival mode where you try not to get mulched by larger and larger enemy waves.

Breakpoint is about a tech guy super colony and Frontlines got canceled. Get Wildlands on sale. You can get a good 50-60 hours out of it, or get it on gamepass, one of the two. Just don’t spent full price for it. The fact that most games these days don’t have a “Greatest hits” price range really burns my ass.

I remember the first time I played Ghost Recon Wildlands.
It was the spring of 2017. I was twenty-two, standing on the edge of adulthood, searching for something vast enough to get lost in.
A friend had been talking about it for weeks, and one evening, almost on a whim, I bought the disc.
But it wasn’t just a game.
It was a map to another world.
It was Wildlands.

I installed it, turned on the console, and Bolivia stretched out before me — endless mountains, dusty villages, rivers glinting under the burning sun.
I spent that whole night learning to move slowly again, to scout, to plan, to breathe before pulling the trigger.
The stealth, the firefights, the moments of pure silence broken only by the wind — it wrapped around me like a second skin.
I wasn’t playing it.
I was living it.

Then came dozens of missions, late-night raids, and quiet helicopter rides over sleeping valleys.
I learned every province, every cartel leader’s stronghold, every path over the hills.
And without any guide — just a map, a marker, and a stubborn will — I built my story, piece by piece.
It wasn’t just a playground.
It was my war.
It was home.

Every now and then, my closest friends would join me.
We weren’t soldiers.
We were just tired kids looking for something bigger than ourselves.
I still remember those perfect moments — when the plan went wrong, when the alarm blared, when everything turned to chaos — and we laughed like madmen, scrambling to survive.
We didn’t need perfect runs.
We needed memories.
It was our refuge.
It was our bond.

And now, eight years later, I go back.
The world has changed. I have changed. I’m thirty-one now.
And those friends? They’ve moved away, chasing dreams in different cities.

Yet every time I boot up Wildlands, it’s like stepping into a painting no one else can see.
The graphics are softer now, the servers quieter — but the heart is untouched.
Every sunset, every thunderstorm, every whispered radio call speaks in a language only my memory knows.
It’s the heartbeat of another life.
It’s the breath of a world where we were unstoppable.

Ghost Recon Wildlands isn’t just a game.
It’s a time machine.
It’s a second chance to feel free, to feel fearless, to feel alive.

And as the rotors whir over the endless horizon, I remain there.
Fingers on the controller...
And a tear I cannot tell — whether it’s sorrow or gratitude.

I've heard a lot of good about this title, and to be honest, it delivered quite well overall.
Still, there are a couple of issues (mechanics, bugs, and game balance) that really soured my experience.

Graphics are pretty decent, often offering you amazing visual treats, as long as you slow down to appreciate the scenery. 
On the other hand, in a classic Ubi fashion, the world map is far too large which in turn forces them to reuse a lot of assests, making it feel a lot less diverse. House interiors are probably the most off-putting as they both look and feel empty, not lived in.

Movement is okay-ish, for my tastes the controls and animations feel too stiff at times, with the cover system working semi-consistently.
Gunplay (from the player side), weapon variety and customisation is very well done, you have a lot of tools at your disposal to use as you see fit. That gives you the options to change up your combat style, keeping the gameplay fresh and fun at the same time.

On the other hand, what I have a serious issue with is a totally unbalanced difficulty scaling, where enemies become all-seeing, no scope bullet sponges as you go higher up. At no point should anyone be able to 3-hit-ko you from over 100m away dual wielding uzis. 
Detection system is a joke as well. Enemies seeing you through walls, from a floor above following with that signature 3-hit-ko is not what you'd expect to find in a "stealth" game. 
Being squishy here is not a problem, the problem is not having a way to move around without enemies noticing you from a mile away (if you're not abusing some game mechanics). I found the second lowest difficulty to feel "the most immersive", as it gives you some leeway in sneaking and being able to move in and out of bases unnoticed.

I liked the story quite a bit. Small group of guerrilla fighters breaking down a large, powerful cartel is fun to see and experience, but it does start to feel like a drag after a while. There's a lot of underbosses and a good chunk of them don't feel all that unique.
Mission variety is okay but often repetitive, mainly the side content, boils down to the same objectives over and over, with a slightly different enemy base layout and a couple of new voicelines here and there.

The world itself doesn't feels all that lived in and immersive, all while that was pointed to as one of the strong suits of this title. As I mentioned above, a lack of variety caused by reusing a lot of the assets gives different locations a same-ish feeling (small pool of car models and colours, copy pasted houses both inside and outside, lack of unique voicelines - from the enemies to especially the radio, etc..).

I usually don't like to compare games from different genres, but I feel it could help make my point here. Division 1 and 2 offer repetitive gameplay in a semi-open world, but they are chalk full of so many collectables that it gives every location a unique story element even with used assets. There's voice recordings, pictures, 3D simulations of certain events, etc. 
All that combined with so so many small details, both on the outsides and insides give the world a bit more oomph. That's what I feel this game is lacking, which is the same with many other open world Ubi games. It just doesn't feel all that alive.

Ghost Recon Wildlands – A Captivating Evil in an Open World

Ghost Recon Wildlands delivers a tactical open-world experience unlike any other. It’s not just another shooter—it’s a story of elite soldiers taking on a powerful cartel that rules Bolivia.

One of Wildlands’ strongest aspects is its compelling storyline. The Santa Blanca cartel, led by the infamous El Sueño, is a force to be reckoned with. His presence is intimidating yet charismatic, making him one of the most unforgettable villains in gaming. Every word he speaks carries a sense of power and menace, drawing players deeper into the conflict.

In terms of gameplay, Wildlands strikes a solid balance between action and strategy. Players have full freedom to choose their approach—whether it’s stealthy infiltration or all-out warfare. The looting and upgrade system feels natural, allowing players to discover weapons and gear organically rather than relying on level-based progression like in Ghost Recon Breakpoint.

Another highlight is the game’s rich and immersive open world. From small villages to heavily guarded cartel compounds, every location feels authentic and presents its own set of challenges. The day-night cycle and dynamic weather add to the realism, making each mission feel unique.

In conclusion, Ghost Recon Wildlands isn’t just a shooter—it’s a tactical experience packed with a gripping story, unforgettable characters, and an open world that truly feels alive. Whether you prefer stealth operations or full-on firefights, Wildlands gives you the freedom to create your own path in the hunt for the Santa Blanca cartel.

Final Score: 9/10

First of all, if you haven’t played Metal Gear Solid V yet, do that instead of Ghost Recon Wildlands. The mechanics are significantly better, enemy AI is more balanced, and the level design is far superior to anything you'll find here. The only major downsides of MGS V are its frustrating boss fights and the game-breaking NVG mechanics.

Now, let’s start with what Wildlands does well. As always, Ubisoft excels at map design. Bolivia looks stunning, and its cities are well-crafted. Even though much of the world follows the same visual formula—brick houses and orange dirt roads—it never feels overly repetitive. The fact that El Sueño’s tomb is visible from most of the map is a nice touch. Ubisoft also handled the hilly terrain impressively, making traversal smoother than in most open-world games.

Given the sheer size of the world, it's clear that individual outposts and bases couldn't receive the same level of attention as those in MGS V. Even within the more constrained map of Afghanistan, every MGS V base allows for multiple approaches—from frontal assaults to sneaky sewer infiltrations. In Wildlands, especially in UNIDAD bases, you usually have only one or two entry points (a main door and maybe a side entrance in a fence). Santa Blanca outposts offer slightly more freedom, but it's evident that level design wasn’t a top priority.

The story of Wildlands is interesting if you take the time to read the Kingslayer files and watch Bowman’s briefing videos. By default, though, the game barely forces the player to engage with the narrative. There’s one cutscene at the beginning, one at the end, and a handful of short, forgettable scenes set in a dilapidated cabin. More could have been done with storytelling, even while keeping the open-ended approach that lets players choose which underbosses to take down first. Another thing is that the ending is preceded by one of the worse missions in the game, completely unplayable on extreme with tier mode as designed - instead of the intended route I needed to drive the train tracks (restart if train appeard), force my way trough the enemy camp in armor car (restart if the car got stuck), disembark few meters before objective, get shot, and run to the cutscene trigger while invincible,

Character-wise, Bowman stands out as a classic CIA spook — organized, precise, and at times, inhumane. The cartel underbosses are grounded and well-motivated, but with most regions only offering two or three hours of story missions, they don’t get enough screen time to feel fully developed. Still, they serve their purpose as stepping stones to the main antagonist, El Sueño. Nomad, the protagonist, isn’t exactly a self-insert, but he isn’t much of a character either—just a government-sanctioned killing machine. Then there’s Pac Katari, whose only redeeming quality is his ending.

Mission design is surprisingly creative at times, going beyond the usual “go there and shoot something” formula. Even with the sparse storytelling, missions don’t feel like mere checklists. The downside? Many seem to have never been playtested for solo play—let alone on extreme difficulty, or worse, with Tier Mode enabled. Some missions are nearly impossible without prior knowledge or outright exploiting the game’s mechanics. Another thing that sucks is respawn points - the game doesn't let you quick save (what else to expect form Ubisoft) but after dying it has no problem respawning me 700 meters from the objective and to add insult to injury I get respawned on the opposite side I was approaching originally. This gets daunting rather quickly. And sure you might think just spawn a vehicle - well for some god forsaken reason the vehicles also spawn hundreds of meters away and often inside enemy base.

Gameplay in Wildlands is solid but unpolished compared to MGS V. It’s a passable open-world stealth-action shooter. I played with most of the HUD disabled—only keeping ammo/item box indicators and occasional enemy markers (especially in areas with civilians to differentiate targets). Surprisingly, the game remained quite playable this way. The progression system is fine, but most upgrades are minor percentage increases that don’t feel meaningful on Extreme difficulty (aside from gaining an extra revive).

Gunplay is decent—stealth kills are consistent, with one-shot torso and head hits, though weapons feel somewhat samey in that mode. When firefights break out, however, differences between weapons become more noticeable. One thing Wildlands does better than most games is allowing engagements at extreme ranges—over 500 meters in some cases. Unfortunately, the inconsistent penetration system hinders this. Sometimes, bullets go through concrete walls and steel floors realistically, but then you’ll encounter a flimsy steel fence that even a .50 cal round can’t penetrate. This inconsistency is frustrating, forcing players to memorize which surfaces are penetrable and which are not.

Your AI teammates are the dumbest squadmates imaginable. It’s baffling how this AI made it into the final release. They’re far worse than those in the original Ghost Recon, where you had similar number of commands + the amazing mechanic of taking over their bodies. In vehicles, they’re useless—struggling to hit enemies just a few meters away. On foot, they’re slightly better, but even with frequent regroup commands, they often lag behind while you clear bases alone. Their main function is as be revive stimpacks and act as wallhack on cooldown—since, in sync-shot mode, they can inexplicably shoot through walls and they spot enemies trough number of obstacles.

Enemy AI is passable. When things go loud, they flank, understand player's suppressive fire, and generally behave well enough. The problem is how engagements start. Sometimes, enemies are oblivious—failing to notice a comrade being shot just a few meters away. Other times, they possess near-omniscience, spotting you through dense vegetation or even walls. The moment you’re detected, every enemy instantly knows your exact position. Reinforcements spawn unrealistically close, breaking immersion. To make matters worse, all enemies, regardless of weapon, behave the same. A random cartel grunt with dual submachine guns will try to snipe you at 200 meters just as confidently as an actual sniper. This issue is particularly noticeable on Extreme difficulty with Tier Mode enabled.

What’s clearly bad is the loot box system. While playing normally I manged to get few crates from prestige coins and out off them not a single weapon. Thankfully, most of the items are just cosmetic junk I don’t care about, but this kind of monetization has no place in a single-player game. The same goes for the anti-cheat system, which exists solely for a multiplayer mode that nobody plays. Worse yet, its presence discourages modding.

As for performance the game runs fine on any semi current hardware. Welcome, tireless gaming enthusiasts!

Thanks to the awesome folks at ForRetroLoop, who lent us one of their retro gaming rigs, we finally got to revisit some classic titles we had only watched others play for years. One of the games on our list was Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon® Wildlands.

Now, this isn't exactly a brand-new release. It’s been around for eight years at the time of writing. But with the rig we had, we were able to crank up the settings to Ultra, and man, that made all the difference. For a game that’s been out this long, the graphics still hold up surprisingly well. The massive open world, packed with life and detail, makes the gameplay even more immersive.

You step into the boots of an elite spec-ops soldier, leading a four-man squad on a mission to take down a ruthless drug cartel ruling over a fictional country inspired by Bolivia. The goal? Take out high-ranking cartel members one by one, gathering intel along the way, helping rebels, and completing side missions that expand your arsenal and skills. The gameplay leans heavily on tactical planning and precise execution, though there are definitely moments when you'll need quick reflexes and a fast trigger finger.

One of the weaker aspects of the game is the AI controlling your squad. While they can be useful in certain situations, their unpredictable behavior can sometimes ruin a perfectly planned mission. However, you can always bring in three friends for co-op, which makes the experience significantly more fun and immersive.

All in all, for an eight-year-old game, Ghost Recon Wildlands has aged like fine wine. If you haven’t played it yet, it’s definitely worth adding to your collection!

To all future Ghosts, we wish you a great time. Regroup, gear up, and we’ll see you in the next review. Over and out!

Ghost Recon: Wildlands Review

Ghost Recon: Wildlands is an open-world tactical shooter that delivers a fun and immersive experience, despite some rough edges. The gun mechanics are definitely a highlight—shooting feels crisp, satisfying, and well-balanced, making every engagement enjoyable. The game's vast open world is stunning, with impressive attention to detail in terrain, textures, and environments. The developers clearly put effort into making Bolivia feel alive, from the dense jungles to the rugged mountains.

That said, the driving mechanics feel a bit off, with vehicles sometimes handling awkwardly, which can be frustrating during high-speed chases or off-road travel. Additionally, while the game offers a variety of missions, they tend to become repetitive over time, following similar patterns of infiltration and enemy elimination.

Despite these issues, Wildlands is a blast to play, whether solo or with friends. The freedom to approach objectives in different ways keeps things fresh, and the cooperative gameplay adds another layer of strategy and fun. If you're looking for an open-world shooter with solid gunplay and beautiful scenery, Wildlands is definitely worth checking out.

I sprinted as fast as I could in the open directly to the objective. Wildlands was also one of those special occasions because despite the numerous reused urban buildings, it still has perhaps one of the best looking open world maps I've seen.
