[b]This review is based on the hardest difficulty of the game because that is all I experienced.[/b]
[h2]Postives[/h2]
[b]High Replayability & Tier Mode[/b]
Multiple difficulty levels and Tier Mode, plenty of challenge and incentive to keep playing and the freedom the player is given keeps things fresh and adds a sense of variety

[b]Stealth Mechanics[/b]
IMO the game does a good job of distinguishing when you are spotted vs hidden the stealth feels pretty polished and makes staying stealthy feel rewarding.

[b]Weapon Variety:[/b]
Tons of guns and attachments to unlock buy or find allowing for deep customization. 

[b]Character Customization[/b]
I didn't mess with it too much, the game allows for a good level of character customization keeping your ghost personalized to your liking and keeping the game immersive.

[b]Vehicles[/b]
Helicopters are super easy to fly which I like. Arcadey controls make it more fun than frustrating.
Realistic vehicle damage which adds to the immersion. Crashes visibly affect your car and can even total it making it fun to chase and crash into enemies.

[b]Story and Mission Structure[/b]
The story is well written requiring you to take down different branches of the cartel before facing the leader. You need to dismantle the cartel security, production lines, social influence, and trafficking ring adding depth to the campaign.
The nonlinear mission structure allows to you take on any objective in any order making the game less restrictive and more replayable.

[b]Gunplay and Bullet Physics[/b]
Shooting feels great and bullet physics are realistic forcing you to compensate for drop when at a distance. You can also shoot through a variety of objects walls and vehicles with certain calibers which is a nice feature.

[b]Content[/b]
Tons of content a huge map packed with missions, side missions, skill points to collect and weapons to find.
Rebel missions and character progression keep the gameplay engaging upgrading rebel abilities is super useful and maintains its strength throughout the entire game.
Ghost mode adds a hardcore permadeath experience, making every decision feel high stakes.
Its also not a live service game. So you can enjoy this game offline for years to come even when there is no more support for the game itself.

[b]World and Atmosphere[/b]
The world feels alive with civilians walking about, cartel soldiers patrolling and fighting Unidad, Rebel soldiers on the move, and aircrafts flying above. The audio is great and immersive with authentic Bolivian accents that adds to the setting and the gunfire and environmental sounds are S tier making shootouts feel intense.

[b]Drone[/b]
Great Mechanic and is well implemented with a range of upgrades and a very nice spotting feature it makes it one of the best field gadgets you could ever need. It can explode so you can take down enemies from afar even high priority targets that are hard to reach. It can EMP nearby devices and even shutdown vehicles and convoys. A noisemaker to distract enemies or make them move position. Or it can even revive teammates and other players which make is super OP when using multiplayer. All around the drone is one of the coolest innovative things added to the game.

[h2]Negatives[/h2]

[b]Unfair Enemy AI[/b]
The Ai is the biggest downside of the game and the age shows through it. 
Enemies spot you way to quickly even from insane distances.
I had enemies in a truck (Facing forward) spot me on a mountain (behind them) while driving away from like 300m-400m
Enemies have perfect accuracy. Meaning a solider with a MAC-10 can beam you instantly from any distance even though its a CQC weapon.
The AI will randomly know your location when hunted, even if you don't make a noise or are spotted instead of searching naturally they will walk straight to you and spot you forcing you to move before they do.

[b]Buggy Team AI[/b]
Ai team will shoot convoy trucks until the blow up destroying valuable supplies you can prevent this by ordering them not to fire but its frustrating.
They will also walk straight into enemy view while in stealth breaking immersion (Even though enemies wont react or spot them)
Sometimes they ignore enemies in fights aswell. leaving you to get shot when expecting support.

[b]Dirt Bikes[/b]
Total death trap finicky bike physics make them unreliable and dangerous. A small rock can send you to your doom.

[b]Mission Restart[/b]
If I get spotted and wanted to restart, I would blow myself up with C4 instead of just having a quick "restart mission" option.

[b]Sniping Limitations[/b]
This might be a big one for some of you, In my case bullets would disappear after around 900m which is far but still disappointing. I would have like Arma-style long distance sniping.

[b]Non Dynamic Cartel Strength[/b]
Even after taking down key cartel leaders and severely weakening the cartel there is no noticeable decrease in enemy presence across the map so it doesn't truly feel like you are dwindling them down.

[b]Graphics[/b]
While the graphics aren't disgusting the visuals show their age. Compared to modern games with ray tracing and next gen lighting Wildlands looks a little outdated though the art style can be seen as appealing for non graphic fanatics.

[b]Bugs[/b]
Ive encountered a few soft locks where I had to kill myself or reload because I was stuck in a canyon or a hill or some objects quite annoying.
Also a bug with the cover system every time you try to peak out of cover the camera switches to the wrong shoulder making it harder to peak properly this has gotten me killed a few times happens mostly indoors while 3rd person aiming.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
GRW is an incredibly fun and tactical open world shooter with high replay-ability, strong stealth mechanics and a good multiplayer. The gunplay stealth drone and mission freedom make it fun to play. The world feels great but the AI and occasional bugs hold it back from perfection like any other game. If you like Tactical shooters you should pick it up. If you are anyone else you should still get it when it goes on sale for less than $6.

If you liked 'Mercenaries 2: World In Flames' from the Playstation 2 era, then you will like this game.
HUGE open world to explore, plunder, and conquer.
You can play by the objectives, but the game doesn't require you to do so;  you can do whatever you want, just like in the Grand Theft Auto series of games.

While the game is designed to allow up to 3 other Humans to play with you, there is an option to play Solo; you will still have your 3 teammates with you, controlled by the computer.
This is important as they will heal you if you take too many hits - but note - they can only revive you ONCE, and if you take more hits after that, you are KIA:  Killed In Action.

There are an un - countable amount of vehicles to use.
Cars, SUV's, Trucks, Helicopters, Planes, Boats, and probably more that I have not personally seen yet.
Point is, there are SO many vehicles to choose from, you may not be able to make up your mind.
Some are necessary to complete certain missions, but as I said earlier, you can do what you want.
The game will not penalize you for not playing the missions, but you may be leaving incomplete missions behind that you can return to later ( if you want to )

Having said that, you must take into account the nature of the game:  If you go around killing members of a gang / cartel, they will immediately attack you and your team.
If you kill someone, be prepared to face the consequences!  -  That's the point.

Weapons are issued to you and your team upon starting the game, but you can change your loadout OR just steal someone else's weapon.
Your ammo count is pretty realistic: you are given precious little ammo and very few frags, so use them sparingly.
Scattered throughout the map ( usually at target locations ) you will find re - supply crates where you can get some lovely new bullets and grenades to continue the fun with!

 The graphics are very good, maybe not hyper - realistic, but everywhere you go on the map you will find highly detailed objects of all kinds.
I recommend NOT using the highest tier of graphics capability unless you have a Gaming computer; it's just too hard on a normal computer ( just like any game ) and you will be decreasing your computer's run time prematurely.

Weapons are just as you'd expect with many familiar names and manufacturers, however you are not likely to find a Jackal ( I don't think there's even a .50 CAL in the game ), a Tank, or any other conventional warfare vehicles.
If you do find some, then I simply have not seen them yet.

Overall the game is a lot of fun, especially because you are free to do whatever you like.
Yes, objectives are there, and the game does reward you for completing them, but you simply don't have to.

TL;DR:
Kill bad guys, or whoever you like, because it doesn't matter.
Steal all kinds of vehicles.
Start all kinds of conflicts.
Get lost, literally, because the map is so HUGE.
The price may be a bit higher on this game, but I've had so much fun playing it so far that I MUST recommend it to you.

Wildlands is probably one of my personal top 5 games of all time. I have nearly 500 hours played over 5+ full 100% playthroughs, and have played nearly everything this game has to offer. The core concept and aspects of the execution are amazing. The map is both quite large and varied, while also feeling realistically spaced. Open areas like the mountains and rolling deserts *feel* open and empty, while still being full of content to interact with. The general gameplay and overall story is very Ubisoft, but executed well. The motley crew of buchones and other npcs you deal with are nicely varied and occasionally interesting. The core gameplay loop of get mission, go to location, scout, kill, then complete, is quite fun and doesn't get boring to me since there are so many different locations that each have their own little differences.

The game also has a fantastic DLC in Fallen Ghosts, which introduces a number of interesting new enemy types that force you to interact with certain aspects of the game that you may not have used (thermals, less drone reliance). When playing on Extreme, this makes the game feel closer to what Breakpoint should have been.

All that being said, this game is not without issues. General bugginess, even years later, still affects the game. Certain aspects of difficulty scaling in Extreme/Tier mode are very odd, and I have stopped playing Ghost mode largely because certain bugs and random other issues can lose you a character very easily. Narco Road is also a DLC that exists, and while I didn't hate the writing or a large chunk of the DLC content, there were many bugs and annoying features (electro jumps taking 30+ tries to work, Los Sin Alma being worse than pre-nerf Unidad)

Overall, I would still give this game a solid 8/10 generally, especially considering the fact that I still can't seem to put it down, That is, outside of the fact that as of today the game is no longer playable thanks to some Ubisoft connect update breaking the launcher. Since this game is literally unplayable at the moment, I will have to say I don't recommend it, ESPECIALLY with the fact that it is still a whopping 50 USD, at least in the US. If they fix it, I would absolutely suggest buying this game on sale for 15 or less dollars, especially if you have some friends to play with.

Ghost Recon Wildlands – Tactical Excellence with Endless Replayability (Player Review – 83 Hours Played)
Ghost Recon Wildlands is an open-world tactical shooter that gives players complete freedom to approach missions their way. With 83 hours of gameplay, you’ve likely experimented with different strategies, perfected stealth takedowns, and explored every corner of Bolivia.

What Makes Wildlands Awesome?
✅ Massive Open World – The detailed recreation of Bolivia offers diverse biomes, from jungles to deserts, keeping missions fresh even after dozens of hours. You’ve probably memorized key locations by now.

✅ Tactical Gameplay – Whether you go in silent with sync shots or unleash chaos with heavy firepower, the game rewards strategic play. At 83 hours, you’re likely a pro at adapting tactics to any situation.

✅ Variety of Weapons & Customization – The Gunsmith system lets you tweak every weapon to your style. You’ve probably fine-tuned your loadout for max efficiency.

✅ Solo or Co-op Fun – Whether you played solo with AI teammates or in co-op, Wildlands shines in tactical team play. If you haven’t tried co-op, it’s a whole new level of fun!

What Could Be Better?
🟡 Enemy AI Predictability – After 83 hours, you’ve likely noticed some patterns in enemy behavior, making them easier to counter.

🟡 Repetitive Side Missions – While fun, certain objectives (convoy hijacks, interrogations, etc.) start feeling similar after long playtimes.

Final Verdict
⭐ 8.5/10 – A tactical shooter with unmatched freedom and replayability. Your 83-hour grind proves Ghost Recon Wildlands keeps players engaged with its immersive world and strategic gameplay. If you’re looking for a fresh challenge, try Ghost Mode (permadeath), increase difficulty, or go full roleplay (e.g., night ops only, no HUD, or limited weapons).

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands - 8/10

Ghost Recon Wildlands is a massive, open-world tactical shooter that puts you in the boots of a Ghost, a special ops soldier tasked with taking down a dangerous drug cartel in Bolivia. The map is huge, and the freedom to approach missions however you want is one of the game's biggest strengths. You can go in guns blazing, sneak your way through enemy camps, or even take out targets from miles away with sniper rifles—there's no one-size-fits-all approach here.

The gameplay is a lot of fun, especially if you’re playing with friends. The co-op mode is where Wildlands really shines. Planning attacks with your squad, coordinating movements, and executing well-timed ambushes is an absolute blast. Solo play is still decent, but the AI teammates can sometimes feel a bit dumb, leaving you to handle everything yourself.

The world of Bolivia is absolutely gorgeous, with diverse environments like jungles, mountains, and deserts that make exploration feel rewarding. The sheer size of the map means there’s always something to do—whether it’s clearing cartel bases, gathering intel, or just driving around enjoying the scenery. 

That said, the game can get a little repetitive after a while. The missions don’t always feel varied enough, and after a few hours of clearing strongholds and taking down cartel bosses, the gameplay loop starts to feel a bit familiar. The story is also pretty forgettable, serving mainly as an excuse to send you on missions.

If you enjoy open-world shooters with tactical elements, Wildlands is a great pick. It might not have the most engaging story, but it’s a lot of fun with friends, and the massive world keeps things interesting for hours. Just be ready for a bit of repetition, especially in solo play.

Ghost Recon Wildlands: The Ultimate Boys’ Trip (With Guns) – 10/10 Would Invade Bolivia Again

Alright, listen up, squad. If Ghost Recon Wildlands isn’t the best game in the series, I don’t know what is. Actually, scratch that—I do know. It IS the best. Period. This game is peak tactical chaos, and I am so here for it.

First off, let’s talk about the REAL experience. Not the story (which, let’s be honest, is basically Narcos fanfiction), not the NPC squadmates who have the reaction time of a goldfish, but the multiplayer experience—aka, me and my friends absolutely botching every stealth mission while cackling like hyenas in a Discord call.

Stealth? We Don’t Know Her
The game tells you, “Approach with caution, take out enemies silently, use your drone, blah blah blah.” Bro, I am rolling up in a stolen Unidad attack chopper, blaring corridos through my mic, and throwing C4 at anything that moves. My homies? One of them just accidentally ran over a civilian (whoops), another got sniped because he was “just looking at the view,” and the last one is 400 meters away, lost in the mountains.

NPC Teammates? Nah, I Got My Clowns
Playing solo? Yeah, the AI teammates will technically help, but they give off the same energy as your friends who say “I’ll be there in 5 mins” and show up an hour late. They’re great at one thing: magically syncing headshots across an entire base like they’re in an aimbot cult. But if you’re playing with real people? That’s when the magic happens. And by magic, I mean absolute pandemonium.

A Map So Big, I’m Basically A Digital Backpacker
Bolivia in this game is stunning. It’s like Ubisoft took all their open-world expertise and said, “Yo, let’s go crazy.” Snowy mountains? Check. Lush jungles? Check. Sprawling deserts? Check. A lake so big I started questioning if I was playing a fishing simulator? Check. It’s so detailed that sometimes I forget I have cartels to dismantle and end up BASE jumping off a cliff for fun.

Vehicular Shenanigans
The driving physics? Oh, they’re special. Every vehicle either handles like a dream or like a possessed shopping cart. Motorcycles are death traps, helicopters fly like I’m controlling them via Morse code, and cars? Let’s just say my squad treats every mission like an episode of Top Gear: Tactical Edition.

Final Verdict:
Is Ghost Recon Wildlands the best in the series? YES. Do I love it? WITH EVERY CHAOTIC BONE IN MY BODY. If you have friends who enjoy both precision and absolute clownery, this is the game for you. It’s Call of Duty meets Just Cause, but with tactical beards and unhinged co-op energy.

An "Alright” game for an open world sandbox, a “Decent” game for the franchise 

Being a military deployed to fight in a desert like those generic American hero movies (most of the times) feels cool. This game does that absolutely great.  

With 93 hours in the game, the Bolivia town still feels alive because how the game was designed. Seeing civilians living their life, enemies patrol, and even a random event that happens randomly along the roads. With all this you can freely roam around the map finding new things like a sandbox. It’s filled with different biomes like jungles, mountains, and desert. which you can freely explore and strategize your attack in various ways. Hit-and-run, sniping, stealth, you call it. 

Due to the game with large amount of biome variety, it came with an enormous sized map and a lot of contents to do in the game. With over 20+ bosses around the map with around 4-5 missions each one. Each boss doesn’t feel exactly like a memorable villain to me like in Far Cry series. They do have personality to each other in each of their cut-scenes but most of them seem to serve more of a sense of progression. That feeling when I have beaten all the small bouchons and finally get the bigger one is pretty satisfying. Like most video games, when there’s a boss, there’s their grunts. There are standard enemies, one with bigger health pool, and a long range with small health pool. Most of the time it’s other obstacles that were around them like an alarm or a jammer. Which really tickles my imagination thinking of how I would approach them. It’s like playing with the same action figures but each time you came up with different scenarios. You might start with just stealth all the way to the mission because you wanted to play it safe and still feel cool like Sam Fisher (which appears in the game at some point). But once you know what to do, all-gun ho is crazy and fun experience to have, like an “American hero movie”. 

This game gets tiring at one point with how big the map actually is. You do have vehicles to travel around ranging from bikes to a literal missile chopper. But travelling across a province just to reach a mission, even with the fast-traveling system, is just absolutely time consuming, especially when trying get that 100% of game progression. More over, the missions feel somewhat repetitive once you have finished some of them. It’s either clip someone, interrogate, or just blow things up with a little detail to each mission to know that they are different. With how sandbox the game can be, differing your approach to each mission, it does make up for that boring feeling of the game but that kind of just it.  

I would say, as much as contents this game has and the possibility on how you can take on the game, it does feels “meh” at some point. Is it a good game? Well, yes, it is. But is it the best? Not really. You would need time and a little bit of commitment to actually beat the game. Comparing this with their old games of this franchise, it does feel underwhelming with how epic or cool those were. It could be due to the old ones being a linear game instead of an open world unlike this one, which means they can go wild with story and cutscenes. But it just kind of gives me that feeling of like “it could’ve been better” but I can’t get it out of my mouth.

"Ghost Recon: Wildlands" is an absolute blast, especially when played with friends. This open-world tactical shooter offers a massive, diverse playground set in the stunning and dangerous landscapes of Bolivia. Whether you’re sneaking through enemy camps, orchestrating coordinated takedowns, or causing chaos with a well-planned assault, the game delivers endless opportunities for strategic fun.

The open world is one of the game’s biggest strengths. Bolivia feels alive and dynamic, with sprawling deserts, dense jungles, snowy mountains, and bustling towns. Each region has its own unique vibe and challenges, and the sheer scale of the map ensures there’s always something new to explore.

The gameplay is a perfect mix of stealth, strategy, and action. You can approach missions however you like—go in guns blazing, sneak through undetected, or use a combination of tactics to outsmart your enemies. The variety of weapons, gadgets, and vehicles gives you the tools to tackle any situation, and the customization options let you tailor your loadout to your playstyle.

But where "Wildlands" truly shines is in its multiplayer. Playing with friends elevates the experience to a whole new level. Coordinating with your squad to infiltrate a heavily guarded base, setting up overwatch positions, and executing synchronized takedowns is incredibly satisfying. The game’s drop-in/drop-out co-op makes it easy to jump into your friends’ games, and the shared progression ensures everyone feels like they’re contributing.

The banter and camaraderie that come with playing with friends add so much to the experience. Whether you’re laughing at a failed stealth attempt, reviving a downed teammate under heavy fire, or pulling off a perfectly timed ambush, the moments you share with your squad are unforgettable.

The graphics are stunning, with detailed environments and realistic lighting that bring Bolivia to life. The sound design is equally impressive, from the roar of gunfire to the ambient sounds of the wilderness.

"Ghost Recon: Wildlands" is a game that rewards creativity, teamwork, and exploration. While it’s fun solo, it’s an absolute must-play with friends. If you’re looking for a tactical sandbox that offers endless possibilities and unforgettable moments, this is it.

Ghost Recon Wildlands is the game that got me into PC gaming, and it’s still one of my all-time favorites. The combination of a massive open world, tactical gameplay, and complete freedom to approach missions however you like was a revelation for me when I first played it. Before this, I had only dabbled in console gaming, but Wildlands was the title that convinced me to dive headfirst into the world of PC gaming, and I’ve never looked back.

Gameplay and Tactical Combat:
At its core, Wildlands is about tactical, team-based combat in a massive, open world. What I love most about the game is the total freedom it offers. Whether you want to sneak around, take down enemies one by one with precision, or go in guns blazing, the game doesn’t force you into a particular playstyle. You can approach each mission in multiple ways, and the outcomes vary depending on your tactics. There’s a satisfying challenge in planning your attack, scouting the area, and deciding the best way to deal with cartel forces.

One thing I learned early on is that tactical combat isn’t just about shooting. It’s about positioning, communication, and timing. And while the AI-controlled squadmates do an okay job at supporting you, it’s the cooperative multiplayer that truly elevates the experience. Playing with friends, especially when you’re coordinating a mission together, is where Wildlands becomes a whole new beast.

Co-Op: A Game-Changer:
Here’s where Wildlands really shines: with friends. Playing solo can be a lot of fun, but the game’s true potential comes alive when you team up with others. The dynamic of having real teammates to plan, execute, and adapt with turns the entire experience into something special. Whether you're flanking enemies, providing cover fire, or reviving fallen comrades, the level of cooperation needed makes the game feel much more immersive and rewarding.

The open world becomes a playground when you have a group of friends to explore it with. You’ll find yourself just as focused on enjoying the chaos of a gunfight as you are on having a blast driving cars, flying helicopters, or causing havoc across the map. The missions can be tackled together with a level of coordination that makes everything feel more intentional and satisfying. Plus, there’s nothing quite like the adrenaline rush of successfully completing a difficult mission as a team—especially when things go off the rails, and you have to scramble to salvage your plan.

Stunning Open World:
The world of Wildlands is massive, and it’s one of the best parts of the game. Set in Bolivia, the environments are diverse, ranging from dense jungles to arid deserts and snow-covered mountains. I loved getting lost in the world, just driving around, exploring new places, and stumbling upon random encounters. Whether you’re scaling cliffs, crossing rivers, or sneaking through forests, the attention to detail is impressive. The dynamic weather system and the day-night cycle further immerse you, as certain conditions can drastically affect visibility and gameplay, making every mission feel different depending on the time of day or weather.

The game’s world also feels alive. NPCs go about their daily routines, animals roam the wilderness, and the environment itself feels like a character. It’s easy to get distracted, whether you’re collecting intel, liberating towns, or simply soaking in the scenery. This open world isn’t just a backdrop—it’s a playground that adds depth and replayability to the entire experience.

Story and Characters:
While the story in Wildlands doesn’t necessarily stand out as a narrative masterpiece, it serves its purpose well enough. The plot centers around dismantling the Santa Blanca cartel and bringing down its ruthless leader, El Sueño. While it’s straightforward and a bit cliché, the focus is more on the action and strategy than on deep storytelling. That said, the cartel bosses themselves are memorable, and taking them down one by one is a satisfying experience.

What I appreciated was that even though the story isn’t the game’s strongest point, it never really detracts from the overall experience. The world and the gameplay were enough to keep me hooked, and the sense of accomplishment in dismantling the cartel is rewarding enough to push you forward, mission by mission.

Graphics and Sound Design:
Visually, Wildlands is stunning. The game runs beautifully on PC, with detailed landscapes, impressive textures, and fluid animations. The lighting, especially at sunrise and sunset, is breathtaking, and it’s easy to get distracted by the view while you're sneaking through a mission. The sound design also stands out, from the realistic weapon sounds to the environmental audio. The soundtrack fits the tone of the game, keeping the tension high during missions and providing a fitting backdrop to your adventures.

Final Thoughts and Rating:
Ghost Recon Wildlands is a game that offers a massive, detailed world full of tactical combat, intense firefights, and the freedom to play your way. The real magic happens when you play with friends—co-op transforms the experience from good to unforgettable. The world is rich with opportunities, the gameplay is engaging, and the sense of accomplishment when taking down cartel members is always rewarding.

The story may not be groundbreaking, but the world, freedom of playstyle, and cooperative gameplay make it an easy recommendation. Whether you're new to PC gaming or a veteran, Wildlands offers hours of entertainment with tons of replayability.

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands has garnered significant acclaim since its release, marking a notable entry in the realm of tactical shooters. Set against the backdrop of Bolivia, the game offers an expansive open world that encourages exploration and strategic gameplay. The attention to detail in the environment is remarkable; players can traverse diverse terrains ranging from lush jungles to arid deserts, all while engaging in missions that emphasize teamwork and tactical planning.

The game's multiplayer functionality serves as a pivotal aspect contributing to its positive reception. Players can collaborate with friends or engage with others online, fostering a sense of camaraderie that enhances the overall experience. The option to approach missions either stealthily or with brute force allows for personalized gameplay styles, catering to both casual gamers and those seeking a more immersive military simulation. This flexibility enables players to experiment with various tactics, which ultimately promotes replayability.

Furthermore, Ghost Recon Wildlands features an engaging narrative centered around combating drug cartels in a fictionalized version of Bolivia. The storyline not only provides context for player actions but also addresses relevant social issues related to drug trafficking and its effects on society. This thematic depth adds layers to the gameplay experience, inviting players to reflect on the moral implications inherent within their virtual missions.

In conclusion, Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands succeeds as both an entertaining video game and a thought-provoking commentary on contemporary issues. Its combination of expansive environments, cooperative gameplay mechanics, and meaningful narrative elements solidifies its status as a standout title within the genre.

If “action-packed sandbox shooter with a hint of Far Cry DNA” makes your ears perk up, Ghost Recon Wildlands might just be your cup of tea. It doesn't aim to be a masterpiece, but it’s got a certain charm that might keep you hooked for hours on end. Here’s my take:

First Impressions
From the get-go, Wildlands can feel like a “dumbed down Far Cry,” loaded with explosions and frenetic encounters. Unfortunately, the plot itself doesn’t match the bombast of the action: there’s a noticeable shortage of cutscenes, and the sub-villains never really get fleshed out. The main antagonist stands out, but everyone else seems to blur together, making each major moment feel fleeting and a bit shallow.

Characters & Dialogue
Your squad might look ready for anything, but their collective personality doesn’t go much further than a handful of voice lines – repeated ad nauseam. Lacking backstories also strip them of depth, which is a real shame, as some more character development and banter could’ve made the story much more immersive.

Gameplay Loop
The core gameplay loop remains undeniably satisfying. Even if there aren’t a ton of mission types, the gunplay feels smooth, and stealth takedowns are fun enough to keep you invested. Unfortunately, from the start, you have access to one of the most versatile weapons in the game, so there’s little reason to experiment with the vast armory. A greater incentive to use and master new weapons would’ve given the game more longevity.

Tier One Mode
Tier One mode is an intriguing concept but jumps in difficulty drastically – you go from story mode to an unforgiving extreme difficulty way too early. Reaching rank 20 is already tough, and beyond that, it feels like you’re just getting knocked out faster without a nuanced increase in difficulty. More stats, more balancing, and a gentler yet still challenging curve would’ve gone a long way here.

Where It Shines
Despite the weak narrative and shallow squadmates, there’s something inherently “comfortable” about playing Wildlands. The setting, the gunplay, and the open-world exploration all blend into a reliable experience that players seem to return to, even if it’s not revolutionary. It’s an excellent title to fire up for a few missions, blow off some steam, and then come back to whenever you’re craving more.

Where It Could Improve
Imagine if it had an extra year of development:

Radio Variety & Interactivity: More channels, more chatter, more life in the world.
Deeper Stats & Visuals: Detailed breakdowns of weapons, vehicles, and regions.
Interconnected Story: Stronger links between sub-villains, with real consequences for your actions in each region.
Dynamic Control: A power tug-of-war among the cartel, Unidad, and rebels.
Enhanced Enemy Dialogue: More situational lines, especially when sneaking around.
Vehicle Challenges & Collectibles: Logging each variant in a collection, stats included, plus improved summoning so vehicles don’t spawn 400 meters away.
Scores
Story: 5.5/10
Barebones plot, lacks punchy moments.
Gameplay: 8/10
Satisfying loop, fun gunplay, though a bit repetitive.
Depth: 5/10
High potential, not enough fleshed-out content.
Replayability: 7/10
Not a ton of variety, but easy to pick up again later.
Mechanics: 6.5/10
Feels smooth overall, some rough edges.
Fun: 8/10
Consistently entertaining despite its flaws.
Final Word
It’s safe to say Ghost Recon Wildlands isn’t a technical marvel or a boundary-pushing epic. But if you’re after an easygoing shooter with a massive sandbox to explore, it still has its appeal. Sometimes, simple can be good – and Wildlands manages to prove that point nicely, even if you’re left wishing for a little more depth and polish.

Overall: 7/10 
but a GOOD 7/10 that you won't regret.

When you add in my time on xbox before i owned a pc, i probably have close to 600 hours in this game. I love wildlands, but it's a god awful ghost recon game. If you want a game that evokes the feeling you got playing any previous Ghost Recon title, this is not it. If you want a wacky narcos game that is more akin to a hybrid of GTA and Assasin's Creed, this is it. I'm happy it exists and I would say it's a little bit better than Breakpoint, but this is when the Ghost Recon franchise fully jumped the shark.

So, while I do recommend this game to some, Wildlands really lives up to its name by having some wild bugs and glitches, and teammate AI is some of the worst I've seen, even by 2017 standards. This type of tactical gameplay needs very competent AI to cover your back, lay down suppressing fire, as well as revive you in a timely fashion; they do not do any of these things most of the time. For example, your AI teammates will watch you eat lead, do nothing, and then will take 30 seconds to revive you because they crouched there looking at you. Furthermore, the driving is god-awful. Now, sometimes it can be entertaining. I played this originally on the PS4, a while after it released, and watched my bike, after going off a hill, fly damn near all the way across the map until I crashed landed and died. However, outside of these rare funny moments, it is often times to janky and slippery; when driving vehicles, or touchy; when flying planes, to sluggish; when operating a helicopter. Whats worse, however, is the story. It is so damn generic and boring, I typically just skip whatever cutscene I come across. Granted, the moment to moment gameplay, when it works, is an absolute blast. There is a great selection of weapons for many weapon types. Most have customization, with a few that cannot be customized for being special weapons. However, much of the map is quite barren, limiting the settings in which gunfights happen and thus not allowing a lot of them to shine. Overall, WIldlands has many problems that cannot be overlooked, but when the gunplay and tactical options come together, TCGR: W's is a fun time, and most likely better played with friends. Thus, I would give it a 7/10, but is something I recommend to get on-sale.

Ghost Recon Wildlands is an Open World shooter that can be played in Single- and Multiplayer in an campain and in competitive PvP modes.
I played solely the campain and I have to say, its incredibly generic, boring, buggy and generally not fun. In typical Ubisoft-manner the idea of the creators was to create a game that stretches as long as possible with almost interesting topics, yet putting in the lowest ammount of effort possible.
You play as an US-Army special squadleader, who is trying to dismantle a drug-cartel in Bolivia by dismantling 4 "big" sections of it, to eventually get to the boss. You do that in various ways, fulfilling missions to annoy little "bosses" till they show themselves so you can either kill or kidnap them. if that sounds like committing multiple acts of warcrimes, that is because it is, which is the most funny part about all of this.
The US has a reason to overthrow the corrupt Bolivian government, but this reason is so incredibly unimportant, that you can solely see it in one of the three trailers that play when you are idle in the main menu, as well as at the very end where it is shortly noted.
So it mainly focusses on overthrowing the corrupt drug-empire that builds the government and help rebells to regain power.
As it is open world you are free to explore everything in the order you want, but it is completely unnecessary and just complicates stuff - instead its likely you clear the area of one miniboss just to travel to the next and do pretty much the same things again.
For the main story that is "travel to place a and kill someone", "travel to place a and sneak to gather intel", "follow person without being seen", "take person hostage and kidnap it", "defend position", "tavel to place a and destroy object". While this can sound alright and typical for such kind of game, you pretty much repeat about 5 of these missions for any of these minibosses, which are 19(!) +4 minibossses with about one of these missions, +4 with about two of these missions till you can get the full ending of the last boss where you do up to two of these missions.
In other words, things get repetitive incredibly fast.
Especially when it comes to rebel-missions, which are seperate and exist to increase reputation among rebels, to level up certain support skills. these consist of 5 different missions that you gotta do about 5 ot 6 different times per area, so up to 21 (if i remember correctly). and then there are also "steal plane/helicopter" missions, abour 2-3 per location, that also all play the same (and only help you gaining a recource to level). So not only do you do the exact same things in the main missions, you also play the exact same things in the side missions. over and over and over again - stretched to the extreme. if you played one of the "steal plane/helicopter" missions for example (works for all the other types too) you pretty much played them all, yet of course are forced to play them over and over and over again. (including another "sidemission" which is stopping a convoy to gain their ressources, but they dont count towards any progression, so i dont count them) And if that wasnt enough, they themselve can stretch a lot as well. Escpecially the helicopter/plane stealing. sometimes forcing you to travel for minutes to complete the mission, in which you do nothing but press forward. straight forward. and if you fail the landing (which with the small runways for planes or sometimes the anti aircraft units that can hardly be dodged or disabled can sometimes happen) you can do the same thing again. cause repetition without any challange is so fun.
Also shoutout to the hundrets of collectibles scathered around the map without any reasoning. that sure was something missing in this game


All of the NPCs feel like cardboard cutouts that would be titled "placeholder for when we can think of something better". And sadly, with the way the game hypes them up, they are the most interesting part of the game, even when there isnt really a payoff for anything.
Rebels say nothing, maybe one line when you pass them per area
enemies repeat the... about 3 same lines every time you encounter them
civilians say nothing
the squad says the same 2 or 3 lines for repeating a similar mission (but with the twist of it being... in another location... but again... whoooooohooo, spooky)
With the minibosses you speak about once and after finishing them, you can forget about them - even when the game hypes every one of them up about being "a key figure in the functionality of the cartel", while after defeating them pretty much nothing changes about the strength or the unfeelable power of the cartel.
Even the endboss feels super empty. the game tells you, almost screams at you "hey, you gotta see this guy as the evil person", yet you encounter him so rarely that the traits the game hypes him up as, are invicible to the player.
And your contractor, while having personality, shifts it at will, especially when in one area of the map she is supposed to be kidnapped and on the other you are supposed to meet her. While her moodswings and teleportation through location she also acts incredibly stupid. threatens enemies where no threatening is needed or tells them things that on one hand nobody is supposed to know (as per story "we are there on secret mission, nobody can know we even exist etc.) or that are against our own interest. Her moodswings get so bad that at the end of the game, the two endings differ in nothing - everything playing out exactly the same - yet she just having a line removed in the other ending. its hiddeous, its bland, its boring, its generic.

At the end there is the lags and difficultytweak, although the difficultytweak is purely summarized with "make enemies bulletsponges, increase their damage, increase their aim, so that the player can only hide and let the rest of the broken ai squad do the heavy work."

sometimes it happens that drones, something very important for the late game, just arent accessable if you use them or guns and scopes being invisible. killed me more than once, and was frustrating and unfun every time.

A Vast Open-World Tactical Playground with Endless Possibilities!

Ghost Recon Wildlands offers one of the most immersive and expansive open-world experiences I've played in a long time. Set in the breathtaking landscapes of Bolivia, this game seamlessly blends tactical squad-based combat with freedom of choice, allowing you to tackle missions however you want—stealthy, guns blazing, or a mix of both. The scale of the map is truly massive, filled with varied terrains, from dense jungles to arid deserts, and each region brings its own unique challenges.

One of the biggest strengths of Wildlands is how it emphasizes teamwork. Whether you're playing solo with AI teammates or in co-op with friends, the synergy between players is key to success. Coordinating takedowns, using drones for recon, and adapting your strategy on the fly keeps every mission fresh and rewarding. There's a real sense of accomplishment when a well-planned ambush goes off perfectly.

The world itself feels alive, with dynamic weather, day-night cycles, and tons of side activities to discover. You'll encounter hostile factions, civilians going about their lives, and even rival cartel members fighting each other. It’s these small details that add depth to the experience, making the world feel reactive and real.

Of course, the game isn't without its flaws—sometimes AI behavior can be a little clunky, and there are occasional bugs, but nothing game-breaking. In the end, the sheer fun of exploring this gigantic world and the creative freedom in how you approach objectives easily make up for it.

If you're looking for a game that gives you the tools to create your own tactical stories, while exploring a beautifully crafted open world, Ghost Recon Wildlands is a must-try. Solo or with friends, there’s always something new to experience here. I've accumulated around a 100 hours of gameplay. Esspecialy worth to play because Ubisoft added achievements to Steam.

8.5/10 - Gear up and dive in!

It's not the most optimized of games and you might run into issues when initiating a co-op session, but at least it's not an always-online title (unlike Breakpoint) so I hope Ubi can't just pull the plug like they did for The Crew. The DLCs are not worth it as they aren't real additions to the existing world and are instead played on separate (smaller) campaigns. 

But if you like the core gameplay loop (basically like capturing outposts in FarCry 5), then you'll get a kick out of this game. I find it re-playable, super satisfying, and extremely fun in co-op. The open world of Bolivia is vast and gorgeous, with varied landscapes ranging from deserts to jungles. However, there's often not much to do in-between points of interest, the world isn't very deep. To go back to the FC5 comparison, there are no sidequests, no hunting, no fishing etc. Most of the time you'll just take in the scenery as you're crossing from one location to the other. 

The main downside for me is that progression (besides the skills and weapons you unlock) is measured in story missions and increased allied presence in provinces, but not in decreased enemy forces. Again, unlike in FC5, outposts are not yours to use once you clear them out — move out and return, and lo and behold, you have to kill everybody again. This is especially frustrating for SAM systems, as in higher difficulty provinces, you're constantly being targeted while flying and it would have been way more rewarding if you could clean the map.

Shallowness and lack of meaningful map progression aside, the gunplay is good, most missions or outposts can be taken either in ultra stealthy fashion or guns blazing, in close range or from afar. Vehicles are ok, I liked the story, and it's a lot of fun with friends. All of that combined makes for a game I regularly come back to.

Ghost Recon: Wildlands is, in my opinion, Ubisoft's most mechanically sound open world experience. The gunplay is tight, the AI is aggressive enough and not nearly as dumb to stealth as most of their work. Fictional Bolivia itself is such a joy to explore through and through, with every single area showing such beauty in design and geography that I have never seen in a game. It is fully playable in co-op (honestly it feels like the intended experience). It's a game you can beat in fifteen hours or one you could beat in thirty... and I wish I didn't take thirty hours with this one.

 The game is more of an open world playground with fun customization with tactical shooter elements than serious gameplay. The heavier gunplay is fun and engaging and the improvements to the Ubisoft formula themselves are so refreshing. No towers at all, just straight outposts and action stealth for the most part, but it does wear out after the halfway point of the game. Even though we opted to keep going after the game did say "hey you can stop here if you want," my party and I were expressing the desire to just get the game over with, lamenting the fact that we didn't stop there despite really vibing with the game's landscapes and combat.

I blame this on the very shallow world building and story completely. While being mechanically dense and diverse in location, there really isn't too much to the world of Wildlands. What you see is what you get, and anything with the Tom Clancy name attached to it (especially with Ubisoft) it's easy to see from a mile away. You either get over the top dad-core in the case of old Splinter Cell or you get something so garish and mean and skirting the lines of morally horrible and crossing the line of what is even okay to cover in a media setting. Ghost Recon spends the entire game positing the Ghosts and CIA member Karen Bowman as "the good guys who have to be a little messed up for the better of the world." By sending them into a fictional Bolivia where, I kid you not, a Mexican mega-cartel overthrew the government and turned it into a narcotics state, player character Nomad and their team are given free reign to turn Bolivia into a no holds barred warzone... or at least that's what Ubisoft wants you to think. The game for the most part was so damn cheezey on the surface that dialogue just slid off of my brain, but upon tuning into the story itself and really started to pick up on what the game was saying I couldn't help but be a little bit pissed. 

Wildlands is very obviously Pro-Service, which I don't think is a bad message itself, even if I don't think that life is the life for me, I understand that the people around me that I love are about this life, and I do support service as a valid lifestyle as I support most lifestyles. It does a really bad job showing that however with how edgy and nihilistic this game is. None of these characters show restraint, none of them follow any sort of laws of war whatsoever, it is all just blatant hypocrisy and brutality. They are exempt of all morals in this setting because the fictional villains, depicted as horrible jingoistic tropes (ffs Madre Coca) instead of actual good writing are just so much worse than the Ghosts themselves. I hate this style of writing from Ubisoft so much, the lack of self-awareness to turn such a dark and nuanced topic such as Black Ops work into nihilistic "if everything is bad, then I'm not so bad" set ups is what plagues this company to its core.

This game crosses the line sometimes and I mean really crosses the line. I don't get squeamish when it comes to violence in media very often, I love DOOM, my favourite game ever is Bloodborne, I grew up on GTA, and on a "realism" sense I can feel the surface level appeal of games like the Black Ops series because of their over the top natures. There is one scene I had to skip because it made me so damn uncomfortable and I am certain if I wasn't playing with people to keep me company I would have just bum rushed the bad ending. Nomad and Bowman capture a drug kingpin and what I can only describe as a tone deaf mood the writers decide to make our protagonist and deuteragonist snort cocaine until he overdoses. There is no justice here whatsoever, this is just plain sadistic and a straight power trip, they already had him and could process him. Most of the dialogue is like this, about how Bowman is willing to use the broken systems of the CIA and the US to break people further, and how the Ghosts are so hardcore for being one step removed from sociopaths, its a wonder how they even care about their country with the way they act. It's the difference between the abstract and concrete feelings of violence, the gameplay itself is abstract and fun Ubisoft BS with heavier gunplay and full four player co-op, but the writing itself tries so damn hard to take itself seriously. 

If you don't agree with me on this then hear me out just once more: shouldn't a pro-service game showcase the restraint and control that it takes to be a soldier rather than having the edgy ideals of a twelve year old's political lens. The mainstream has such a hard on to promote American military life as "ultra violent narcissism" over the multiple nuanced reasons people join the military that I can't but feel like it has had an effect on our youth. As a twenty year old myself, I've seen so much misfitted guys around my age range get sucked into the rhetoric of these games that special operations is so good for these guys because it allows them to get rid of their moral obligations because they don't fit in, and I hate that so much.

Let me be clear, the "thumbs-up" I give this game is just here for the sake of the gameplay and the sandbox carrying the game. As a mechanics first experience, it is very solid. If you can do yourself a solid and turn all of the dialogue off and skip the cutscenes and find friends to play with, you will get a vastly enjoyable game. If you decide to engage with this game's braindead and worthless narrative, then god, or whoever you pray too or if you don't, bless your soul

A Truly Immersive and Beautiful Adventure – Ghost Recon Wildlands is a Masterpiece

I’ve sunk countless hours into Ghost Recon Wildlands, and honestly, it’s one of my favorite open-world shooters of all time. From the very first moments, the beauty and sheer scale of the world captivated me. Bolivia’s vibrant, varied landscapes—from dense jungles to vast deserts and snowy peaks—are nothing short of breathtaking. The environment feels alive, with dynamic weather, day/night cycles, and wildlife that all add to the immersive experience. You can literally get lost in the world, just exploring, taking in the views, and soaking up the atmosphere.

The story mode is incredibly well-crafted too. The plot of taking down the Santa Blanca cartel is engaging, with a variety of missions that allow you to approach them however you want. Whether you prefer stealth, tactical assaults, or full-on firefights, Wildlands offers an incredible sense of freedom in how you approach every situation. The missions are varied and consistently rewarding, making every completed objective feel satisfying, especially as you see your team and the world around you slowly change for the better. The progression system keeps you motivated to improve your skills and gear, with a real sense of accomplishment when you take down major targets or liberate areas.

Now, let’s talk about Ghost Recon Breakpoint. I honestly don’t understand what happened there. Wildlands took everything that made it great and added a sense of polish, depth, and fun that Breakpoint just couldn’t match. Wildlands gave you freedom—freedom in how to tackle missions, how to explore, and how to have fun. Breakpoint, on the other hand, felt like a grindy mess. The world felt lifeless, the story was forgettable, and the whole survival mechanics thing was just unnecessary clutter.

I’ve found myself going back to Wildlands time and time again, and honestly, it’s hard to even consider Breakpoint as a sequel when Wildlands does almost everything better. The open world is richer, the story mode is more engaging, and the missions are way more satisfying. Ghost Recon Wildlands truly shines as a game that’s both fun and rewarding, and I absolutely love it. If you're on the fence about this game, just take the plunge. You won’t regret it.

The Chilean peninsula this game is situated in is Fictional, but based on superb real world research that includes wildly differing regions varying from Andean snowcapped Alpine peaks to humid swamps and heavily wooded rolling hills, all with industry and town locations fitting to their regions.

This accentuates the background to a rather excellent storyline which is wonderfully voice acted and I presume mo-capped. The production values are impressive across the board in this regard.

While it is clear many locations have buildings copy/pasted, their interiors and exteriors are all individual removing "repeated dungeon" fatigue common to many titles. The indistinguishable primary bases scattered throughout this world sized....world immerse one even further.

The World itself really feels alive with AI citizens wandering around on foot, plane, train or automobile and commenting on story driven events, alongside radio broadcasts setting the scene and enemies commenting on their lives and postings or patrols. All have reactionary based animations and behaviours. Your squad even comments on regions you enter, adding further to the experience.
[hr][/hr]
Combat AI is...an interesting one. Depending on your difficulty level which ramps up dramatically if you choose the endgame ranking system in order to unlock more toys, skins and cosmetics, you can end up in one shot instadead territory if discovered. Which does bring forward the GHOST intended nature of the game, you are not really meant to be seen at any point!

One can however, allow full degeneration into CQC combat, but the realism kicks in here with you being as squishy as most of the enemies. First shot wins. While playing with the AI teammates who are essentially gods and effectively give you a "life" (later 2) if you are downed, your Co-Op experience will vary in this regard. If your idiot buddy stirs a hornets nest, it really is best to run and hide to return to resurrect them, or let the timer run out and they teleport back.

Death merely loses you your most recent XP, resources and objectives earned before the last autosave. Autosaves occur on Teleportation, and entry into fresh combat zones, so its pretty good in that regard.

Avoiding all that is done by playing the game as intended. Careful reconnoitring of the objective, enemy patrol patterns, resources and backup potential allow you to select your infiltration point be it via BASE, HALO, ground assault or even using the Rebels to attack and distract.

The Rebels you are assisting can be used to call in Mortar Strikes, entire backup squads, auto-recon, or do distraction attacks on command. Your squad, can also to a degree be controlled in this manner, sending them to specific points, holding zones or going stealth or full combat.

This leads to the coolest feature of the game, Synchronised Shots. Sync shots with AI are a bit overpowered and can be used to reach all sorts of locations, while doing it in co-op is a lot more satisfying and a true art form. Marking targets, you then wait until all are lined up for their shots and call a simultaneous hit dropping them all without alerting the remaining enemies. Very effective.

While the better weapons and attachments are hidden across the entire map, usually in Points Of Interest, some are inside main bases or mission areas. One can attack mission bases outside of the Mission to gain access to the loot, and when you return on the Mission you'll find enemy layouts and triggers dramatically different. POI's are not required to be fully cleared to complete the game, unless you enable the endgame scoring system in which case you'll be hunting for every advantage possible!

To be clear, [b]Tier One[/b] (endgame scoring) is totally optional, and just ramps up the difficulty while forcing you to then invest in upgrading your weapons to match enemy armour levels. A bit of fun and not terribly complicated, but totally unnecessary to finish the game.

The Rebel Leader, Pat Katari is a bit of a miserable qunt. Whenever you do call the chap to drop in a vehicle for you, the clown will do his best to confound you by placing your called in item either halfway up a cliff face, in the middle of traffic, or on top of an entire enemy squad. This feature though is best used when clear of obvous pitfalls where it then behaves as intended, and makes for trudging your way on foot from a random location you found yourself in, back to civilisaton far less tedious (or just teleport to a base...but break your immersion).

[h1]Overall, one of my most favourite gaming experiences. Highly recommended both solo and if you can find a friend who isnt a gung-ho looney![/h1]

This is a free-roam stealth-inclined open world game.
Best short description I can give is "GTA with stealth elements" - it plays exactly like free-roam GTA, except it also tries to spin itself as a stealth game.
The combination works, and the core of the game is very solid, but there is serious "ubisoft cancer" in it, too.

The main core of this game - navigating the open world, driving various vehicles, stealth-optional combat - all works quite great and is typically fun to engage with.
It definitely nails this whole " just a team of 4 dudes by their own deep in enemy territory" feeling.
It is possible to clear areas with a much higher enemy count without them ever noticing you, or just completely blow it and go guns blazing (optionally in a rocket-firing helicopter or cannon APC).
Either option works, but obviously in the latter the enemies will attempt to pressure you, which, depending on the difficulty, area, and your equipment (including vehicles), might be weak or downright crippling.
The game does not really iterate on itself or progress in a meaningful capacity much, but I found that it was good enough for the time the game required my attention for.
There is co-op play available, and I happened to have a friend who is fan of the game who joined me often so that definitely added to the experience.
Solo play is definitely possible though, and the AI squadmates that you get are downright cheating at times.

Everything around the core of the game is what I want to refer to as "ubisoft cancer".
Open worlds having slow moments is definitely not something specific to ubisoft, but there are definitely signature elements.
There is an absolute metric ton of various side objects and collectibles you can get, most of which do not really do anything for you.
Since there is a form of resources you can collect, collectibles for these resources just continually respawn all around you.
There are a lot of guns, a lot of which are locked behind ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ loot boxes of all things.
Loot boxes and premium currency, in a damn single-player/co-op game.
Though, at least the guns do not really distract that much as while there are a lot of them there really isn't much of a reason to explore the arsenal - I kinda stuck with a completely overpowered sniper rifle and the same assault rifle for the whole game.
The core of the game does not change all that much as I mentioned above, this can be a huge negative if you are expecting progression or being forced into different scenarios - the approach is always the same, and the strategies are always the same.

Overall, despite the "ubisoft cancer" this is a really solid game.
Most of the cancer can be ignored, and if you can look past that (and have a friend to play with) this can be a really fun experience.
Would not recommend buying at a full price - there really isn't that much content (it just feels like there is because of open world), and just to spite them for putting extra monetization.

This was such a fun concept in theory and I feel they pulled it off pretty well. It mashes the tactical nature of the first games while implementing the GR Future Soldier gameplay core. And it works like a charm. I had a huge gripe with the gameplay of GR FS, its movement and lack of any requirement of tactical thinking even in the highest difficulty. I am happy to say, this game solves those parts.

The story is pretty simple, set in a fictional setting of the real state of Bolivia. However, the execution of the story is done very well with mature themes intertwined with them sparingly, but effectively. Considering the huge amount of bosses this game has, and the limited time we get to meet them (mostly when we shoot them in the head or capture them) - most of them are pretty well fleshed out. The gameplay is well intertwined with the story and even if one doesn't take in the lore, the nature of the missions within each of the bosses' territory effectively manages to tell you a lot about your adversary. We don't have a Vaas or a Pagan Min in our hands here, but those games have a tendency to become boring in gameplay within the first playthrough itself.

And that brings us into the gameplay. And I have to say, GR FS walked so this could run. The core gameplay is the same. 4 soldiers, not directly controlled - only controlled through in game commands. But this works much better in this open world setting, especially since they did fix the movement and did away with the forced cover-to-cover sprint movement. Each fight is tactical and somehow felt fresh right up to El Sueno. This is facilitated by the variety of environments which forces you to switch tactics. Some has thick foliage that make sneaking up a bit easy and sometimes you are in a nigh barren wasteland where you cautiously avoid open spaces. The gameplay is significantly different during the day as compared to that during the night as well. It really gives a feeling that the world is alive - only broken by the respawning of enemies (a necessary evil).

This is the best Ubisoft exploration experience among all that I've played. Each collectible has a reason to exist and the dynamical gameplay make the process not feel repetitive at all. Moreover, the exploration is adequately accentuated by well spaced side-missions that, although similar in set-pieces - never feel overbearing. 

I am actually pretty impressed with this game and feel this game really went below a lot of our radars when it came out. Play it. I recommend it wholeheartedly. 

IMPORTANT: However, the does still suffers from a lot of optimisation issues that can really ruin the experience for you especially during Ghost mode runs.

Here are the things that stood out to me (good and bad) while playing GR: Wildlands. See the last point for what I think is the most glaring issue.

Pros:
- Very large map with divers biomes
- Many options for map traversal (i.e. vehicles)
- Pretty good loadout customization (weapons, gadgets, clothes, accessories, etc.)
- Go it alone or with up to 3 mates (or strangers)
- AI squad is optional if you do want to go solo, though it is more difficult, I think
- Guns are based on irl counterparts instead of made up garbage
- Weapon customization is pretty good, though somewhat limited
- Decent plot
- Okay cover system, but doesn't always work
- Nice graphical quality
- Adding a suppressor does not affect damage (albeit after a skill upgrade)
- Sam Fisher crossover is pretty cool
- Overall pretty fun

Cons (IMO):
- Ubisoft
- Devs seem to know little about weapons, such as the difference between an AKM and an AK-74 or where to mount an optic or foregrip, etc.
- "Standard" capacity magazines are 20 rounds on intermediate cartridge rifles; should be 30
- Ubisoft script writing
- Movement is sometimes stiff or does not respond well
- Skill upgrades requiring skill points AND specific supplies is a little much
- The BIGGEST complaint I have with Wildlands is the enemy AI and the way they respond to threats. For instance, you plant some explosives on an enemy vehicle or hardpoint and then relocate somewhere on the opposite end of the area. Then you detonate said explosives from the safety of your new spot to create a diversion or something. Somehow the enemy AI knows exactly where you are and attempts to engage you. To me this removes a great deal of the immersion, and by extension, much of the fun. I could deal with the other issues I have with Wildlands if this problem had been addressed or never existed.

One of the great things about Ghost Recon Wildlands is the variety of missions and activities available to players. There are dozens of different missions to complete, ranging from stealthy infiltrations to all-out firefights. The game also features side activities, such as hunting and gathering resources, which add to the overall experience.

Quite possibly one of worst stealth shooters I've seen. The premise of the game is meant to be a tactical shooter with the idea of being as covert as possible in an open world environment. Instead, we have GTA style stealth game with spicy diarrhoea DRM and Ubislop connect on a seven year old game to remind the people they don't own their games.

The AI is smoothie of frustrating and abysmal awareness. Enemies are omniscient enough to see the player through dense foliage whilst the player can't effectively track. AI teammates are too inaccurate and unreliable without heavy, unnecessary grinding. Rebels are so dense, they have a bone in their brain. They either give away your position or commit explosive suicide by grenading the road they'll drive over if there's an enemy in front of them. Unidad patrols are annoying. No matter how fast you kill them, it results in swarms of patrols, sometimes in sparse rural areas as if they wear trackers on them. The end result is a poorly designed swarm shooting gallery which typically ends when you find cover or die. There is no other possible outcome. The worst feature they put in is "on the spot revivals". This basically means where you die is where you are revived. It would be fine if my team cleared the zone, but what typically happens results in a near instant death from where you are revived with a maximum of being revived twice.

The gunplay has not been improved since it came out. Far Cry 5/New Dawn, Ghost Recon Breakpoint (yes, I know it came later) are a few other examples of what the basic gunplay boils down to. It may be satisfying for many people, but it does not satisfy me. Most sniper scopes do not seem to work. The game offers no instruction how to aim with them other than to guess. I've used AI and manual search queries and found a brain drain of people who could have taught me but don't exist. You've reached peak laziness, Ubisoft; when will we be able to calibrate the sniper scope and get real laser rangefinders?

The map design makes me upset. Objectives are often intrusive such as one stealth mission spawning underneath me when I was flying a helicopter. The mission failed because everyone was on orange alert and I lost my helicopter, forcing me to walk. There's another set of missions where you have to find parachuted boxes all over the map. Mountain climbing doesn't work, meaning helicopters are required. The rest of the game is playing Christoper Columbus and walking to objectives you can't exactly fast travel to.

And for the other sources of frustration sync-shots take forever to coordinate and are unreliable. Invisible walls soak up bullets if you try to defilade in a firing position in some places. Tagging enemies in helicopters has become so unreliable, I often hide behind cover and use my drone to fly into the helicopter rotors instead of trying to shoot at it. As someone who loves stealth and precision, **Ghost Recon: Wildlands** hits the mark for me in every way. I thrive on planning my approach, and this game gives me the freedom to do that perfectly. I’ll spend time scoping out enemy bases, using the drone to mark targets, and then move in quietly, picking off enemies one by one without anyone knowing I was even there. There’s nothing more satisfying than syncing up shots with the squad and taking down a whole outpost without raising an alarm.

What I really enjoy is the flexibility. If I want to snipe from a distance or go in close with silenced weapons, I can. If things go wrong, I don’t panic—I adapt, using the environment or vehicles to escape or reposition. I’ve had moments where a perfectly planned mission goes sideways because of an unexpected patrol, but that just adds to the fun. It forces me to think on my feet, and those unscripted moments make every mission feel unique.

With the **Fallen Ghosts** DLC, the difficulty ramps up, and I love that challenge. The tougher enemies make stealth even more crucial, and I have to be smarter about how I approach each mission. It’s the kind of game where patience pays off, and every successful stealth operation feels like a personal victory.

For me, **Wildlands** isn’t just about completing missions—it’s about doing them my way, with precision and control. It’s the perfect blend of strategy, skill, and chaos when you need it. Whether I'm sneaking through the jungle at night or taking down an enemy convoy, the game gives me the tools to do it all, and that's why I keep coming back.

The engagement distances are pitifully low, the stealth is a joke thanks to that (no one hears suppressed gunshots, ever), and the aircraft controls are absolute trash, especially helos. It's basically a modern Farcry game, bar climbing any towers. There's also a 4-player limit, which is exactly the kind of limitation that ended up killing Codemaster's OFP games.

BUT.

The character and weapon customization is genuinely pretty great, since you now get all the Ubisoft Club weapons and gear for free, it seems, and, being a AAA game, it has a lot of features and details you just don't get elsewhere. Being able to shoot out of vehicles from the passenger seats, having nice animations for almost everything, and having detail without murdering framerates (looking at you, Reforger and Squad) is just super nice. There's also a lot of civilian life and ambient animations for both enemies and civvies, as well as wildlife everywhere. Again, looking at you, Reforger :P

I think if you're the kind of person that likes playing the campaigns of Arma games, or liked goofing around with friends back in the OFP days, you'll like GRW. Likewise, if you like Farcry and want something more grounded, coop, and with a larger open world, you'll like GRW. Otherwise, it's a hard sell for anyone looking for anything serious.

o, I jumped into Ghost Recon Wildlands and put in over 30 hours, thinking it would be my next big obsession. At first, I was really digging it—the open-world setting felt huge, and the idea of taking down a drug cartel one mission at a time sounded like a blast. But it didn’t take long to realize this game is just another standard Ubisoft open-world experience. The missions are pretty much ripped straight from the Assassin’s Creed playbook: go here, take out these guys, blow this thing up, rinse, repeat. It’s like they just swapped out the hooded assassins for military gear and called it a day. After a while, it felt like I was just going through the motions, and it got old real quick.

Now, the co-op missions? They’re okay. Nothing groundbreaking, but they at least add some fun if you’ve got friends to play with. But don’t even get me started on the AI partners. They’re just downright awful. It’s like playing with a bunch of clueless interns who have no idea what’s going on. They can’t follow simple orders, get stuck in the dumbest situations, and half the time, they’re just a liability. And as for the enemy AI? They're beyond stupid. I could be hiding in the grass, and they could literally be touching my body, and they still wouldn’t see me. It's like I’ve got some magic invisibility cloak. The whole thing just kills any immersion and makes the game feel like a joke. In the end, I just lost interest. It had potential, but between the repetitive missions and the brain-dead AI, it ended up being more frustrating than fun.

Full disclosure - I'm at about 1300-1400 hours into the game on PS4, and still purchased the game and all DLC on PC. I've also purchased everything possible through microtransactions on console, from vehicles to weapons to cosmetics. I have not purchased anything with microtransactions the second time around on PC.

With that out of the way, Wildlands delivers a visually stunning and truly living world, where enemies have a day/night cycle, civilians will get in cars and drive off, and the presence of an unholstered firearm will have AI react differently. These features are all absent from the 2019 sequel, Ghost Recon Breakpoint, in which I have about 1000 cumulative hours invested between console and PC. Though the story is contained in a multitude of tight arcs in Wildlands, it's connected well enough to be able to approach it from any angle and in any order. The freedom of choice makes for an incredible sandbox game that doesn't have the traditional Ubisoft "go grind for 10-15 hours" segment in the midgame. I highly recommend this game to anybody who's a fan of tactical shooters, casual MilSim enthusiasts, and even chaotic, high-octane players who can't help but pull out a machine gun and grenade launcher when they see a large enemy base. No matter your playstyle within the genre, you'll have people with whom you can matchmake, and most of the missions will support your approach. 

My only complaint is that some of the microtransactions do have mechanical advantages over items available in the base game, though within that metric, shooting an enemy in the head will just kill them, so it's not a huge deal if you get the hang of what you have available.

Overall, I'd give this game a nostalgic 9/10, or a more objective 8/10. Hopefully the next game in the franchise that Ubisoft launches - following the dead-in-the-water Ghost Recon Frontline free-to-play battle royale - will be more reminiscent of Wildlands and its scenic, living world. Should you grab this game on a more modern rig, enjoy the 2017 graphics on maxed settings and don't be shy of trying out a few mods down the road. Happy hunting, Ghost.

You play as Nomad, a male or female Ghost of your choosing, with some light customization. While theres not much to start with, theres a solid variety of clothes or accessories to wear and A LOT of different, fully customizable weapons. You also get some control over how your teammates look and what weaponry they use. straying from standard shooters, you can carry two primaries and a secondary, allowing more freedom of approach. your central ability is the sync shot, a carry-over from Future Soldier, where you can mark targets to take down at the same time; in singleplayer, your AI team will execute with perfect timing but need to line up first. In co-op, this mechanic works either naturally through voice chat, or through a ping system.

virtually any stealth mechanic you can think of is here, from detection and takedowns, through to lures and camouflage. As a shooter, its also competent, with toggles for first person view, snappy automatic cover, and plenty of offensive gadgetry.

where it stops being great is basically everything else. Voice acting is fine but at the risk of coming off prudish just seems too vulgar. the word ♥♥♥♥ is fantastic but its used in such a way that interrupts dialogue flow, and your own character will call virtually everyone something nasty (remember, you're supposedly an agency professional, not GD Mickey Rourke in Rogue Warrior). The story is just distinctly forgettable, and is paced in such a way that the game feels overwhelming. the best open world games intentionally start out small (Grove Street in San Andreas, Broker in GTA4, Valentine in RDR2, Riverrun/Whiterun in Skyrim, etc) so as to not do that. This game just drops you in the middle of nowhere Bolivia and its HUGE.

Loot is basically always a weapon part or clothing item, meaning you have to find the red dot sight _for the gun_ you wanna use, or whatever. its fine because each chest is like "ooh whats this" but then sucks because 9 times out of 10, its something you dont need or want. I do think that intel is a pretty OK system, if basic and not well utilized. 

Theres a unique lack of things to do or see in this world too. It looks good but never fantastic, its decently designed but never memorable, and theres no interaction with NPCs or side activities. Theres not even like really any missions, side or otherwise, where you directly help the people you are "helping" (America in a nutshell). the story wants you to believe that this country is under the grip of a cartel but aside from a checkpoint every now and a bit, civilians are just goin about it.
