[h1] "Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon® Wildlands" Review: A Tactical Open-World Adventure [/h1]

"Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon® Wildlands" offers a rich and immersive experience that kept me engaged for hours. I thoroughly enjoyed taking my time with this game, collecting everything I could find and exploring every corner of its vast open world. The game-play is smooth, providing an immersive shooter experience that feels satisfying and fluid.

What sets "Wildlands" apart is the freedom it offers. With mods, the game can be transformed into a first-person open-world sandbox, giving players countless options to tackle the buchons. The story also impressed me, with each take-down making the narrative more compelling. The cameos from the "Rainbow Six" team and the legendary Sam Fisher were a delightful surprise, and I enjoyed the short missions featuring these iconic characters.

The environment is beautifully crafted, with each region boasting its own unique flavor. Exploring the different areas was a joy, as the diverse landscapes added depth to the open-world experience.

However, the game isn't without its flaws. The crates, a common annoyance in modern Ubisoft games, were a bit of a frustration. Additionally, having to play on harder difficulties to unlock certain skins and weapons felt unnecessary, though the base game does provide a good variety of weapons.

Overall, "Ghost Recon® Wildlands" is a standout title with a well-crafted world and engaging game-play. Despite a few gripes, it's a game that offers plenty of fun and tactical excitement.

I can't really understand why this game is so popular especially with how buggy it is and how overpriced it is for a game of this quality. I'm gonna list off the issues I have with the game.

- The game is 70 GB, and while compared to modern games, for a 2013 game, that's MASSIVE. For comparison, Cyberpunk2077 is the same size, and has much better graphics, a larger map, story and way more features.
- I have the game on ultra graphics, and it still looks worse than the original Tom Clancy's Division, which released a YEAR earlier (2016)
- The AI is terrible. Your squadmates can barely function on their own (can't get into a separate vehicle), and the enemy AI is even less realistic. 
- The shortcuts the developers took to make the game "run smoother" takes away the immersion that it's supposed to have. An example: AI can shoot through walls and mountains (but only when you're not looking at them, to give the illusion they're "moving to get a better shot")
- The checkpoints for story missions are terrible. I can quit the game halfway through a mission, and once I load back in, I'm 5km away from the mission area, and there aren't checkpoints for VERY IMPORTANT sub objectives (stealing a helicopter, or turning off SAM launchers)
- It's so incredibly buggy, and these should be FIXED! It's a 7 year old game (as of writing) and it's also LIVE SERVICE. IT IS STILL BEING SUPPORTED! Why do I need to deal with getting stuck in rocks?
- The side missions are terrible too! Convoys sometimes spawn immediately after you load in, so you have no time to set up mines or any kind of organized resistance.
- Mines don't work half the time, like they literally don't explode! And when they do work, they're terribly impractical because there are always civilians in front the convoy! That means that there's again, no time to even use these mines. Sure, you can use them to set up traps in other bases, but you'd think mines should also be able to be used on vehicles!
- You can't kill civilians, which is TERRIBLE AGAIN for any kind of side mission. Convoys? Too bad, your mines blew up two cars, you are now reset.
- Your squadmates can get spotted by enemies, but instead of only knowing where the squadmate is, they now know where EVERYONE is. How does that work? Again, this covers the point of the AI being TERRIBLE.
- The missions suck, boring repetitive, the vehicle controls are terrible, the gunplay is terrible, the voice acting is terrible, how is this a triple A game? 

In conclusion, the game does not deserve the positive reviews it has. In fact, I'm 90% convinced that it has good reviews simply because the other Ghost Recon is EVEN WORSE. I'm thankful I bought this during the Summer Sale, so I didn't pay the full S60 for this bugged out, over hyped game. I got Cyberpunk2077 in the same sale, and I got a more fleshed out game, with better combat, better graphics, better story, and it costs the SAME! In fact, I got the same frames on Cyberpunk as Ghost Recon, which is insane if any of you reading this have seen Cyberpunk's graphics. Do NOT get this game unless you're itching for a Ghost Recon game. It is terrible.

I've played my fair share of tactical shooters, but Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands is a complete disaster. I came into the game expecting a polished, tactical, sneaky shooter experience, but what I got instead was a mess of poorly executed ideas and frustrating gameplay.

AI Nightmares: The AI in this game is shockingly bad. Your squadmates act like they’ve never seen combat before, often getting stuck or wandering into enemy fire without a second thought. Enemy AI isn't any better—they alternate between being oblivious to your presence and having psychic knowledge of your location.

Gunplay Woes: The gunplay is another major letdown. It feels clunky and unsatisfying, with guns lacking the punch you'd expect from a military shooter. The lack of precision and weight to the weapons makes every firefight feel like a chore rather than an exciting challenge.

Tactical Blunders: The game bills itself as a tactical experience, but the mechanics to support that are nearly nonexistent. The stealth elements are poorly implemented, and planning a coordinated attack with your team is nearly impossible thanks to the aforementioned AI issues. It often feels like brute force is the only viable option, defeating the purpose of a tactical shooter.

Bugged Missions: As if the gameplay wasn't frustrating enough, the missions are riddled with bugs. Objectives fail to trigger, enemies spawn out of thin air, and mission-critical NPCs disappear at the worst possible times. It feels like a game that was rushed out the door without proper testing or polish.

In short, Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands fails to deliver on almost every front. It's a tactical shooter that forgot the tactics and a stealth game that doesn’t understand stealth. Unless you're looking for a lesson in how not to make a shooter, I'd recommend steering clear.

[h2] I am really conflicted about this game. [/h2]

[h3] The good stuff: [/h3]
On the one side this game makes you feel like a super soldier dashing from cover to cover never being seen and taking out an entire cartel in a beautiful open would. And it does that wonderfully. 

I also really enjoyed the variety in weapons and gear, though there are some problems with them which I'll address later.


[h3] The not so good stuff: [/h3]
But on the other side this games has so many moments where I just wanted to break my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ keyboard. I played this game on the highest difficulty and yes, in stealth everything worked perfectly. But the moment you where put in a position where you were in a firefight, like through missions, this games mechanics just fails. Being outside cover makes the enemies instantly shoot you, with you having no time to react, not to mention that they kill you in a single burst and almost never miss. This makes it nearly impossible to change cover mid battle, which should be a big part in a cover shooter (I have no idea if Tier One was the reason, but even then this shouldn't have happened). Yes, I understand that this might just be a "skill issue", but when there are missions that auto engage you, it just feels almost impossible and more importantly, frustrating.

The AI of your team also brought me a bit a frustration. When you are not directly giving them orders they just feel useless or even get in the way.

There is no quickload. This is the greatest sin. I sometimes don't want to get picked up by my team two times to get back to the last checkpoint.

Even though the open world is designed wonderfully, it just feels empty. After the first few hours, you will most likely have seen everything there is to see. That is not to say that you won't see many different and unique parts of the map, but that what the player is given to do is almost always the same, or at least it feels like it.

The weapons like I said are a part of the game that I really liked, but even they fall short. I will primarily point out the FN 5.7 for the obvious reason that from the point you get it, there really isn't a better pistol for you to get.

I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hated Unidad at moments. These guys somehow managed to ♥♥♥♥ me over at the worst possible moment 20 minutes into a mission with no checkpoints. I understand why they exist and I like the concept, but the execution just misses. 


[h3] The things I feel nothing about: [/h3]
The story was okay i guess. I can still remember what most of the different cartel members did and what made them unique, but the overall story, especially Bowman were just meh. I never really felt like I liked Bowman or could understand her decisions, so the end mission just never hit.

The Vehicles are "okay". I think the handling is a bit off but this isn't a racing game so who cares. The bigger problem is that helicopters just are too widely available at the click of a button. This leads to less exploration of the map and even the skipping of entire sequences (the final mission).

The HUD is okay. The problem is more that you have to play with the settings the get to a state where the game feels "fair". I am talking about enemy clouds in piticular here, because in my opinion the kinda ruin the game. The game is about recon, which you don't really have to do if you can see where all the enemies are.


[h3] So what? [/h3]
After playing through this game i can say that is is alright. If you like these kinds of games, more power to you. But for me it was one of the most infuriating experiences I've had in recent history (And I started playing Tarkov again so that has something to say). I am happy to be done with this game and don't really intend to play it again.

Ghost Recon Wildlands is yet another installement of a long series of tactical shooters, offering both solo and cooperative multiplayer modes. The core gameplay loop involves gathering intel, planning missions, and executing them with precision. There are numerous ways to approach each mission, whether through stealth, all-out assault, or a mix of both.

[h1] Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*] Open-World Freedom: The vast open world allows for a high degree of freedom in how you approach objectives. You can choose your path and strategy, which adds replay value.
[*] Co-op Experience: Playing with friends enhances the game significantly, as coordinating tactics and executing plans as a team is where Wildlands truly shines.
[*] Variety of Vehicles and Weapons: The game offers a wide range of vehicles and weapons, which can be customized to suit your playstyle.
[/list]
[h1] Cons: [/h1]
[list]
[*] Repetitive Missions: Many missions follow a similar structure, which can become repetitive over time. The game could benefit from more variety in mission design.
[*] AI Issues: Enemy and teammate AI can be inconsistent. Teammates may not always follow commands effectively, and enemies can alternate between being overly perceptive and frustratingly oblivious.
[*] Solo Play Limitations: While the game is designed with co-op in mind, playing solo can feel less satisfying. The AI teammates lack the tactical depth that human players bring.
[*] Bugs and Crashes: Despite numerous patches, the game still suffers from occasional bugs and crashes, which can disrupt the gaming experience.
[/list]

[h1] Final verdict: [/h1]

Wildlands is a mixed bag. Its expansive open world and cooperative gameplay offer a lot of fun, particularly with friends. However, the repetitiveness, AI issues, underwhelming solo experience, and the bugs hold it back from greatness. If you enjoy tactical shooters and have a group of friends to play with, Wildlands is worth checking out. For solo players, it may not hold your interest as long.

Can't recommend it for the "regular" price of $120 for the ultimate version, but since this is easy to find deeply discounted ($24 at the moment of writing, I think I got it for cheaper a while back as part of a bundle) it gets a tentative thumbs up from me if you want to play this as a single player experience which is how I played it.

In my experience for single-player, the base game is more than enough and I probably wouldn't bother with anything beyond it even for $10 or so.

On the pros side, the map is phenomenal and can make you pause once in a while to admire the vistas as you traverse the terrain. The level of detail in the map and the impression that there's been actual care put it into is pretty great. The graphics and art direction are otherwise OK, except for showing their age in some circumstances, mostly when you're traversing the terrain from up high in the sky in an helicopter or when zooming in with the drone or binoculars - in those cases you see obvious details clearly missing or popping in as you move (even with max graphical settings).

On the cons side, the cover system is iffy where it's easy to be visible without realizing, and a lot of times being unable to tell how the character is going to pop out, or not, out of cover when aiming at someone. Also, there's a randomness factor with any engagement near a road where you can be engaged by the Unidad faction (militarized police) if they spot you when you're focusing on sneaking on some cartel enemies.

You have to go into the game with a certain mindset, that while it's fine to start encounters with stealth and thin out resistance that way, a lot of times you'll either be spotted, or some rebel ally from even the last mission will start causing mayhem and things will descend into chaos. Just stay back, order your squad to fire, and take potshots at enemies before they detect you - otherwise, if you're detected, and particularly on higher levels of difficulty, you're not bullet-resistant at all and can't have the typical shooting contest of a lot of games.

Completion-wise, if you play the game straight starting at regular difficulty and clear out all provinces as you go along (of objectives, not enemies as those always come back), you'll reach lower 20s tier if you keep increasing the difficulty as you unlock it (counting down from 30 to 1). You'd need to grind to go beyond that if you really want to unlock more stuff or just get to tier 1. Personally I won't bother as the gameplay alone isn't enough to keep me in it once all the story content is done.

Difficulty spikes to a point where you really must change the way that you play, but it's still mostly doable as long as you're careful (except for the last mission where you have to cheese it to have a chance, at least as a solo with controller - I doubt even four actual players with mouse and keyboard could clean that one in a legitimate way). Just keep using your squad and rebel assistance as those are crucial.

Edit: just a small addendum, I've actually been having fun with the daily challenges so far. The challenges introduce variety compared with how you'd typically approach missions and I may check back for a bit more until they start being more repetitive. Still not bothering to grind all the way to tier 1 though (even completing the challenges daily it'd still take forever).

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Although the video game market is saturated with military shooters where you play as [b]the[/b] Billy Badass who can shoot their way to victory, very few of them touch on the subject of the drug cartels and narco culture as a whole. In Ghost Recon Wildlands, you'll spend your time in Bolivia, a gorgeous and once free country that was recently turned into a narco-state by one of the most ruthless criminal organizations depicted in fiction - the Santa Blanca cartel.

[h1]The Story[/h1]
In Wildlands, you play as Nomad, the team leader of a US Special Forces unit known as The Ghosts. Nomad and his team are sent to Bolivia, after an undercover Drug Enforcement Administration agent is exposed, tortured, and subsequently murdered by the Santa Blanca cartel. To top it all off, the US embassy in Bolivia is bombed in a terror strike. Throughout the game, you roam through the vast open world of this beautiful South American country, dismantling the Santa Blanca cartel with the help of your team, your Central Intelligence Agency handler known as Karen Bowman, and the Katari 26 (Bolivian freedom fighters). The Ghosts also fight a much more powerful group known as La Unidad, a special faction of the Bolivian government created specifically to combat Santa Blanca. The two groups reluctantly end up calling for a truce - Santa Blanca stops killing civilians, and Unidad allows them to produce and sell their cocaine. The odds seem to be stacked against our heroes... Or so it seems.

[h1]The Gameplay[/h1]
Ghost Recon Wildlands gives you complete freedom. There are four areas of the Santa Blanca cartel that need to be destabilized: Production, Smuggling, Security, and Influence. Each operation or section plays an important part for the organization, and crippling them is pivotal to your success. All sections are ran by an Underboss, the Head of the section, and four "Buchones", who are more or less high ranking thugs. In order to take down an Underboss and the Head of an operation, all Buchones must be killed or captured (usually, your CIA handler asks you to kill them). In order to go after the leader of the Santa Blanca cartel, you need to take down two Underbosses and two operation Heads, though it's highly recommended that you dismantle the entire cartel. You can attack the Santa Blanca operations in any way you see fit, and the game doesn't force you to follow a predetermined path. I myself destabilized Security, then Influence, Production, and finally Smuggling. You can do it in whatever way you prefer, and you can even partially destabilize an operation, go to a another one, then return. Or go ♥♥♥♥ up another branch of the cartel. The choice is yours.

The gameplay loop of Wildlands consists of exploring the region of the map that you're currently in, searching for intelligence that could give you a lead on the local operation, and once you have the lead, you go to work. You start attacking the objectives one by one in order to draw out the Buchon, and then you strike. Like I said before, once you deal with the four Buchones, it's time to go after bigger fish. Most missions boil down to the same thing: kill a high value target, destroy a location, interrogate a special target, rescue an important person, etc. There's enough flavor in the game to keep you entertained, though, so you won't feel like you're doing the same thing over and over again, until the last three areas of the game (assuming you're going for 100% destabilization).

The most repetitive aspect of the game, however, are the Rebel Ops. There are side missions that need to be completed in order to assist the Katari 26 rebel group, so that they can provide you with better support during gameplay. They can deliver vehicles to you, provide mortar fire during combat, create diversions, and spot for you during stealth. Completing rebel ops reduces the support timer cooldowns and they improve other aspects of their skills.

Wildlands also features a skill point system, where you can earn XP to level up certain skills in different branches. You can upgrade your squad mates so they have more health or so they kill enemies faster. You can upgrade your drone to give it an explosive charge, thermal vision, or a noisemaker to lure enemies. You can upgrade your own skills to reduce the speed at which enemies detect you, increase your health, or upgrade your equipment. Weapons and attachments can be found all over the world by looting boxes in order to add the item you found to your inventory. You can customize Nomad, your character, by changing their clothes, their appearance, and even their gender (though canonically, Nomad is a male).

[h1]Notes[/h1]
-Wildlands can be played solo, with AI partners, or you can play with three other friends to help you take down the cartel.
-Sometimes, the map can be too big for it's own good. This is a pattern followed by a few other Ubisoft games. I recommend having the Katari 26 bring you a helicopter for most of the missions in the game. You'll quickly get tired of driving, trust me on that.
-Apparently, the game has a PVP mode called Ghost War. I didn't try it, but you probably could, assuming anyone is playing it.

[h1]The Final Verdict[/h1]
Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands is one hell of a game that tends to go on sale quite often, and for a great price. It's a breath of fresh air from most military shooters, and the Wildlands experience gives you freedom to play the game your way, something not many other games truly let you do. Play like a Ghost, sneak in the shadows and make the enemy scared of the dark... Or go in, guns blazing, and destroy everything and everyone with your skills. Whatever play style you prefer matters very little, because you're going to have fun even if you leave your comfort zone to try new tactics.

Wildlands is one of the few games I've wanted to replay just after finishing. It sparked my interest in the history of the Mexican drug trade and the peoples of Central and South America. After reading books about these topics, I realized how much thought went into the making of this game. The developers incorporated many elements from real life. It's like the history of the War on Drugs compressed into a fictional Bolivian setting. 

In terms of gameplay, I love the open world and the freedom to tackle the cartel bosses in any order. The landscapes of the different provinces are gorgeous and diverse, from jungles to deserts to lakes to salt flats. Compared to other tactical shooters, Wildlands is a populated world, with civilians and bad guys all over the place. It's similar in some ways to Sniper Ghost Warrior 3, which came out the same year and is another great game, but I prefer Wildlands. One of my favorite elements is the interaction with NPCs. Sure, the backstories could be more fleshed out, but the characters in Wildlands Bolivia still seem like people who could actually exist, with real motivations. In fact, I often wished I could slow down and absorb more of the atmosphere, because after spending a lot of time taking out the small bosses, the bigger ones were done in a couple of missions. 

The main thing I didn't like was the fact that the enemies always respawn even after you've "liberated" a province. If completing more rebel support missions increases the number of rebel patrols, why can't the cartel presence decrease as you get rid of more cartel bosses? I would have liked that element of realism, but I've seen similar complaints about games like Far Cry 6, so maybe game development isn't at that level yet. Other than that, I highly recommend Wildlands. It's a lot of fun!

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: A Tactical Masterpiece

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon sets the bar high for tactical shooters with its gripping gameplay and strategic depth. As a seasoned fan of military simulations, I found myself thoroughly immersed in the realistic environments and intense firefights that define this game.

From the outset, Ghost Recon impresses with its attention to detail. The weaponry feels authentic, each gun meticulously modeled to reflect its real-life counterpart. This realism extends to the game's environments, which are not just backdrops but dynamic landscapes that influence gameplay. Whether navigating dense jungles or navigating urban sprawl, every mission presents a fresh challenge that demands careful planning and precise execution.

What truly sets Ghost Recon apart is its emphasis on strategy. Success hinges on teamwork and coordination, requiring players to leverage their squad's unique skills and adapt to evolving threats. The ability to command squadmates adds another layer of complexity, allowing for coordinated assaults or stealthy maneuvers depending on the mission objectives.

Graphically, Ghost Recon remains impressive even by today's standards. The attention to detail in character animations and environmental effects enhances immersion, drawing players deeper into its richly crafted world.

However, the game is not without its challenges. Some missions can be punishingly difficult, demanding patience and strategic thinking to overcome. Yet, these hurdles only add to the satisfaction of mastering the game's mechanics and achieving victory against overwhelming odds.

Overall, Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon stands as a testament to the tactical shooter genre. With its blend of realism, strategic depth, and intense action, it offers a compelling experience that will appeal to both fans of the series and newcomers alike. Whether you're a military enthusiast or simply enjoy a well-crafted shooter, Ghost Recon is a must-play that delivers on all fronts.

Although the game's concept, destabilizing a drug cartel in a South-American country, seems somewhat interesting, the game itself is hellishly clunky...
The AI teammates sometimes successfully target enemies through walls from a hundred meters away and then fail to see someone right next to them. The enemies aren't really any more clever though, as teammates can often be seen "sneaking" in front of them in plain sight without being noticed
When driving or flying vehicles, teammates often teleport into the vehicle if you don't wait for them to enter it before driving away or taking off. Although this might seem helpful to not be required to wait for them every time, it gets even more strange when driving a motorcycle, as they simply won't accompany you at all then and just spawn right next to you when getting of the bike
Spawning brings me to another aspect, as the game lacks a jump mechanic. The climb mechanic provided as a replacement works reliably in most cases, as almost anything can be climbed in fact, from fences to walls to roofs to shipping containers. More often than once did I end up between a bunch of knee-high rocks though, of which the game allowed me to climb exactly none. Any human being able to jump would have easily escaped the situation, but as the player character lacks that trait, respawning at the nearest quick travel location was the only option in such cases

In addition, my expectation for Ghost Recon gameplay lies somewhere between Splinter Cell and Rainbox Six on the sneaking/shooting scale. This game requires the player to cover almost the whole range though, sometimes even back to back within a mission and without any checkpoints in between
For example, some missions require you to infiltrate some mansion or camp for an "observation" of some high-rank cartel or military traitor. After sneaking into the location, carefully putting down guards one by one so they don't notice, the target scriptedly jumps into a car and drives of. When inevitably following the target, the roads are suddenly packed with enemies wanting to see the traitor dead. So, you need to make sure that a) the target doesn't notice you, b) you don't let the target get away, c) the target isn't killed and d) you aren't killed
Another example, and an even worse one, is a crossover mission with one of the other mentioned franchises, that has you sneaking into a military base staffed with about 30-40 soldiers, without being noticed and without touching any of its inhabitants. Halfway through that mission, hell breaks lose and you have to fight through the aforementioned soldiers and their reinforcements to an extraction point

Easily the best part of the game is its open world, and I literally mean the world. It's still quite pretty, considering its age, and I'd even call it beautiful in some regards. It has swamps, forests, deserts, snow-topped mountain ranges and even a huge salt flat, all combined with weather conditions and a day-night-cycle
Flocks of birds can be seen in the sky or on larger lakes and other animals such as deer and llamas are encountered regularly, sometimes in herds, reacting to the player when approaching them. Humans inhabit the villages and towns in somewhat believable numbers or drive around in vehicles throughout the countryside

The game naturally has some of the usual Ubisoft open world stuff as well, such as hidden collectibles and places to explore, although all those are at least combined with some kind of historical or narrative background either regarding real world events or the story. Funnily, some of that stuff simply can't be collected or completed though, if you choose to disregard specific playstyles and their relevant equipment
If you like to play stealthily, you might be lacking C4 or mines in some situations. If you like to play aggressively, you might be lacking an EMP or distraction lures in some situations. Then you can either ignore those situations entirely or complete other stuff first until you have those items available, even though you might not need them for your usual playstyle

The available weapon arsenal is a whole other story instead. Providing everything from SMGs to LMGs, from assault to sniper rifles, from semi-automatic to automatic pistols, shotguns and even a crossbow, there's a weapon available for every situation right from the get-go. The thing is, there's just too much to choose from, as nearly every category sports 20 or more weapons with sometimes just minor statistical differences. Some can be customized with different weapon parts, such as grips or scopes, some are pre-defined trophy/signature weapons
You'll quite probably not use more than one or two from every category though, even if you regularly change your loadout to match the situation. To even have a weapon loadout bars any explanation on the other hand, as you can even switch equipped weapons when crouching directly behind an enemy's back. Regularly encountered ammo chests show a GUI option to change the loadout, which indicates that loadout changes were not intended to be possible all the time, but that limitation was seemingly removed from the game either before release or sometime later

TL;DR:
If you manage to grab the game during a sale and really like the franchise, it might be worth your time
Otherwise, keep your hands off of it

Original Review:
Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon® Wildlands is the best "mid" game you will get to play, and on sale, it is well worth the money.
What got me to spend over 100 hours in this game are the gunplay mechanics with a satisfying sound that confirms a successful hit. It doesn't hurt that the world is quite pretty most of the time.
The overarching story is boring and quite problematic, to be honest (it paints Bolivia in quite a bad light and has that "white savior" trope).
Regardless, the game is mad fun in co-op. Me and a friend had a blast.
I wish more games had gun mechanics such as changing the fire rate of your gun, having a scope with a moving 2nd scope for extra zoom (EXPS x G33 Assault Rifle Scope, my beloved), and more. That really made the game fun for me—fiddling with the gun assembly, and then getting to use it in a successful raid on an enemy compound.
To summarise; this is a half-decent game with a solid amount of effort put into it. The core gameplay is well-fleshed out—and while it is repetitive, the challenge is varied enough to keep you engaged.

It's a very complete third-person shooter experience. Shooting, sneaking, vehicles. Cool villains. Lots of things to do. Feels kind of like playing a Far Cry title but with third person and milsim. My only complaints are that I find the game pretty easy, even in the beginning with few tools unlocked, playing singleplayer, on extreme difficulty. Matchmaking is dead.

I mean, at the very deep discount that it has currently (Summer Sale), it probably is worth it especially if you can rope a couple friends into buying it with you and then playing through it in co-op, in which case it's a good "pop open a cold one, open a bag of crisps and talk ♥♥♥♥ with your mates for an hour or two of a decent stealth-action game", but at full price or as a single-player experience where you actually want to focus on the game, it's just super bland and boring, even for a post-Black Flag Ubi game,  and in a pretty bad technical state to boot.

Pros:
- solid amount of content (activities, gun selection, vehicles, etc.)
- the open world locations are pretty varied

Meh:
- story, lore, characters - overall very uninspired, generic, safe - really, the story is just a B or C grade action movie forced onto an open world game
- sounds - all very bland, the guns sound distinct enough from each other, but a lot of them sound "subdued" for a lack of better term, vehicle sounds just sound like stock sounds you buy on a digital marketplace for a couple bucks, they are decent from technical standpoint, but again, they don't really elicit any emotions - if you've ever sat in or been near a supersport or a muscle car or one of those high-tier off-road beasts, even if you are not a car person, I can 100% guarantee that during the start up or when the accelerator was down to the ground, you had goosebumps on your skin - you sit in the fake-lambo in this game, it sounds like just another car
- music and in-game radio - ranging from forgettable to annoying, turned off within 30 minutes of playing the game, although I guess there was at least some effort put in to make it match the setting, at least as far as I was willing to listen to it

Cons:
- technical state of the game is rather poor, even after multiple years of patches - stutters, crashes, objects stuck in other objects and freaking out physics, T-posing NPCs, "deliver me a vehicle" ability spawning vehicles hundreds of meters away, in unreachable spaces, in the middle of an enemy base, etc.
- some cutscenes are unskippable for some unknown and extremely stupid reason
- while the open world content is serviceable, the setpieces are pretty much all bad with a very few exceptions, especially their balance is really bad, having basically two levels - retardedly easy and retardedly hard. "story" missions can be either completed easily even on the hardest difficulty with little to no effort (majority of them), or they will require multiple attempts for reasons ranging from "the mission designer said ♥♥♥♥ you" to "here, have ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ RNG, several times in a row". As an example - you are put into a forced stealth situation, no disposing of enemies to, supposedly make sure no one finds out you ever were in that place. Only, after getting reaching the objective, suddenly you are told to just start shooting because of some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gimmick reason. Why the actual F U C K did I just spend nearly half an hour dealing with your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stealthing a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ designed location???
- the voiceacting is atrociously bad, there were better voice acted games made in garage by two people back in 1987

The ability to plan and execute strategies on the fly adds a layer of depth and replayability.

Wildlands is fundamentally just not Ghost Recon, it plays more like a tactical GTA mod.  Nearly everything about the game is a technical step backward from previous titles--movement is janky, the gunplay is stiff, the stealth is a mess, game physics overall are off (especially for air vehicles), most vehicles handle poorly, and enemy AI scaling for difficulty is comically bad.  Using and moving around cover is stiff and inconsistent.  Your teammate AI requires constant handholding and will routinely just not enter gunfights without your command, even after you're detected.  Rebels will arrive at random and spoil ambushes, block the roads, and generally be a pest.  While previous GR titles aren't renowned for their dialogue, they never actively pulled me out of my suspension of disbelief like Wildlands does; delivery runs from completely passable to totally wooden (sometimes from the same actor), a lot of the team dialogue is written and delivered with no rapport between characters, and the attempts at humor usually fall flat.  Almost everyone's attempts at Spanish sound like a Boomer ordering Taco Bell.

Compare it to Future Soldier or GRAW on mechanics alone and it fails entirely, but somehow the gameplay loop of exploration keeps this an interesting experience for the whole game.  The fictional slice of Bolivia they created is rich and interesting, with absolutely gorgeous vistas that will keep you flipping to photo mode constantly, and the story is pretty fun to dig into.  It's good fun solo, great with friends.  Player and weapon customization is detailed and feels like playing with virtual GI Joes.

As a PC port, however, the game is a bit rough.  The already-stiff controls are even worse without a controller and I strongly recommend playing on a gamepad.  Controlling vehicles, especially flying, is really awkward on keyboard, and aiming on a mouse is a juggling act with shoulder and perspective switching.  Visuals will be a bit intensive on mid-level cards, and I get weird moments of actual lag, not framerate hitches.  Not game-breaking, but noticeable.  I've had one crash so far in 24 hours of gameplay.  Get it on sale, buy copies for your friends, have some good co-op fun.

This one is hard to like.

It seems to be an increasingly recurring thing with the studio's titles. For at least 15 years, it has become increasingly difficult to keep returning to these franchises so mistreated by Ubisoft.

They are like the M. Night Shyamalan of games. Living off questionable successes of the past and a nostalgic attachment that fills fans with the hope that someday, somehow, despite the insanity of expecting anything different, something truly interesting will be released.

Who isn't tired of knowing how precarious the company's productions are? That they have already adopted such a hateful, creatively bankrupt, and invasive business model that any person with the slightest bit of common sense should never continue buying their products?

But they keep taking my money with these absurd 95% discounts. Go figure. 

The result is always the same. Unfortunately, I played enough not to be able to request a refund.

So, I'll leave a positive thumbs up, like a good loser.

Here we have a mechanical patchwork of things we've already seen in 2012, in Future Soldier, with the unwelcome addition of a huge and redundant open world and a subtraction in the traditional futuristic/hard sci-fi aspect of the franchise.

They gave up a practical and streamlined structure, with well-designed missions that balanced moments of action and stealth in a dramatic rhythm and offered a striking sense of style that encapsulated the propagandistic futuristic military power fantasy of a global terrorist hunt. And instead, they provided impractical natural landscapes, which are not very immersive and mechanically boil down to huge purposeless empty spaces that unnecessarily stretch the experience, and hundreds of small generic missions that work as micro-doses of the more linear and scripted stages of FS.

The game feels completely scattered and unfocused.

Future Soldier was as stupid as one would imagine, and it was an abandonment of the franchise's more grounded and strategic roots in favor of adhering to the simplified conventions of the time, but at least it was a game with personality. It had a sense of style in its presentation and executed its entirety with competence and confidence and with technical merits that Wildlands struggles to rival.

FS didn't linger more than necessary, and every minute of its duration had a reason to be. Now just look at the hour count needed to complete all objectives in Wildlands to find out it's exactly the same as all the others. The same thing they did with Assassin’s Creed, Far Cry, and the like, they did with Ghost Recon.

Increase the size, decrease the quality. Fill those open worlds with a swarm of icons and banal activities made with the creativity of an ant to inflate the duration. Then force players to do these activities to feed a lazy upgrade system that almost never adds anything to the game experience but is essential for the full functioning of your character.

Collectibles! NEVER forget the collectibles.

Wildlands has no soul. It has no atmosphere. It has no humanity. And its theme is executed so flaccidly, poorly, and unbelievably stupidly that you wonder if the writers are 12-year-olds. It’s a “systematic war on drugs” that tries its best not to touch on the specifics of the subject or discuss anything remotely associated with it.

You, conservative friend, who learned about drugs from sensationalist news and the speeches of hysterical hypocrites, and have a comically childish and fantastical view of how this “war” is fought in the real world, would be able to write something more substantial, if not at least more entertaining. 

They didn’t even try to tell a story. They didn’t even try. 

What you have here is just a toothless amalgam of vaguely associated concepts with a theme emptied of any meaning.

As if that weren’t enough, the technical quality of the game doesn’t surprise at all either. Wildlands definitely doesn’t look like a cutting-edge 8th-generation game. Graphically, it’s not surprising, some of its animations are laughable, and the lack of personality and style in its presentation make the game feel strangely generic. 

Like something that cost a lot to make but wasn’t polished properly to make good use of that money.

As for gameplay, the game doesn’t offer anything particularly innovative or different. Except for the addition of the open world, there was nothing surprising in the technology employed there. It’s more of the same, only worse, somehow.

And I’m not kidding. Just play a mission of Future Soldier, and you’ll see that things in Wildlands haven’t gone far.

Far be it from me to demand that other games offer the same standards for vehicle control as the GTA franchise, but you have to wonder if it’s acceptable that a 2017 AAA game, made by one of the largest studios in the world, appears to be worse and more primitive than things found on the PS2.

Driving and flying in Wildlands is a horrendous experience.

And despite all this, the game manages, somehow, to be fun. Not very fun. But fun enough to be passable.

I think this has to do with the sharp rules of gunplay on high difficulties and the inherent satisfaction of devising dynamic plans and executing them within a tenuous fantasy of professionalism.

The small doses of stealthy and occasionally bombastic action (when the plan goes wrong), somehow never got old.

You end up getting used to the brutal banality of most of the content and inevitably narrow down to the best parts that the experience can offer. They’re not amazing and exciting moments executed elegantly, but they work well enough for you to be satisfied. If everything else goes wrong, at least the rules are consistent.

You plan, execute, and adapt very easily, but the high lethality (both yours and the enemies’) prevents it from becoming brainless and monotonous.

Add a handful of friends to the chaos, and everything becomes even more interesting.

Even the grind for collecting resources seems to have been made easier, with collection points always conveniently close to the places you have to go to do the main activities.

Occasionally, the game even manages to reach introspective notes, with beautiful landscapes accompanied by the game’s minimalist tracks.

That said, ultimately, it’s an average game. Mediocre in almost every sense. Incompatible with its own era’s peers (and previous eras’). It’s also not a notable improvement over its predecessors. 

It’s a mediocrely enjoyable game. Don’t have high expectations.

I liked Wildlands, but if I were to be honest... I’d say it’s still not worth it.

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands is a thrilling open-world tactical shooter that masterfully blends strategic gameplay with breathtaking visuals. Developed by Ubisoft, the game takes players to a sprawling recreation of Bolivia, where they must dismantle a drug cartel using their wits, skills, and teamwork.

World and Atmosphere
The world of Wildlands is vast, diverse, and alive. From towering mountains and dense jungles to arid deserts and bustling villages, the environment feels immersive and vibrant. The day-night cycle and dynamic weather system add another layer of realism, affecting both the gameplay and the mood. Whether you're infiltrating an enemy base under the cover of darkness or navigating through a storm, the atmosphere never fails to impress.

Gameplay
Wildlands strikes a fine balance between tactical strategy and action-packed combat. Players can approach missions in a variety of ways—whether through stealth, all-out assault, or a mix of both. The ability to coordinate with AI teammates or human players in co-op mode makes every operation unique and highly engaging. The sheer number of weapons, gadgets, and vehicles ensures that players have plenty of tools at their disposal to tackle any situation.

Story and Characters
The narrative revolves around the team’s mission to dismantle the Santa Blanca cartel. While the story isn’t groundbreaking, it’s solid enough to keep players invested. The cartel bosses are diverse and memorable, each presenting unique challenges and insights into the world of Wildlands. The banter between Ghost team members adds a touch of humor and camaraderie, making them feel more relatable.

Multiplayer and Co-op
One of Wildlands’ strongest aspects is its cooperative gameplay. Playing with friends elevates the experience, as teamwork and coordination are crucial for success. The synchronized takedowns and shared strategies create some of the most satisfying moments in the game. Even solo players can enjoy the game, thanks to competent AI companions who follow your commands effectively.

Graphics and Performance
Visually, Wildlands is stunning. The attention to detail in the environments, character models, and animations is commendable. While some minor bugs and glitches might occur, they rarely detract from the overall experience. On powerful hardware, the game truly shines with its sharp textures and fluid performance.

Conclusion
Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands is a remarkable blend of tactical depth and open-world exploration. It rewards creativity, teamwork, and strategic thinking, making every mission feel like your own unique story. Whether you’re a fan of stealth games or action-packed shooters, Wildlands offers something for everyone.

Overall I'd say it's... meh? It's your average Ubisoft open world game with too many things to pick up, although here it's not really a big issue. 
My thoughts that I randomly collected:
Story feels more like it's here so we can have a reason to do things but it's not bad. 
Shooting feels meh which isn't a great thing but it could be worse. Some weapons are better for stealth, others for going in loud (kinda surprised me). You can collect a bunch of guns but really only need a DMR and LMG to flesh your kit out. The rest is just flavour. 
Missions are ok in terms of diversity BUT the car escort and Sam Fisher missions are just bad and frustrating. Difficulty is a mixed bag; hard with AI isn't really hard, even without any upgrades as they die rarely and revive you every time without fail (only once per fight tho) but in solo you have to pay attention to your positioning and your flanks, so you can easily get overrun if you aren't paying attention.
Movement feels odd. You can walk sideways but not run sideways. There is no jump and you have to climb in order to get over or on top of some things. Wouldn’t be bad if it worked on everything but it doesn’t. Some things that look climbable aren’t and you have to go around. You also can’t use the parachute unless you jump out of a plane or helicopter, So landing on tall structures and then jumping down is straight up impossible.
Speaking of moving, driving is very serviceable, plane flying is meh but Helicopter flying is awful. Since some have guns you might want to use them from time to time. But aiming with a mouse is either super slow or way too fast.
Respawning is also not quite there. Often it puts you in ok places, but multiple times I’ve respawned at places where I had to walk waaaay too long to get back.
If you cat it for 5-10 bucks it’s a perfectly fine game. If you have some friends who would be into those games it will likely be more fun too.

I was keen on playing a ghost Recon game for the first time. I remember seeing breakpoint and it's bad reviews so I went to take a look at the predecessor and play that one instead, hoping it would be better. It started off strong but over the course of the entire game, it spiraled down into complete trash. I have played this game on and off since 2020 and I have finally finished it in 2025. After five years, I have finally finished this torture of a game. You may ask why I put myself through this. Without going into detail, the game has some aspects that I liked about it that made me keep on playing it.


[h1]Positive:[/h1]

[b]Concept:[/b]
I really liked the concept of being dropped into a world and being tasked with taking out a big cartel.

[b]Weapons:[/b]
I like the weapon customization. You open a menu where you can see the entire gun disassembled. You can see every part of the gun exposed. You can change the barrel, the stock, the mag and the scope. Some weapons support under barrel attachments like grenade launchers.


[h1]Negative:[/h1]

[b]Servers:[/b]
Every time I boot the game up, it tries to connect to some server it never reaches. I have to wait in the menu for about a minute before it decides to load my single player save.

[b]Hardcoded Map Key:[/b]
Out of all the keys, the map key is hard coded to "M". I have to stretch my hands to reach it.

[b]Audio:[/b]
The audio quality of sound effects and voice lines sound low and compressed. They sound quite bad for a 2017 game. The music is nothing special. Only the menu music sound decent

[b]Borefest:[/b]
The game took me years to beat. I played it on and off because it gets quite boring after a short time. The game is flooded with targets you have to take down. It felt like the game had 50 targets and let me tell you, it gets really boring after the first five

[b]Optimization:[/b]
This game uses more resources than it should. It doesn't even look good. The entire image looks like it's over sharpened. yes, I tried everything. I went through the game's graphics settings and my AMD graphics driver settings. Nothing helped.

[b]Facial Animations:[/b]
The facial animations are God awful. It's so uncanny. The faces look so plasticky. Even a game like Half-Life 2 had better facial animations than this 2017 game. Animations that don't look horrifying.

[b]Balancing:[/b]
The balancing is what kills this game for me. If you die in a mission, it gets entirely reset. I'm over here sneaking around in the base, messing up and getting killed. That's fine but don't make me go through that whole base again. When that happens, I do what I always do. I just rush through the whole base an gun everyone down without thinking. I just throw the slow stealth out the window. Another thing that's really annoying is how enemies (like dual SMG wielding cartel members) can gun you down at a distance of 30 metres while my invisibility backpack is active.

[b]Unidad:[/b]
The Unidad get their own spot here in this list. They're probably the worst part about this game. They work like GTA cops. If they see you, they instantly start to attack you. You can get a wanted level and then they won't stop respawning. The only way to get rid of them is to flee. But that's not always possible. Especially in small bases that have only one road as entrance. They pin you down hard. You have no choice but to kill them but that will raise your wanted level. More and more enemies will spawn with stronger gear. You're just gonna be stuck there and the only option for you is to die after trying to fight them for 10 minutes. You probably think that you should just try to avoid them. Well, good luck, because they spawn in story missions too and will instantly attack you when you drive by their cars. They're actively sabotaging the campaign. I'm not joking. The game would be 20 times more enjoyable if they were never implemented. I like to compare them to gum you have accidentally stepped on and is now stuck to your shoe. Not even GTA cops attack you on sight.

[b]Vehicles:[/b]
Driving cars and flying planes feels awful. 

[b]Bugs:[/b]
The game is filled with bugs. When I go down, my AI teammates will come to revive me. Their pathfinding can be broken and they can't find me, bleeding out on the floor. Some side mission wanted me to fly a plane 15 kilometers away from my current position. When I got there, nothing happened. I was at the exact spot where the arrow pointed me to. I've just wasted my time. This is not a biggie but it happens too frequently. It drives me mad.

[b]monetization:[/b]
This game is filled with monetization. It has all the usual suspects present. A premium currencie, loot boxes and tons of skins.  some of the skins looked pretty cool like the operators from rainbow 6 siege but they're all buried in loot box pools.  Such a shame.

[b]Final Mission:[/b]
Contains the worst parts of the entire game combined into one mission. Enough said.


[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
It shouldn't come as a surprise that I won't be touching a Ghost Recon game ever again. The idea behind the game got me interested in the series but the execution was pathetic. This game was already outdated on multiple levels when it came out. I do not recommend to play this game at all.

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands
Release Date: March 7, 2017

Developer: Ubisoft Paris

Publisher: Ubisoft

Setting and Story
Setting: The game is set in Bolivia, where a fictional drug cartel called Santa Blanca has taken control of the country. The game world is a vast open environment with diverse biomes, including mountains, forests, deserts, and salt flats.
Story: Players control a member of the Ghosts, an elite special operations unit of the United States Army. The Ghosts are sent to Bolivia to dismantle the Santa Blanca cartel and its operations. The main antagonist is El Sueño, the cartel's ruthless leader.
Gameplay
Open World: "Wildlands" features a massive open world that players can explore freely. It is one of the largest open-world games created by Ubisoft.
Missions: Players can approach missions in various ways, including using stealth, tactical planning, and direct combat. The game allows for a high degree of freedom in how objectives are completed.
Cooperative Play: The game supports up to four-player co-op, allowing players to team up and tackle missions together. It can also be played solo with AI teammates.
Customization: Extensive customization options are available for both characters and weapons, allowing players to personalize their gear and loadouts.
Features
Realistic Combat: Emphasis on realistic military tactics and combat scenarios. Players can use drones, binoculars, and other equipment to gather intelligence and plan their attacks.
Vehicle Usage: Players can use a wide range of vehicles, including cars, motorcycles, helicopters, and boats, to traverse the vast map.
Dynamic Weather and Day/Night Cycle: The game features a dynamic weather system and a day/night cycle that affect gameplay and strategy.
Reception
Positive Reviews: "Wildlands" received generally positive reviews for its open-world design, cooperative gameplay, and the freedom it offers players. Some criticism was directed at its story and mission repetitiveness.
Commercial Success: The game was a commercial success, selling well and becoming one of the best-selling titles of 2017.
Post-Launch Content
Expansions and DLC: Ubisoft released several expansions and DLC packs, including "Narco Road" and "Fallen Ghosts," which added new missions, challenges, and content.
Updates: Regular updates and events were introduced, enhancing gameplay and adding new features.
Legacy
"Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands" laid the foundation for its sequel, "Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Breakpoint," expanding on the open-world tactical shooter experience with more survival elements and a new storyline.

Overall, pretty good sandbox version of a Clancy game. Overall, if you like the Rainbow Six and Ghost Recon games, you'll probably enjoy this. I do recommend holding out for a killer sale, though. I haven't gotten very far into Narco Road, but it didn't have the "undercover" depth I was hoping for and I noped out after a couple hours. Fallen Ghost DLC is a bit better, in a way like NG+, but you get everything from the vanilla playthrough by default. It has some new OP skills, and some new semi-sci-fi baddies that slightly up the difficulty. Basically, 4 new tangos: 1-shot high-perception snipers, head-shot-only heavy troops, mobile emp jammer guys, and predator wannabes who only show up on thermal. Below are the cons I ran into:

AI teammates are a bit broken in both directions. Too good: sync shots shoot through barriers and can randomly spot a guy 3 stories down in a sealed bunker. Too bad: they will randomly blunder into patrol routes on "don't get spotted" missions even when you told them to stay put in a safe area while you infiltrate. They also will stand by and watch you get gunned down because you didn't have time to give a "fire" command, or open fire and blow up a chain of cars, killing the guy you're supposed to intimidate or the vehicle you're supposed to capture. Whether for challenge, immersion, or just avoiding idiotic mission failures, it's just better to play with real people or get rid of the AI and roll solo.

The gameplay can get a bit dry and repetitive, even moreso than many other sandbox style games. Every area has slightly varied versions of like the same 10 or so missions, with an occasional slight twist . . . like a twist written by a 13-year-old who aspires to be a filmmaker and thinks M. Night Shyamalan is the ONLY director worth studying.

They didn't put much thought into progression in the game as far as weaponry and equipment unlocking. Most of the best equipment is available to equip as soon as you start playing, with a couple slight upgrades or lateral trade-offs unlockable through exploration and mission completion. The best long-range scope? Unlocked by default. All the others have lower magnification and no visible benefit over their default peers. Vision modes transfer automatically to all the scope views, so high magnification is the only real selling point for any of the scopes. For the battle sights, handling is everything, especially once you unlock thermal vision. Damage doesn't matter much really, a handgun bullet or a .50 bmg round both 1-shot an unaware enemy, and alert enemies likewise take similar damage from all rounds. Just equip yourself from the get-go with a good cqc weapon and a semi-auto sniper rifle with the 6x scope (all the others cap at 5x or 5.5x), and occasionally swap the sniper rifle for a lmg for those "hold this position" missions.

I personally hate "realistic shooters" that ignore chambering of their weapons and have generic ammo pools of "Handgun bullets", "Rifle bullets", "Shotgun Shells", "LMG bullets", and "Sniper Rifle Bullets". You can carry X amount of each type, rather than any sort of capacity based on the remainder of your equipment (LBV, pack loadout, etc., they're all just cosmetic). If an operative COULD carry a DMR and an LMG in a functional manner, you better believe he'd select 2 that were chambered in the same round, so he didn't have to tote two kinds of ammo and risk grabbing the wrong one, or being out of one when the situation called for it. The devs also did the annoying thing of having multiple weapons chambered identically dealing drastically different levels of damage. That's not how bullets work. If a 7.62x39mm cartridge is fired from a handgun, a rifle, an lmg, or a pipe and nail boobytrap, the round still does the same level of damage. Only the accuracy, recoil, and round stability vary.

For me, Ghost Recon Wildlands is the best game in the series. It has an interesting story, engaging characters, a rich environment, and most importantly, excellent stealth gameplay. Breakpoint never reached that level of stealth for me due to its futuristic setting with drones and robots, and I didn’t find the story interesting at all.

“Wildlands: Where Ghosts Roam and Legends Are Born”

Welcome to Tom Clancy’s Ghost Recon Wildlands, a game that’s less about being a ghost and more about causing a ruckus that even the dead can’t ignore. This is not just a game; it’s a journey into the heart of Bolivia, a land so beautifully rendered you’ll forget you’re on a mission to dismantle a drug cartel.

The map is a behemoth, a sprawling digital canvas that’s a love letter to geography. You’ve got jungles, mountains, deserts, and salt flats that aren’t just there for show—they dictate your tactical playbook. Want to play hide and seek with the enemy? The foliage is your friend. Prefer to snipe from a distance? Find a desert. And if you’re feeling particularly athletic, the mountains offer a high-altitude workout with a view.

But let’s talk about the vehicles, because in Wildlands, they’re not just transport—they’re an adventure in physics. Cars that handle like they’re on ice, helicopters that demand a PhD in aerodynamics to fly straight—it’s all part of the charm. And by charm, I mean the kind of challenge that makes you question your life choices.

The missions? Oh, they start off as exciting as a new romance, full of promise and adrenaline. But after a while, they settle into a comfortable routine, like a long-term relationship where you finish each other’s… objectives. It’s co-op where Wildlands truly shines, turning repetitive tasks into a party. Because nothing says ‘teamwork’ like accidentally blowing up your buddy with a misplaced grenade.

And the story? It’s a classic Tom Clancy cocktail—part political thriller, part action blockbuster, with a twist of ‘what the heck just happened?’. You’re a Ghost, but this isn’t Casper’s friendly neighbourhood. You’re here to take down El Sueño, a man whose name literally means ‘The Dream’, but the only dreams he’s interested in are the kind that come with a side of narcotics.

In conclusion, Ghost Recon Wildlands is a dramatic, fun-filled romp through a land of beauty and chaos. It’s a game that asks the important questions, like ‘Can I drive this tractor off a cliff?’ and ‘What happens if I shoot that explosive barrel?’. It’s a testament to the spirit of adventure and the enduring appeal of blowing stuff up.


Remember, this review is written with a dramatic flair and should be taken with the spirit of fun it’s intended. Ghost Recon Wildlands has carved its niche in the gaming world with its expansive open world and engaging co-op play. So gear up, Ghosts, and dive into the Wildlands!

Ghost Recon Wildlands is a mostly casual, yet engaging open-world third-person shooter.
The setting of a fictionalized "Bolivia" is pretty much the perfect location for an open-world game set in "a real place". It has more or less every major environment on earth in a non-overwhelming package - anywhere from dense hilly jungles, snowy mountains, desert plains, and even Caribbean-feeling lagoons. Every region feels visually unique.

The campaign taking place in this great environment however, leaves something to be desired.
The premise of a joint CIA-DEA-JSOC operation against a major cartel is an excellent idea, but the execution of said idea is far from perfect.
Almost every single character, friendly or otherwise, is rather unlikable, and the majority of the game's dialogue is absolute cringe. The non-set piece dialogue (random conversations) also get annoying and repetitive very quickly.
Even so, the story isn't all bad and can be quite interesting at times and as long as you can deal with the cringe dialogue you can get some semblance of immersion in the game's world.

But even as poor as a lot of the dialogue and characters are, the gameplay itself is good.
The stealth gameplay and the majority of the game's missions are excellent - though whenever you are in open combat it can quickly fall apart.
The experience is very unique and its hard to put into words that give it adequate credit. It's not without its flaws, but the overall gameplay experience is great, especially if you team up with friends in CO-OP.
Another selling point of the game beyond the pure gameplay is the relatively large customization options and ability to play "tactical dress-up" with your character(s), though just like the rest of the game, it's nowhere near perfect.

I positively recommend this game to anyone who is, for whatever reason, willing to deal with Ubisoft's nonsense.

Ghost Recon: Wildlands is a great third-person shooter. Its open-ended mission design and quick time to kill for players creates a satisfying loop of planning and executing strategies. This thoughtful, consequential gameplay is then further escalated by Wildland’s feature-complete cooperative mode, which allows up to three friends to join you in the chaos.

Every mission in Wildlands can be completed in a variety of ways, with the player being given complete choice in what weapons and vehicles they decide to bring into the fight. This freedom extends to moment-to-moment decision making, letting the player decide if they want to stealth their way through a compound or go in guns-a-blazing. There is a lot of room for creativity in how you tackle objectives, with different types of weapons, gadgets and vehicles providing different benefits that triumph or fail miserably depending on the mission.

Whether you are prepared or not, gunfights in Wildlands are typically very quick encounters thanks to the low time to kill for both players and enemies. This makes head-on engagements on higher difficulties a greater challenge and rewards stealth play more, but also is incredibly satisfying when you manage to brute-force your way through an enemy position. The game also features a permadeath mechanic for the truly hardcore which deletes your save if a squadmate fails to revive you in time. As a life-long MilSim and Arma 3 fan, this mode is one of my favorite parts of the game because it requires the use of strategy and tactics to defeat every encounter.

While Wildlands’ gameplay is outstanding, the narrative is a mixed bag. The premise of being a U.S. special forces member actively working to decapitate a narco state is great, but the execution of the story itself falls flat. There is no character development or intrigue, just cutscene after cutscene of the game trying to convince you how evil your targets are. I didn’t start playing Wildlands because I thought it would have some amazing thriller story, but I was surprised to see how many cinematics were in the game despite the narrative being in the backseat. I was expecting the finale of the campaign to be very satisfying and so I rushed through missions to finish it faster, which I can confirm now was a mistake. Play this game for the gameplay and you cannot go wrong.

The campaign took me close to 40 hours total to complete, and most of those hours were spent playing with a full team of friends. If each member of your team specializes in a specific skill tree, you can have some fun moments where you have a medic player and a drone player and a heavy weapons player, each fulfilling a specific role on the battlefield. There isn’t an explicit class system in the game, but self-imposing rules upon yourself and your team can lead to a lot of fun in Wildlands.

It should also be mentioned that Wildlands is a visually and audibly gorgeous game. There were several times playing with friends that I felt obligated to point out how pretty a view was or how atmospheric the storm that we were flying through felt. The map is ginormous and features a lot of variety, including mountains, salt deserts, swamps, forests, rivers, lakes, large towns, small villages, and open fields. The weapon sound effects are also very punchy and appropriately cinematic, although perhaps not very realistic. The presentation is superb overall.

I fully recommend Wildlands for its excellent cooperative and tactical sandbox gameplay. It goes on sale often for $9.99 which is a bargain and definitely helps to convince a party of friends to buy it along with you. The game requires installing and creating an account for Ubisoft Connect which isn’t preferable, but the experience Wildlands delivers is absolutely worth it.

I am a big fan of Tom Clancy's series since 2000s and I never understood all the critics of this game when it came out. I read some reviews by different famous videogame magazines where authors had been criticizing the game's story, open world and stuff like that. But in my opinion this is one of the best Ghost Recon games ever released. The story here is just as deep, as it has to be for a game about Ghost Recon squad eliminating yet another major threat/target somewhere in the world where they have been sent. And the story has more than enough depth - it has amazing voice acting and some notable characters. Dialogues are written very well too - basically I can say that authors do know how real military talk to each other. I am not part of military myself but I am very much into the topic still. I watch a lot of content related to it, both documentaries and fiction, and play airsoft for couple of years already. So, I think the game recaptures the vibes and the atmosphere just perfect. Another thing I really liked about it, it's the fact that it has very grounded and realistic plot. Cartels with such massive power and influence do exist in real world and they indeed can challenge national governments. For me the events in the game look much more real than, for example, civil war in Mexico in GRAW 1-2. If we talk about open world and respectively the gameplay, it's probably one of the best things we ever had in Ghost Recon series. One of most notable features here is that you can play the whole game in coop - it allows 4 players in total, which is amazing, but even if you will play the game alone you will enjoy hearing interactions between the Kingslayer Team members - Midas, Weaver, Holt and you, Nomad. But I especially enjoyed officer Karen Bowman - she is one of the best characters I've ever seen in military video-games. Talking about gameplay it can be said that while these series always were giving player a lot of freedom to approach mission tasks with different tactics and strategies, here it achieves a brand new level with player having possibility to complete the mission in different ways with different vehicles and different gear. And the gear itself, oh, man, it was so mind-blowing for me to see so many different types of plate carriers, tactical vests, ammo pouches, etc., available in character's customization, as well as weapons attachments and weapons customization! It does not go into simulator category but for AAA game made for mainstream audience all this is just amazing. No to mention that there are even real brands present in the game! I wear 5.11 Tactical myself while on airsoft game or just on daily basis and so I respect this collaboration. To summarize my review, I think that this is an amazing game and is easily one of the best in Ghost Recon series. The artdirection, the soundtrack, the gameplay... Ghost Recon Wildlands nails the atmosphere and delivers an ultimate Ghost Recon experience!

CO-OP / ONLINE PLAY
The biggest question you'll probably have concerning this game is how co-op / online play works. I have good news; it works just fine (in my experience. This MIGHT be different for you).
In the 60 - 70 hours I spent completing the base campaign plus some side content on co-op with 1 other player, my game crashed / broke / disconnected perhaps two to three times total. Each time it was a matter of starting the game up and rejoining, which doesn't take too long.
At times the game will give you notifications about how it cannot synchronize online contacts, preventing you from joining another player's game, but that never lasted than a minute for me. It looks like being in a menu (adjusting your character, gear or looking at the map) prevents others from joining your game. Close the menu, wait for your mate to join and you're good to go.

GAMEPLAY
The game is fun. You can easily sink many hours into it and you can probably replay it on different difficulties. The base difficulty isn't too hard, nor is it too easy. The varying difficulty levels of the zones will ensure you're going to have a tougher time here and there. 
There's a great amount of weapons and customization options for these weapons. It really doesn't matter which gun you pick; every single gun is viable. Hell, you can easily beat the game with the guns you start with. Guns also aren't locked behind levels or progression points; you can jump into a plane, car or heli to travel to any point in the world to grab a gun you want. 
The drones, the rebel support options and the various throwables in your arsenal will allow you to be flexible in every engagement. I know it's commonplace to forego using all items in your arsenal, but the EMP drone is crucial for engaging convoys; the explosive drone is great at taking out holed up enemies; the healing drone will allow you to ressurect your mate from a distance and the various throwables come in handy at all times. The flashbang is particularly useful when you have to clear buildings. 

STORY
The story is alright. It's the least important part of the experience imo. The gunplay, strategizing, travel and collection are the things you'll spend the most time doing. As these are all excellent, you really needn't worry about keeping up with the story.

VEHICLES AND TRAVEL
Get used to flying helicopters, because they're by far the most reliable option in this game. Planes are viable, but less flexible, although better at dodging missiles than helicopters; they don't come with weapons though. Helicopters come with gatling guns, rocket pods, really BIG rockets and some helicopters are gunships that have guns AND rockets. It's kind of unfair how good helis are.
Cars are very hard to control. They have very intense reactions to every input and seem to have a tendency to steer to the right all the time, even without input. They break quite quickly and the cars that come with gatling guns have very narrow fields of view that are horrible in chases. Cars are however very viable for chases where on person leans out of a window. 
Bikes are great if you want to get down a mountain real fast. They're nimble and steer better than cars, but it's going to be bad for your health if you take them into combat.
Boats are useless for the simple reason they are restricted to water. You are better off flying a helicopter. 
Then you have APCs, military vessels and the attack helicopter; these are rare to come across, but wield great firepower. The APC is a bit weak for my taste but the gun shreds. Military boats are few and far inbetween and have the same handicap normal boats have. The attack helicopters is very powerful, but spaws only in very secure UNIDAD bases (and they're not even guaranteed to be there, so it's not a reliable strategy to seek them out.

DIFFICULTY
The last thing I was to touch is difficulty. The difficulty scales with the battle pass thingy. Higher difficulties initially make enemies more spongey (though often still easily killable with headshots), while also making them do more damage. At some point the difficulty starts to make spotting harder. Enemies no longer appear on minimaps as washed out dots that approximately give away their position. From that point onward you either have to start playing a lot more strategically, or consider lowering the difficulty at expanse of earning no more reward. There certainly is a difficulty for every type of gamer; whether you wanna have a chill time or feel like being a sweaty tryhard.
