I would recommend this game with a few caveats:

Be aware that there is no cross-platform service in any way, shape or form. Ubisoft wants you to spend your money on a copy of the game for each platform (which is reasonable, if that's where you're going to play it) and then link these accounts to a central Ubisoft account on the Ghost Recon Network that is largely defunct, but no progression, save files, or unlocks will be shared between systems. As far as I can tell, the credits that you earn to buy loot boxes (yes, it relies heavily on those) are limited to what system you purchase them on. If you buy on Xbox, you won't see your credits (or loot box "rewards") on Steam.

They force you to use their launcher-in-a-launcher to connect with friends and to simply play the game, and it requires mental gymnastics to operate, sync, and make purchases that cause the whole thing to be a giant mess.

It still contains Day One bugs and glitches. This game came out so long ago that it's outlived many people's housepets and they still haven't updated anything that keeps your characters from making splashing noises while walking on stone or "clonk" footsteps as if you're on a catwalk while walking through grass. Your character's voice will simply loop through lines in the Narco Road DLC when you're no longer in the situations that trigger them. A lot of voice lines will be me missing to you as the host of a game while your guests will hear them without trouble. You will be spotted through boulders, trucks, dumpsters, bulldozers, and 100-foot mine shafts, then forced to run 3km until you're no longer "hunted" and can fast travel. Et cetera.

Did I mention loot boxes?

Ghost War and other gameplay modes are required in order to get the really neat cosmetics (mainly through loot boxes) and the daily challenges typically require massive skill, friends to play with, incredible luck, and a lot of slogging in order to get your reward... typically loot boxes.

The game is no longer in development and is, therefore, basically unsupported. The mentality seems to be that "we have other games you can spend your money on; now here's some micro-transactions for in-game currency to buy loot boxes" and that's typically incentive to just not spend more money, in my book.

Your AI companions only operate as a single unit, moving in a "blob" when ordered. There is no fine-tuning anything, so grab some trusted friends for best result. Especially since Holt can stand next to a target without being spotted but you can be half a klick away through dense jungle and behind a bulldozer but that guy on the hill will spot you and rain mortars on your position for the next hour of your life.

The AI is either cheatingly-cunning or completely moronic. Nothing in between.

Have I mentioned loot boxes?

If you can overlook all of this, the shameless cross-promotion of other titles, and the price after it's been out so long and abandoned (grab it on sale), Ghost Recon: Wildlands will find ways to dazzle you with beauty, challenge your tactical skills, thrill you with its action, and leave you itching for the next mission. I sank hundreds of hours into this game on Xbox ONE, having unlocked nearly everything obtainable through progression and purchase (prior to the decision to implement loot boxes) and playing entirely by myself.

Picking it up years later to play with a friend (and then my wife... and another friend... and another...) has been a real treat for us and given us a sense of nostalgia. It has also provided a way to unwind after a rough week and new reasons to swear at one another when someone's fat head gets in the way of a scope, or their poor driving sends the armored SUV off a cliff. Half the fun has become yelling into the microphone in a voice bordering on pure rage/panic/giddy joy as the plan either goes completely to hell or goes off without a hitch.

You can play on intense difficulty levels with complete newbies and all feel like you're elite operators given total operational control thanks to independent difficulty scaling and progression, which is a huge bonus when playing with someone who can't seem to stop shooting the dirt during stealth missions or who doesn't know how to run (looking at you, Barre!). I play on Advanced while my wife (not a shooter fan but loving every moment) plays on Casual and I actually think that I'm holding her back, despite the number of times I've had to pull her out from behind a burning truck (or the number of times she dropped a mortar on the squad). Completing a mission in Solo play doesn't lock it out; you can help a squaddie with their version and still gain the rewards along with them, or continue your own story missions across the map while the rest of the squad tackles other threats and challenges.

The weather effects are wonderful and, combined with time of day, can dramatically affect nearly any mission. Showing up to an Unidad base around noon will see soldiers at the chow hall. In the mornings, they will be crawling from their bunks and ambling about for PT or morning cigarettes. Afternoon will have them more active as they move out on patrol or begin tending to tasks about the base. At night, slip through the gaps in patrols while everyone is asleep to cut the power and leave everyone in the dark, but don't get caught, or the spotlights will blind you and turn you into an easy target! Night operations have become a favorite for my group and we will deliberately putter around with random tasks before nightfall, just to strike in dramatic fashion during a late-night thunderstorm. We are the things that bump in the night... mostly into one another, but the bad guys don't need to know that.

I recognize that the game is aimed at coop, but I don't know anyone who plays it and it has an AI team system so it seemed fair to play it and review on that basis. If you have friends, your experience will differ. That said, I'd have appreciated more reviews of the SP experience, so I'm going to write one.

The SP is not good, mostly because of the friendly AI.

Friendly AI has no respect for walls or physical space whatsoever. It can see & shoot through walls, (but not reliably - meaning that sometimes you get superman and sometimes you get dipshitman) teleport anywhere, and become invisible to enemies. At first I thought I was just not seeing them move and not finding the path they did, but with time I did manage to spot them pop through walls, spot enemies inside windowless buildings, and stand in plain sight without alerting enemies. 

Do not, however, think that this is going to make them overpowered. If you set up the synced shot mode, their aim is always perfect, always 1-shots, and can often hit through walls, but you can only use it every 30(?) seconds with preparation - reminiscent of the assassin trainees in Assassin's Creed. Outside that mode, their aim is atrocious, will never get headshots, and does far less damage than yours even with the same weapons, leading to the 3 of them combined almost never getting more than 1 kill to my 5. I can kill a normal enemy with 3-5 centermass shots from basically any weapon, where I've watched them put dozens of rounds with no effect - especially infuriating when in a vehicle where you can't shoot and have to just let them grind down the enemy with their BB guns. They're also virtually invincible, even without upgrades, taking entire magazines to the chest without bothering to walk behind cover as compared to your extreme squishiness.

All this combines to make them essentially inert in combat, existing solely for the setpieces and to draw fire or revive you if needed. 

A few other nitpicks: 

* The starting guns are more than enough to do the job and can only be upgraded at the expense of increasing sound. If you want a stealth set, your starting sniper rifle/smg combo is the best available, and the attachments are imperceptible changes. It's also entirely capable of handling standup fights, with the sniper 1-shotting most enemies with a chest hit and the smg capable of killing half a dozen enemies in one magazine even suppressed at fairly respectable range. 
* Lots of graphical bugs and memory leaks leading to CTD on long sessions.
* Missions get repetitive, especially when you get the hang of the mechanics. 
* Car physics are weird, like every vehicle has a lift kit from hell.

Gameplay and Tactical Depth:
Wildlands excels in providing players with a deep and tactical gameplay experience. As a member of an elite Ghost Recon team, players are tasked with dismantling the Santa Blanca drug cartel. The game offers a wide range of tactical options, including stealth, long-range sniping, and coordinated team assaults, allowing players to approach missions in their preferred playstyle.

The open-world nature of Wildlands adds a layer of freedom and exploration rarely seen in tactical shooters. Players can navigate the massive and diverse Bolivian landscape on foot, by vehicle, or even by air, uncovering hidden objectives, gathering intel, and engaging in dynamic encounters. The game's attention to detail, including realistic ballistics, weapon customization, and equipment choices, further enhances the tactical depth and authenticity of the gameplay.

Cooperative Multiplayer:
Wildlands shines when played cooperatively with friends. The game supports seamless drop-in, drop-out multiplayer, allowing players to collaborate and tackle missions together. The cooperative gameplay mechanics, such as synchronized takedowns and coordinated squad maneuvers, make for thrilling and rewarding teamwork experiences. Whether it's infiltrating enemy compounds, coordinating synchronized shots, or executing complex strategies, Wildlands offers a dynamic and engaging cooperative multiplayer mode that greatly enhances the game's replayability and enjoyment.

Open-World Environment:
The expansive and detailed open-world environment of Wildlands is a standout feature. The Bolivian landscape is breathtakingly recreated, featuring a diverse range of biomes, from dense jungles to arid deserts and snowy mountains. The world feels alive, with civilian and cartel activities occurring dynamically, providing opportunities for emergent gameplay moments. The attention to detail in the environment design, combined with the day-night cycle, dynamic weather, and realistic lighting, adds to the immersion and authenticity of the game world.

Narrative and Character Development:
While Wildlands' narrative may not be the main focus, it successfully sets the stage for the player's mission in Bolivia. The game's story unfolds through mission briefings, cutscenes, and character interactions. While the plot may not offer groundbreaking storytelling, the character development within the Ghost Recon team adds depth and emotional investment to the experience. Each member of the team has a distinct personality and backstory, creating a sense of camaraderie and attachment as players progress through the game.

Visuals and Audio:
Wildlands boasts impressive visuals, with stunning landscapes, detailed character models, and realistic animations. The game's attention to environmental details, such as flora and fauna, further adds to the immersion. The audio design, including weapon sounds, environmental ambiance, and voice acting, is top-notch and contributes to the overall realism and atmosphere of the game.

Conclusion:
Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon® Wildlands offers a compelling and immersive tactical adventure set in a vast open-world environment. With its deep tactical gameplay, cooperative multiplayer, and attention to detail, the game provides an engaging experience for fans of the tactical shooter genre. While the narrative may not be the game's strongest aspect, the expansive world, realistic mechanics, and cooperative play make Wildlands a standout entry in the Ghost Recon series.

This is an open-world Ubisoft game. If you've seen one, you've seen them all. 

Combat: The combat mechanics in this game could be best described as 'just fine'. The guns lack any real sense of impact and are startlingly accurate at virtually all ranges that are practical to test. When you pair this with overly-generous health even at higher difficulty levels and AI companions that rarely miss, you end up with a fairly boring combat experience that feels far too easy. 

Traversal: In my playtime with this game I was able to experience a variety of the game's methods for traversing the open world and my general impression was that most are poorly implemented. The land vehicles feel as though they're constantly sliding around on ice. Additionally, Ubisoft have demonstrated time-and-again they are spectacularly incapable of implementing aircraft in a way that feels at-all realistic or fun. All of the aircraft show aerodynamic properties roughly akin to those of a firmly chucked brick. To compound the handling difficulties, the companion AI has a supremely hard time pathing to and embarking on player controlled vehicles. This makes the experience of shepherding your trio of moron teammates about the level excruciatingly slow and painful. Further, the friendly AI is seemingly incapable of piloting vehicles by itself and so any action that requires putting an additional person into a 4-seater vehicle results in a team-mate being left behind and simply warping to the player's location. Character movement on-foot feels fine throughout, however. It is just a pity that there's no practical way to traverse the map on foot given its size. 

The Map: The size of the map in Wildlands is its most impressive asset. However, that size isn't necessarily indicative of any particular depth. While visually enjoyable, the environment is largely empty save for the smattering of enemy outposts and bad-guy-pouring-petrol-on-civilians random events that Ubisoft games like to spawn every 2 to 3 metres along the roadside. 

Story: I didn't get very far, obviously. As a result, I will refrain from commenting on this aspect of the game. 

Performance: Game performed fine on my machine. Obviously your experience with this will vary though. For reference, my computer is running a 1080ti, 16GB DDR4 RAM, and an intel i7-8700. Stable 60+ frames at 1080p. 

I see many reviews suggesting that this game is best picked up on sale. As someone who picked this game up on sale, I wouldn't recommend it even then. If you're not absolutely sold on the Ubisoft open-world formula, I would say that you'll have a better time just avoiding this game in general. Go play an actually good Ubisoft game like R6: Siege instead.

While the missions can at times feel repetitive, particularly if you are a completionist who wants to do all the side ops, there is a lot to like about this game.

Gunplay and weapon customization is where this game shines. You begin the game with a handful of weapons and build your arsenal as you explore the map, finding both new weapons as well as modifications. Each weapon has its own unique feel to it in terms of rate of fire, damage, accuracy, range, and so on. As you unlock more modifications and weapons, you get a better sense of what works best for your playstyle and tactics. I frequently found myself playing around with different combinations of guns and oftentimes revisited past favorites after unlocking different modifications. The unique guns that you unlock from defeating the game’s various bosses, as well as the multitude of unique loot box-only guns, provide some nice variety ranging from the subtle and practical to the downright over the top and outlandish.

Combat in this game feels rewarding, whether you opt to play aggressive or stealth. The variety of weapons in this game easily caters to both playstyles. By the time I reached level 30, the max character skill level, I felt like a one-man army. Once I opted into the tier mode, unlockable at level 30, I quickly felt less unstoppable. Tier mode is how the player unlocks additional cosmetics and the premium currency to buy loot boxes. As the player's tier increases, the difficulty level required to keep earning unlockables and premium currency increases, eventually requiring the player to play on extreme difficulty. At the hardest difficulty, the player is usually eviscerated by enemies almost immediately if not being careful. Enemies likewise only appear on the player’s minimap once they have been tagged. This increase in difficulty felt like a great counterpart to the more powerful skills and guns that the player has access to in the late game. 

Players will immediately notice when starting this game is the sheer enormity of the map. The map in Wildlands is huge and diverse, leading players through mountains, salt flats, jungles, swamps, and everything in between. The ability to visit any section of the map at any time and complete its missions helps create a more cohesive experience. Each portion of the map also includes plenty of collectibles scattered throughout in the form of guns, gun modifications, and pieces of lore. Each map section also includes its own set of missions and rebel ops.

The size of the map does come with a drawback, however. While the terrain is varied and diverse, the rebel ops are unfortunately not. These ops constitute the game’s side missions and are mostly optional. That said, completing the rebel ops is the only way to level up the rebel skills, which come in very handy, particularly in the harder difficulties. This leaves the player completing the same five mission types over and over again, just in different locations. While completing these missions can be rewarding in leveling up the different rebel skills, this still means that the player has to do the same mission nine times for each of the five skills in order to max them out. It almost felt like there just wasn’t enough content to pad out the size of the map.

The story of the game is simple and the cutscenes are rather limited. The country of Bolivia has been taken over by a cartel, which is now exerting power across all levels of government and it is up to the CIA and the Ghosts to save Bolivia. If you’re familiar with history, you might be aware of the fact that the United States has a complicated relationship with South America, particularly as it applies to military adventurism and destabilizing governments. This makes the entire plot seem almost farcical in this regard. I do recognize that the story is a work of fiction, but I do think the story missed an opportunity to address the elephant in the room and demonstrate the nuances to America’s relationship with South America. 

Overall, the game is extremely enjoyable. I bought it when it was on sale, and honestly feel like I still would have gotten my money’s worth had I purchased it at full price. Playing it solo was a lot of fun, and I can only imagine that it is even more fun with friends. Although the gameplay can feel repetitive at times there is enough content to allow the player to explore a variety of different play styles and tactics, helping keep the game fresh and exciting. I would definitely pick this game up if you are a veteran of the Far Cry and Just Cause series.

This is a great shooter for the solo player as well as a group of friends. I'd go so far as to say it might be one of the best.

This is a third-person shooter with the ability to aim down the sights while aiming your gun. It is not a looter shooter, so no need to worry about weapon damage beyond some guns being realistically more powerful than others, and every headshot will be a one-hit kill. You can find weapons and weapon parts in the field, increasing your lethality, and you can modify your wardrobe to make your character unique to you, adding to the enjoyment.

The premise is simple, yet effective: dismantle a cartel piece by piece , taking out key figures and flushing out the big players, working your way up to the jefe himself, El Sueno. The game literally drops you into the middle of the map with a story mission that'll guide you along the route you'll take for the rest of the game: gain intel of the current province of Bolivia, dismantle key infrastructure of the cartel, flush out the member responsible for overseeing the province, and eliminate them. It's a fun concept, and while simple, it constantly gives you different missions based on the target, with rich story elements mixed in. You feel like you're taking down the cartel piece by piece, not just some grunt told to go here and kill this dude or shoot that place up. It's wonderfully pulled off, and for those that enjoy story in their game, you'll love it.

With friends, the tactics available to you grow, and you'll find many missions become much easier with creative thinking or superb coordination. Added on the fact that you'll frequently have laughs at mishaps and the accidental friendly-fire, and you'll see enjoyment from this game much more than solo.

I purchased this product for ~$10 during the Steam Winter Sale.

Would I buy it again? For $10 yes, for $50 NO.
____________________________________________________________________
The story:
This is basically Far Cry 4. The story is forgettable, but you aren't playing for the story, you are playing for the experience. Certain aspects of the game are fun but you definitely don't feel like you accomplished anything. 

It is much less refined than Far Cry. Example: enemies and friendlies will not fight each other unless you "make" them - they will drive right past each other and not bat an eye. There is one mission where your handler is captured. If you click on any other mission she calls you and gives you a run down for the other mission - it's just weird. You can't actually capture regions or bases, enemies just respawn. Enemies never stop coming - I killed HUNDREDS of enemies at a military base that all walked at me in a semi file line. The list goes on.

My specs:
2080 Super
i7-9700k @ 3.6
32GB DDR4 Ram
Raid0 Storage
____________________________________________________________________
Difficulty Settings: Advanced (2nd highest)
Graphics Settings: Very high (highest settings), locked on 75fps. I had an issue where the game was stuttering but the GPU/CPU usage was around 70% and temps were just fine. The only thing that fixed it permanently is by locking the frames. The graphics look great on the highest visual settings.

____________________________________________________________________
The bad:
-After playing the game for 10 hours, you've pretty much seen all that the game has to offer. A large proportion of missions are the exact same mission, just re-skinned and in a different location. Examples: go here and extract HVT, go here and destroy X, go here and kill X, go here and defend X for 5 minutes. A few of the missions are stealth based - "go here and get the intel without being detected" - these are the worst part about the game.
-Enemies can smell you fart down wind from 3kms away. Playing missions during the game day time is not do-able sometimes. There are a few missions that I ended up playing 10 times because helicopters would spawn (with no alarm or call outs) and not leave the mission area, leading to me being spotted while under a bush 400m away. This was with a gillie suit and sometimes tactical camouflage (that makes you nearly invisible). No, helicopters do not have heat vision. 
-The story is forgettable and terrible. I finished the game yesterday and don't remember any enemy figure except Sueno. Finish-able in 30 hours.
-This game is regularly priced at $50... It is not worth $50.
-Enemies are easy to kill while you are stealthing, typically one hit kills anywhere in the body. They turn in to the terminator after you are spotted. Laser bullets and 5-10 rounds to kill.
-This has the old style spotting system where if one enemy sees you the entire complex knows EXACTLY where you are instantly. Even if you move 100s of meters away without being spotted. There are much more fair and realistic ways to implement a spotting system... and Ubisoft has already implemented these systems in other games.
-Cars handle great for a Ubisoft game. Which is good. Because you are going to be driving a lot.
-Still weird bugs. My character couldn't pull a gun out a few times requiring a reset, the drone would very typically glitch and not deploy until resetting, enemies can shoot through objects that you can't shoot through (bullet proof glass and no, the glass wouldn't break), I soft locked the game once, and the game crashed 3 or 4 times during one mission. Guns would float, enemies would spawn a few hundred meters away directly in front of you, enemies would fall through the map (you could see them falling under the map if you tagged them), enemies will see you through hard walls for 300m+ away.
-There are still areas that drop frames like crazy. I have no idea why. It seems to be explosions.
-The RNG makes this game crazy. Sometimes defending a location is hilariously easy (10 enemies or less), sometimes impossibly difficult (2 helicopters and 50+ enemies). This happened on the exact same mission that I failed when it spawned 50+ enemies. The enemies just didn't spawn the second time?

The good:
-Tons of content. Not much of it good - but wow there is a lot to do.
-Map is large and beautiful.
-The online co-op system is interesting if you can find someone to play with.
-The game breaking bugs that did exist in this game are mostly solved.
-Tons of guns and gun modifications.
-Some of the tech is really interesting. Active camo, the different drone modes, etc.

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands is a PvE spectacular 3rd person shooter. It is framed in enough realism echoing the US war on drugs in South America as well as beautifully crafted environments to hold up even five years later. Though not without its faults, the core gameplay experience and empowerment fantasy sees the player take on the fictitious Santa Blanca drug cartel and Unidad military forces as they assume the role of the "quiet professionals" - the Ghosts. 

As a single player, narrative experience, the game has stretches of great immersion. Supported by three AI team mates the superiority of the Ghosts is obvious as the player uses high-tech gadgetry such as a deployable reconnaissance drone, night and thermal vision modes, as well as a host of upgrades to ensure tactical superiority. A quick-select scroll menu allows for limited commands to be given to the AI teammates - though not individually - and a 'sync shot' ability allows players to eliminate up to four targets simultaneously which is a tremendous help in stealth operations. 

The open world experience spanning a good chunk of Ubisoft's necessarily scaled-down vision of Bolivia is large enough to feel expansive, whilst dense enough to feel engaging. In addition to main story quests divided into strings of missions across distinct, yet seamless zones, side missions, random encounters, targets of opportunity, and loot opportunities give the player plenty to do for over 100 hours of gameplay.

The gunplay central to the experience can be very satisfying, particularly for players with previous experience in snap-aim, and confident FPS/TPS skills. Certain features of the gunplay such as penetration of rounds through different materials makes for some interesting tactical options, as well as a welcome nod to realism, though falling well short of true realism. (Certain bushes can stop .50BMG rounds from anti-materiel rifles, for example)

Vehicles are also a well-fleshed out part of Wildlands, with a myriad of vehicles available to the players as unlocks, provided by friendly, rebel forces, commandeered at gunpoint from civilians (lo siento, senor), or 'appropriated' from enemies. These include cars, trucks, APCs, helicopters, and even gunships. If your dream was to strafe bad guys from a Blackhawk with a door-mounted M134 minigun, good news! Wildlands may be right for you.

A range of missions and objectives will keep the gameplay engaging and force the player to hone both stealth skills as well as run-and-gun skills - particularly in the case of Unidad or base assaults where prolonged engagements will draw increasingly more hostile forces over time. Get in, get out, get on with life - linger and die, is the mantra. 

As a multiplayer experience, the gameplay is quite different. Rather than three AI team mates, the game adjusts to 2-4 player co-op, but makes no accommodation for the tactical handicap of having fewer team mates in the 2-3 player experience. A slight desync between players and Ubisoft's servers can have a profound affect on accuracy and timing, but in the lower difficulties this will rarely be an issue. 

The players and the narrative are helped along by CIA handler and no-nonsense bad ass, Karen Bowman (not that kind of Karen). Bowman is the all-American, all-jeans, all-business woman coordinating the downfall of the Santa Blanca cartel behind the scenes whilst the player is the hands-on operator. This interplay, helped by radio traffic and cinematic cutscenes including video montages for exposition, helps ground the open-world experience and provides direction. She won't micro-manage players interested in a sandbox experience, but she will align on-the-ground objectives with the narrative arc when necessary. As a link between the player and the action on the screen, Bowman was very well implemented, and her jaded sense of humor feels on-point for a hardcore CIA handler. 

There are a host of problems ranging from mildly annoying to rage-quit levels of frustration, but if you steer clear of Ghost mode and Tier mode, this remediates the harsher edges of these problems in most cases. 
What follows is a list of some of the gameplay issues that, to my mind, break immersion and/or negatively effect game enjoyment. Your mileage may vary.

* Civilian AI reacts to gunfire (and strange ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with guns in their presence) but their behavior does not tip-off enemies, not do they flee combat zones. This is particularly true for civilians on roads and/or in vehicles.

* Additional enemy spawns tend to be too close, appearing in the most heinous of cases in areas cleared by the player moments before. In urban warfare, that is usually immediately lethal. 

* Enemy AI accuracy and target acquisition are unrealistic in the extreme, and despite claims made by Ubisoft that lighting conditions and foliage aid cover, only hard cover seems to work correctly. On higher difficulty, expect gangbangers brandishing twin machine pistols to snap snipe you from 100 meters away, from a moving vehicle, at night, with no problems.

* Enemies can and do respond to being fired at - for example running for cover if you miss - but once intent on the player's demise, they will shrug off suppressive fire from a 7.62 machine gun, or near misses with a .50BMG rifle, and rush you. Some enemies will also collect body and even head hits(!) without it so much as disrupting their aim. 

* Aggro is strongly prioritized to the player to the extent that an enemy can be surrounded by all three AI players at close range and it will still try to shoot the player, in cover, at rifle ranges of 200m+ instead, even if they were previously unaware of the player. 

* The player cannot jump, and the climbing mechanic is not great. 

* Interaction with objects is finicky. This can sometimes from preventing the player from getting in a vehicle. 

* Player-spawned vehicles can spawn quite far away, as well as in places where they are inaccessible, or will self-destruct (particularly true for helicopters)

* For players looking to snipe, the render distance and load distance limitations means getting closer to your intended targets first before backing away and shooting at highly pixelated environments where the target used to be and hoping they didn't move. (Generally the render distance cut off is around 500-550 meters and the load distance closer still)

* Enemy AI is a hive AI. If one enemy knows where you are, they all do, always. This includes enemies firing non-line-of-sight 80mm mortar rounds, which is a problem. Similarly, if enemies are pinned and can't reach your position, they will call for patrols who will unerringly know your location. 

* Friendly AI is too basic and cannot adequately cover the player's flanks or rear. Even when told to move to a specific location, and told to engage the enemy, they will allow certain enemies to penetrate their fields of fire as they seek out the player (due to the aforementioned aggro issue).

* Although sci-fi, digital active camouflage exists in the game as an unlockable item, this does nothing to stop the player from being spotted. 

* Guns are generally modeled on real-world small arms, but do not necessarily behave as expected. 

Ubisoft has since moved on to the next installments in this franchise, but the collaborative effort between Ubisoft development studios across Europe makes this one stand out as one of their better efforts.

[h1][b]Introduction[/b][/h1]
The last time I played the first installment of the Ghost Recon series was over a decade ago, so coming back to its successor felt naturally exciting. The differences between Wildlands and the original are vast. Thanks to that, I enjoy exploring the game more than I could ever hope for. This review will surely give you heaps of insight into the game, without a single spoiler.

[h2]Summary[/h2]
Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon® Wildlands (GRW) is a PvE-focused military tactical FPS, where you assume the role of special forces operators, known as Ghosts, in a reactive and immense recreation of Bolivia to take down the savage drug organization known as the Santa Blanca Cartel.

[table]
[tr]
	[th]😇Wins[/th]
	[th]💀Sins[/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
	[td]- Massive playable areas.
- Diverse, detailed, and beautiful ecosystems with realistic weather conditions and day/night cycle.
- Lifelike NPCs with schedules and practical actions.
- Fully customizable Ghosts Squad.
- Military role-playing.
- Well-assorted weaponry and satisfying gunplay.
- Sandbox gameplay.
- Limitless replay value.
- Playable without internet connection.
- Accessible to casual, hardcore, and immersion-oriented players.
- Seamless (for the most part) and unrestricted co-op experience. [/td]
	[td]- Unmemorable, no-stakes story.
- Repetitive and predictable mission objectives.
- Inactive PvP.
- Seldomly unresponsive AI teammates.
- The lack of tactical elements like camouflage, corpses interaction, disguise.[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

[h1][b]In-depth Analysis[/b][/h1]
[h2]How Open World Should Be[/h2]
GRW features 21 provinces inside eleven highly detailed and realistic ecosystems, making each visit to these areas feel like a whole new experience. From shallow swamps, open green lands, elevated forest valleys, lakes, waterfalls to snowy mountains. With the character creation available at any time, you can customize your whole squad - composed of Nomad (your playable Ghost leader), Midas, Holt, and Weaver (your AI teammates) - to alternate their appearances and fade into nature’s background. While most locations and the geography of the world are purely fictitious, a few recreated landscapes are based on their real-life counterparts, like the terrifyingly accurate Death Road, or the beautiful shallow salt lake Red Lagoon, and many more for you to explore. 

Although made up, all other locations still feel believable enough to be indistinguishable from real life, with NPC civilians all having proper interactions with each other and the environments, like celebrating in costumes, playing football, or simply swiping the floor. Watching them react is fun and intriguing, which is something I rarely enjoy in any other games. Sincerely, I think this fictional version of Bolivia has become my new standard of how an open-world game should be. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2702247587
[h2]Choose How to Operate[/h2]
Since the world is reactive with weather conditions, day/night cycle, along with enemies and civilians acting accordingly to their set daily routines, you too can choose how to handle them and use the environments to your advantage. Almost all cartel thugs, even the Unidad - dirty government soldiers - sleep and eat at night (except during special operations), making them vulnerable to a stealthy operator. During nights, enemies are harder to see, and so are you. It'd be wise to scout out the whole area using a binocular or a drone. With night-vision goggles equipped, you'll be the unseen ghost, silently striking enemies' bases when they are at their weakest. And operating in the dark during a thunderstorm or mist? That’s when the immersion hits through the roof!

Or perhaps you’re just a casual player who wants to shoot bad guys and blow things up to have fun? Then, go loud, spray and pray with LMGs in broad daylight, when you can see everyone and become the spotlight for all guns pointing at you. 

Be warned though, as carelessly acting like that is not favorable in higher difficulties like Extreme, aka simulation mode. And for any hardcore, [strike]masochistic[/strike] players or Ghost Recon old-timers out there, Ghost Mode with permadeath is awaiting to challenge you. Always planning, strategically maneuvering, paying attention to your surroundings, and being precise with your bullets are the keys to enjoying GRW. Playing on Ghost Mode, Tier One (increase the challenge, earn exclusive rewards) with Extreme Difficulty, and limited HUD (Minimap, Ammo, and Items shown only) brings me back to the punishing experience of the original game. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2702252676
[h2]Wide Variety of Guns to Choose and Love[/h2]
GRW provides you with over a hundred firearms, with the option to carry one primary, one secondary, and one handgun, so choosing your favorite can be tough. Each gun is made distinct, not only on the model but also in the sound, both suppressed and unsuppressed. Bullet drop, recoil pattern, penetration power, and attachments contribute to that factor, too.

Gunplay is easy to learn for the most part, but hard to master if you, like me, prefer to use sniper rifles and attack from afar. Sniping over 500 meters and watching the enemies confusingly running and hiding behind cover is amusing, as they are clueless to find you since the gunshot source is too far away from them to know where to look. But if you shoot loudly about 150m close to them, they will hear, react to your shot and try to run towards the sound, so don’t camp and be on your toes.

That being said, sometimes they can magically spawn a vehicle to pursue you if you are too far away even though logically, they shouldn't know where you are, which ruins the immersion. Oddly, corpses disappear way too quickly, in under 30 seconds. The fact that you can't carry them around to hide or dump in a trash can [spoiler]where they belong to[/spoiler] feels unpolished and lackluster in a AAA tactical shooter like GRW.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2702271902
[h2]Jolly Cooperation[/h2]
GRW allows you to co-op with your friends or resort to public matchmaking to find randoms, so you can role-play together or have some dumbass ruin your plan by not communicating and exposing your position. The best thing about the co-op is that no matter where you and your friends are, all players’ progress contributes to each other. This means you can operate on one side of the map, while another player is at an airport over 15km away, to steal a resource plane and fly to the finish point. All of the players in the match will receive the same rewards.

This review is a few years late, the game came out in 2017, but this is still one of my absolute favourite games of the modern era. It was a real sleeper. This is a game I can always pick up and just enjoy. I put hundreds of hours into this game on Xbox and I would absolutely still recommend this for anyone looking for an open world tactical shooter than can be laid back and casual, guns blazing crazy (sort of), or a stealthy challenge. Loads of different environments and a ton of different tactics.

[h1]Campaign[/h1]
The solo campaign is awesome. It'd recommend playing with a friend. The story is interesting, but the real magic is the map is truly open world. You can go anywhere and do anything, in any order you please. I don't normally find that to be particularly interesting, but most games aren't truly open world. They block off certain sections of the game until you've reached a certain level or completed a certain amount of the game to "unlock" it. 

I had a lot of fun exploring the map, looking for weapons, attachments, and collectables. There is enough of the main campaign to keep you busy for a while, but not so much that it gets tedious or repetitive. Each mission is unique in some what and you will end up using all of your skills to complete them. 

I don't recall any major difficulty spikes or boring stretches. The game maintains a consistent balance throughout the campaign. I think what makes this work so well is the progression system. You don't necessarily level up your character, but you unlock new skills and abilities, you upgrade your weapons, and find more powerful weapons as you explore. The skills, abilities, and upgrades make combat easier, but they aren't totally necessary. You can start a fresh game and travel to the most difficult province and still hold your own. It's a challenge but absolutely possible.

The gameplay mechanics are great. The mechanics and controls will take some getting used to, especially if you're coming from CoD or Battlefield, but once you do they become second nature. At no point did I get frustrated with any of the movement mechanics and or anything like that. It's just that fluid and natural. I will say, however, that they're not the best for outright combat. It's easy to get scrambled and panic a bit if you're under a lot of fire, but that is kind of the point. This game doesn't lean too much on the stealth aspect but more-so than outright action.

[h1]Ghost War[/h1]
The real joy here though is the Ghost War PvP. This has to be the most complete and balanced PvP experience I've ever seen in a video game. It's not even close. All in all I think the combination of features really made this a good experience. With a focus on cooperation, communication, and teamwork, this had the extra benefit of keeping toxic players out. I never had a bad experience with other players online. To this day, the only game I'll play where I'm happy to be in the game chat. I've met some really great people online that were a blast to play with.

Each class comes with a limited set of available weapons and a static set of gear. They screwed this up big time in Breakpoint by allowing classes to use whichever weapons they wanted. Each fills a certain role and each has a special ability which is uniquely advantageous. There isn't really any class that's truly OP and each takes some practice to be truly effective. At the start of each round, you don't know which classes your opponents have chosen until they've been spotted or killed. Half the fun is picking a class to both complement your teammates and to counter the opponents.

The normal games are 4 vs 4 and best of 3 rounds. There's a few game modes, uplink, elimination, extraction, and sabotage. Uplink is easily my favourite. There's no radar and you don't know where your opponents are until they're spotted. You can really play some mind games with your opponents and catch them off guard, especially if you have good communication with your teammates. 

It's too bad this game kind of fell under the radar. There was no Ghost War at launch and maybe that hurt the game's reach. I haven't tried to play on PC recently but I'm expecting the population to be low. I wish Ubisoft would update this game for 2022 with some new content and basically re-release it as it is to spur the player population.

[spoiler]Thinking of the core mechanic of being a special ops team infiltrating and disrupting a cartel's operations along with a corrupt military force and just ruining their day by destroying their camps. This all works well within the game and outside of missions the missteps that lead to pulling you out of stealth and making your day more difficult is most of the time your own fault. So props on creating this part of the game, and playing the game on the easier difficulties, and perhaps even Advanced, most parts of the game can be an enjoyable experience solo. However playing in Tier One Mode which eventually leads to playing on Extreme, doing this solo is no bueno. I believe most of my grievances with this game is because I enjoy the stealth and strategy part of the game so much that all the flaws revolving around them, ruining my experience, just makes me so disappointed and frustrated.

The game becomes extremely punishing, no pun intended, and in the end I think the only remedy is playing with a full group of competent players, perhaps not even that. Doing it solo really highlights how completely useless the AI really is.

Enemy AI has you at the top of their priority list at all times, and they have a hivemind. If you are in a big battle with your team and about 20 rebels that have all been noticed by the cartel and / or Unidad, enemies will still always choose to shoot at you the second they've seen you. The effect of this is that most Radio Station missions you are barely allowed to participate in, either with full team skill points you will end up on the ground 3 times and wait 10-30 seconds each time before you get to play again. And friendly AI DOES NOT clear the area before you are revived so you will be surrounded and have to deal with them all by yourself which often ends up with you on the ground again and have to wait for the AI to help you up again, which by the way, they don't always do even when standing right next to you (Happens very rarely so, not a big point).

There are several missions that are completely overtuned for Extreme difficulty;

Sam Fisher, immediately surrounded and automatically engaged, the event lasts for what at least feels like 5 minutes with continuous air support and reinforcements pouring in, stuck in a building with 5 different entry points, second part you are still chased.

El Pulpo is BARELY doable, either there is a certain distance you need to keep from him in the last part or you just have to be lucky as af.

El Muro, the traditional thing you adopt doing solo extreme is going completely gungho with a helicopter and it ends up alright because the AI doesn't manage to find you in time.

The finaly mission in the story, not gonna spoil anything, but to keep it short, too many enemies, too much vehicle damage despite fully skilled, not enough replacement vehicles, basically only doable in Extreme in one way.


One of the biggest frustrations in this game is Ubisoft's choice of drop off for air vehicles, they incessantly choose the drop off point to be the worst one in the game for about 6 or 7 side missions, despite it sometimes being 9 km away, that really made me irritated.
During Extreme it often felt like Ubisoft themselves were watching and found new ways to mess with me. Sometimes when requesting land vehicles they would spawn on higher ground, roll off, and end up upside down. Rebel Ops to tag enemies sometimes don't get all tags within their zone so enemies catch you off guard when there SHOULDN'T be anyone there. Unidad forever watching and just sticking their nose in EVERYTHING you do, one of the most tedious things easily.
The AI team are so unreliable often times I wished they weren't there, sometimes the most they did was add commentary that was just unsavory in my time of frustration, they bring nothing to the immersion or story, I don't care about who any of these people are. Better way to do it would be the option of hiring your own team members using resources to replace them with teammates with better stats that actually become useful the more you play.[/spoiler]

Sort of meh moments:

[spoiler]In my initial review I talked about driving and flying and different control aspects and other minute issues, if you are an adaptive gamer a lot of this can be overlooked and you can get used to it. But a simple comparison, GTA V came out in 2013, 4 years prior, the driving there is 100x better, and if you try to go off-road in Wildlands, most often you are gonna have a bad time.[/spoiler]

Some of the positives:

In spite of all these frustrations, the game clearly does offer a lot of content for someone like me that likes to do things 100%, a lot of the content is repeated however when it comes to side missions but hey, that happens sometimes.

Shooting and sneaking for the most part feels good, sometimes enemies become bullet dodgers and in Extreme that gets really annoying, despite that not many issues there.

Playing through the game you do get a lot of weapon and customization options, however, some weapons are so clearly better than others it might not matter, but it does let you and your team (of actual people) assign yourselves roles with different loadouts which makes for a cooler and more immersive and inclusive experience, and you can unlock all of these in any order you like, either if you like to progress naturally through weapons or if you want to get your optimal setup immediately. Player Agency, I love it.

The map is gorgeous and versatile, many different biomes that seem to meld together at points, some very cool landmarks, the AI while patrolling seem to greet each other and talk about random things, makes for a really nice and feeling alive touch, much of the world has something going on, randomly spawned resource "missions" on the side of the road or in the hills, good choice by the developer. Speaking of visuals however, there is an interesting choice in loading in assets that make them sort of grow out of the ground, its OK in a huge forest but when looking at a metal fence about 20 meters away it's quite jarring.

In summary, here are recommendations on how to set yourself up for a good experience:

Looking for fun: Play on the easier difficulites, bring friends, mess around with the world.

Looking for a challenge, but something still good: Play Advanced and go into Tier One Mode eventually and see Extreme that way, set you and your team up with different loadouts to complement each other and strategize, very giving way to play this game.

Looking for torture, stressing yourself out, and ripping your hair out: Play Extreme difficulty solo.

Score if picking choice 2: 7/10
Score if picking choice 3: 2/10

I still choose not to recommend this game because of a lot of the choices made here, I will however as mentioned recommend option 2, set yourself up for success unlike me.

And a few words to the developer:
Ubisoft, please polish, the world is great, but the minimap deals with unreliable information (use vision cones on enemies, have indicators for if something is above or below you), and add better footsteps sounds for enemies, just these three changes would have a massive positive effect on playing the higher difficulties, look into how things play and feel in every setting (Extreme Solo is imbalanced and needs tuning, especially in Sam Fisher's mission.)

It's like Metal Gear Solid 5 if it were painfully mediocre, had an even more insane amount of content, annoying microtransactions, and co-op. All in all a win, despite all that. What can I say, I like repetitive virtual murder.

To be real, the biggest highlight of this one is probably the absolutely gorgeous open world. Insane biome variety, hella good looking, got some mad pretty erosion ♥♥♥♥ going on in the hills - you know what it is.

Makes you think that if Ubisoft made games as fun as they made worlds pretty there'd be no stopping them.

Ubisoft™ has a massive hard-on for a lot of things. But you will notice that those things are usually either open-world games or anything they can slap a Tom Clancy™ logo on.

Tom Clancy's™ Ghost Recon: Wildlands™ is your standard fare Ubisoft™ Open World Third-Person Military Espionage Stealth Action Shooter game set in an exotic backdrop where you, an operative with years and years of experience, are deployed to do some hardcore balls-to-the-wall "operators operating operationally" type of missions.

Now that sounds pretty fudmuckering exciting. And it bloody well is, for the first few hours of the game.

As you go on and learn the mechanics, the lay of the land and how you fit in, the story unfolds before you.

I won't talk much about the story but if you've ever watched any kind of spy / war / drug war films or at least played Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell™ series, you'll pretty much know what I mean. (EXCEPT THE STEALTH OPTIONS ARE MINIMAL)

You got two primary weapons, a sidearm, a drone and 3 AI companions that you can dress up use as meat shields. You can change their gender too if that's something you were looking to do. You could now be the military equivalent of the Spice Girls™ if you really wanted to. But clothing options are limited to mostly military themed stuff.

Personally, I put everyone in Ghillie Suits because it looks ridiculous but at the same time it also looks kinda cool as you stalk the forested areas, picking off targets one by one with a suppressed sniper rifle.

The gunplay mechanics feel a lot like they do in Tom Clancy's: The Division™ and Tom Clancy's: The Division 2™

Except you won't generally run into too many bullet sponge-esque enemies early in the game. Those come around later when you start fighting targets that are a bit more armored. 

The animations feel a little dated but they still look good and the addition of a photomode makes it so that you can take pictures of your operator operating operationally for whatever reason. 

Co-op is of course fun with friends because you're all trying to get to a unified goal and the journey getting there is pretty fun. Doing it with randoms is a mixed bag and your mileage may vary.

There is a lot to do in the game and sometimes it might feel like a chore but I really liked how most of the things you do will always contribute to the overall scheme of things.

Intimidate that thug? The word gets to his boss that he's a ♥♥♥♥♥-ass culero and he has to get his ♥♥♥♥ shot off.

Steal a helicopter full of drugs, guns and other miscellaneous supplies? The underboss gets his ass spanked with a nail board. Presumably.

It all adds up until the boss of the bosses of that area comes out and you get to ruin his day by either killing or capturing his ass. Results may vary.

You should give this game a shot but only under three conditions.

1. It has to be on sale.
2. You can afford like 2 McChickens™ cause that's usually the cost.
3. You are willing to spend for the cost of said McChickens™ to get the game.

If you wanted a numerical rating cause that's the sort of thing you are in to (I'm not kink shaming you.)

I would rate this game at an 8/10. As you can see from my playtime, I got to about 50-ish hours of play from what amounts to literally McChicken™ money.

Sure, I could have gotten a literal McChicken™ instead but eating that same thing for 50 hours compared to playing this game for an accumulated 50 hours, you kinda get which one I'd rather be doing.

You get pretty damn OP by the end, but it all feels earned, and you're never bulletproof -- you gotta use cover, concealment, and an advantageous position.  Taking the time to plan your first strike on a base is important.

However, that is not the point of this title. Indeed, it shines especially in cooperation mode, taking you - you and up to 3 of your comrades - on an adventure in a giant sandbox.
The map is huge, quite vertical, offering many splendid & varied landscapes, vehicles of all kinds, and both vertical and horizontal gameplay.

Behind this superb appearance dear to Ubisoft, there are still some shortcomings. The gameplay is fun, adaptable and precise, yet it is often heavy, choppy and little polished. Driving is rough, and the title's PC optimization leaves a lot to be desired at times.

The servers are however stable; the customization of skill trees, of the character and his arsenal is quite extensive; and the lifespan of the game is quite substantial (long main quest, and a lot of side missions - despite a few repetitions in the latter: the worst example being the outposts, with their spawns and absolutely identical positionings ...). The wide choice of difficulties is also a nice plus, with the last selectable level which will give you a lot of trouble.

TLDR: This game is absolutely correct, fun and long. I would advise however, because of its few flaws, to buy it during sales in its' gold edition. It still remains way more enjoyable than its' successor ...
=> 14-15 / 20.

This game saved my life.

I am 31.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.

After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.

Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.
After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.

Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends.

I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together.

Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Mary Berry's Banoffee Pie:
Ingredients

For the base

150g/5½ oz digestive biscuits (about 10)
75g/2¾oz butter
For the toffee filling
75g/2¾oz butter
75g/2¾oz light muscovado sugar
1 x 397g/14oz full-fat condensed milk (see tip)
1 tsp vanilla extract
For the topping
300ml/10fl oz double cream
3 small just-ripe bananas, sliced
50g/1¾oz dark chocolate, melted or cocoa powder

Method

Line the base of a deep 20cm/8in spring form tin with baking paper.

To make the base, crush the biscuits to fine crumbs and melt the butter over a low heat. Pour into a bowl and mix to combine. Spoon into the base of the tin and press down with the back of a spoon until level. Place in the fridge for 15 minutes.

To make the filling, heat the butter and sugar in a small non-stick saucepan and stir over a low heat until combined. Add the condensed milk and bring to the boil, stirring for 2–3 minutes – do not over-boil or it will become grainy and fudge-like. Add the vanilla and pour into the tin. Place in the fridge for at least 1 hour.

Whip the cream in a bowl until soft peaks form.

Arrange the banana slices in neat rounds on top of the toffee. Spoon or pipe the cream on top and level. Set in the fridge for an hour.

Remove from the tin, and zig zag the melted chocolate over the top or dust with cocoa powder.

The game play is good overall. It feels like they took the Farcry game and modded it to make it work in the Ghost Recon world. I like Farcry a lot so I'm happy with this. You get the same special abilities like "guns for hire", as well as a few others, like a mortar strike, or summoning a helicopter or armored vehicle. There are a lot of guns and gun mods to unlock. Lots of collectibles of all sorts. There is a big map to explore with distinct zones. Most of it is empty of course, but nice to look at. They offer a good selection cosmetic customizations to make your character look cool. 

You can even dress up your AI teammates, which is a nice touch, although you cannot give them specific guns. This doesn't really matter though because they either 1 shot everything anyway or just stand there in the open like idiots, not shooting anything at all. AI teammates are a bit brain dead. The developers were self aware about how poorly they coded the AI teammates so they made them (mostly) invisible to enemies. You'll often see a teammates standing right in front of enemies, both acting completely oblivious to each other.

The story is a bit cringe. Basic plot: American patriots using enhanced interrogation on cartels. There is a lot of pro American propaganda, e.g. that the war on drugs is moral and justified, and winnable by only 4 federal agents.

There is also an in game store that sells weapons etc via loot boxes. This is a completely ridiculous money grab on a full priced game. Shameless capitalism and money grubbing on display. That said, they do provide an in game way to earn points to purchase loot boxes, although in reality you get very few points and the system is designed as a gateway drug to get you into the store and to manipulate you into buying stuff. Very sinister. 

Also you have to be logged in to do the solo campaign. This is really stupid. It's also inconvenient because it takes like 30 seconds just to connect to their stupid servers when I'm trying to do a solo campaign. 

On harder difficulties you get 1 shot constantly by enemies so it becomes really important to rely on stealth or your AI teammates, as well as the resistance fighters that you can summon. You are eventually forced to play on harder difficulties if you use their "tier one" system to level up past level 30. 

The stealth mechanics are pretty good and I especially appreciate how you can tag enemies for your AI teammates to shoot for synchronized shots. Synchronized shots are about the only thing your teammates are useful for. 

One complaint is the driving is weird. It's like there is some weird reverse correction on the steering. Like when you press "A" to turn left, then release the "A" key, the car will turn back to the right again. It's really annoying and I end up sin waving down the road. The flying is much better, especially since you can just summon a helicopter at any time. 

Overall enjoyable game.

I'm writing this review after completing a majority of the game. I'm unsure I'm I'll finish it- probably, but it's easy to step away from. The first 8-10 hours is interesting game. As well, there appears to be a lot of customisation- albeit partly locked behind lootboxes. You can totally go through the game without buying into it. 

Unforunately, the biggest killer is how awfully repetitious the game is. Unlike other Ubisoft games I've played, such as the Far Cry series, the same three steps of of going to enemy base, killing enemies, getting into to do main story missions becomes a slog and acts as a fun-sponge. Instead of enjoying the game, I'm trying to think of how to most efficiently get all the items (like medals, weapon attachments, upgrades, etc). Finding all the collectables falls in this same vein and there are a huge number to find scattered widely throughout the map. Making your adventures more frustrating is that the AI is inconsistent. Somehow your squadmates are passive lobotomites who will not shoot back to save their own life, let alone your's; oppositely, cartel members are aggressive and decent shots. I've experienced some minor glitches, but nothing too terrible. 

I did get the game when it was on a good sale, but that would be the only time I'd recommend picking it up. The less you pay, the more fun you'll have, and the easier it'll be to put back in your library if/when you get bored.

That brings me to my only real issue with Wildlands: it’s too ambitious for its own good. Ubisoft has repeatedly said that this is the biggest open world game it’s ever made, and it truly is a stunning achievement as a final product, but the sheer size and depth of every aspect of the game has left many, many crevices for bugs to creep in. It’s not just the phantom AI soldiers having conversations in your ear. It’s the fact that the radio and NPC conversations aren’t synced for both you and your real-life co-op partners, the surprisingly frequent glitches that prevented me from reviving my allies in battle, and the bug that made me appear to my partners to be running behind every car I hijacked, when I was clearly in the driver’s seat on my own screen. 

None of those recurring glitches or other, one-time bugs I experienced were game-breaking, and most of the time they resulted in a fit of laughter rather than any actual frustration, but they’re definitely present. Still, it’s hard to look at those shortcomings as anything other than the small unwanted side effects of building a game as massive, detailed, and rich as Wildlands is. In fact, Wildlands is so far removed from what most have come to expect from a Ghost Recon title that it could have benefitted from shedding its sub-franchise namesake and simply standing on its own. It’s certainly got the legs for it.

Tom Clancy’s Ghost Recon: Wildlands is equal parts new approach to a storied franchise and familiar and well-trod open world systems. While it doesn’t break a great deal of new ground for the genre, when played with friends this cooperative open-world game can be an amazing amount of fun. Those moments are tempered by technical mishaps and inconsistencies. Military-minded co-op fans will find fun playing with friends, while solo players can also expect up to 50 hours of open-world entertainment.

- Magnificent illustration of Bolivia
- High level Tactical Stealth Gameplay
- Enjoyable co-op but also provocative single player
- Great variety and number of missions, offering many hours of fun
- Beautiful graphics and huge game world
- Excellent creation of a realistic world, good presentation of history and its support, satisfactory and complete finale
- Arcade helicopter-boat driving and fun handling
- The joy of the sniper player who must calculate the Bullet Drop in his shot
- Collectibles are part of the gameplay as they contribute to the evolution of the character

Cons
-------
- Various bugs, glitches and frame drops (especially while driving)
- The destruction of the Stealth approach from the release of captive rebels during the missions. It is recommended to leave them for last
- With the exception of El Sueño and some Bosses, the rest of the NPCs are moderate
- The portrayal of all proud Bolivian NPCs remains unfortunate
- Driving behavior of the cars that takes getting used to

The game truly is one of rinse and repeat quests, and there really isn't much going for it. 

MGS:V has everything that this game has, but with base building, and it is cheaper. This game fails to implement a truly engaging stealth system worth utilizing, and this is solely due to nonsensical AI sensory abilities. 99% of the missions you go on will end up going loud, and it will mostly be because an enemy saw you through an obstacle rather than any fault of your own. 

Get it on a big sale, and when I say big I mean 80% off or more. If you're new to the franchise, I'd say spend $40 on it at most. Just don't complain when the gameplay gets stale after eight hours, because you were warned.

**This game features microtransactions, BUT**

This game is done well in so many ways.

Ubisoft has always had talent an effort put into the world. This is no different. The world of Bolivia is presented with sometimes excruciating amounts of details. Worth $5 on its own.

The gunplay, character customization and everything else present in the world is very good. You get a wide selection of customizable weapons, clothing and game mechanics. The last one refers to the fact that certain items of clothing give you new animations or, for example, game effects like a different NVG filter. There are a lot of these mechanics to explore and the selection quality ranges from awesome to very poorly executed, but such issues are minor.

The story is realistic. It would never happen in the real world, but you can imagine it happening, and the missions are aligned with that idea. They don't feature any over the top mechanics or scenes, so you can fully immerse yourself in the story and the gloriously hammy characters. The missions have a great deal of variations, but usually involve either shooting, driving or sneaking, or all of the above. Many missions have a lot of alternative ways of completion and sequence breaking, never punishing the player for trying.

A special mention goes to the vehicles, which are like driving a block of ice in a desert. You get used to the controls eventually, but they never really grow on you.

Yes, this game has a ♥♥♥♥ ton of cosmetic, but also functional items hidden behind either payments or lootboxes, or both. But to Ubi's credit, the game actually sidesteps the problems with most of these. At 300 hours in, by doing daily challenges and playing the game, I was able to get literally every item in the game I care about, that being all lootbox weapons, functional cosmetics and vehicles. Voice lines and special characters I never cared about, and they are still in the lootboxes. I never spent a cent on the microtransactions (bought the DLC Ghosts for 5 buckls, which contains new story, new areas and new weapons).

The game difficulty is interesting. The base game is well balanced, with the enemies and missions being perfectly playable at any level, but some areas of the game offering a substantial increase in challenge. The Tier Mode, sadly, does not add more enemies, but instead just makes the enemies require more bullets, to the point where weapons that have been a one shot kill even on vehicles will fail to kill a person at lower (higher difficulty) Tier levels. This is Borderlands difficulty and it's just a pain to play, and requires immense amounts of grinding to function the same way as the base game.

There are interesting mechanics like the Unidad. You have your standard array of enemies to shoot at, and whether you do so quietly or loudly, they will eventually end. The Unidad offer a very interesting mechanical challenge by functioning like a GTA style police system and quickly overwhelming most players, but also being very easy to get rid of if you just move positions. Unlike GTA police, and contrary to Ubisoft's usual style, the Unidad are just as beatable as the regular groups of enemies if you choose to fight them, but the skill and effort required makes this a long, arduous and ungrateful task. It is in your best interest, as the player, to avoid them. This is great game design, and such mechanics are at the heart of Wildlands as a shooter.

This game has absolutely amazing Coop play. Flawless drop in and drop out multiplayer with very, very few issues. This is a great game to play with up to four people.


***The Bad***

Ubisoft Support. If you need anything from them, be prepared that they can't solve it, since this game has been abandoned by Support and Ubisoft in general for a while.

I have a love/hate relationship with this game. It's not a bad game, but there are some issues. First of all I've gotta say that the gunplay feels good, the map is huge and have different enviroments (biomes). Most missions are interesting and it's alot of fun to combat the drug cartel. It's also nice that you basically can try a mission guns blazing or through stealth. So that is a lot of praise for the game, what about the issues?

The personal issues I'm having (which incidentally is the reason I rage quit and uninstall the game) is with the AI. I haven't played on any lower difficulty so I cannot say anything about that. The AI always know exactly where you are once you are detected. It doesn't matter. You can sneak into a base and plant C4 charges; sneak out while staying undetected; detonate the explosives from a safe distance - BOOM: and then the AI knows exactly where you are. And seeing how they have almost godlike accuracy, it makes it even less "fun".

Another issue is that there are a lot of bugs. Most aren't game breaking but I've experienced a few crashes. There is also - as with every Ubisoft open-world game - alot of invisible walls, where there really should be any. You can only climb up specific cliffs/rocks, but most of them not (even if the rock is at knee level). This often makes it frustrating and even if you do manage to "bug" yourself up certain rocks/cliffs, there is a risk of getting stuck.

The invisible walls sometimes forces you to go a specific way and not being able to tackle objectives from any place. It removes advantages and options. Frustrating. This is standard Ubisoft though since the Far Cry series suffers from the same thing. I've also seen people bashing the driving in the game, it's not good but I didn't mind it too much. You'll just have to learn.

Anyhow, that is my take. Not a bad game - but sometimes incredibly frustrating to the point that I rage quit. I recommend buying it if you like open-world games with tactical elements. It's not the Clancy games of old, but don't let that get in the way. You'll have a lot of fun with this one. Thumbs up!

[h1] Brilliant game with some fatal flaws [/h1] 
I think this is one of Ubisoft's best games and efforts into making something really good.

POSITIVES
[list]
[*] First of all a large and gorgeous game world. This is one of the strongpoint of Ubisoft in general but Wildlands is way above any Far Cry games I've played before. Very diverse and detailed nature and areas.
[*] Very fun gameplay and effortless compatibility for both solo and online squads with friends.
[*] Nearly complete freedom in picking missions and your approach to playing the missions. This really is a free choice game, however that also means there is going to be less emphasis on a story that drives the events in the game. There is still a story but you pick the order in which it plays out so don't expect a movie-like cinematic experience.
[*] Very nice gunplay and nice ballistics model.
[*] Cars are better made with full damage models than in The Crew 2, ironically enough.
[*] In general a very fun game to play with friends: [url=https://youtu.be/chdvIA6opgw] PROOF [/url] 
[/list]

NEGATIVES
[list]
[*] Basically all the major flaws in this game start showing in the highest Extreme difficulty which is eventually forced onto you if you reach max level and want to level up the Tier 1 mode as well. But they exist to some extent on the lower difficulties as well.
[*] HORRIBLE, TERRIBLE, DISGUSTING aimbot accuracy on the enemies which is simply ridiculous and totally unreal. [url=https://youtu.be/4FlClXcVjY4] I mean just look at this. [/url] Combined with realistic damage on this difficulty it is a recipe for disaster.
[*] Loud gameplay impossible. This is a result of the previous point and the fact that once you get the enemies on alert, there will be infinite waves of reinforcements coming at you so your only chance is to flee if you can. This means that the only viable tactic is full stealth, which brings me to the next point:
[*] Stealth is broken. If you are detected ONCE, the enemies will ALWAYS know where you are, even without seeing you. They also behave like a hive mind so once one guy in a massive base sees you, ALL the enemies will magically know where you are, even when they don't see you and you change position. In some cases you don't even need to be detected in the first place. For example I completed a mission from 200m away in hiding by blowing up the mission objective with a drone and all the enemies immediately knew where I was despite never seeing me.
[*] Then there's some nitpicky stuff about controls such as not being able to switch to underbarrel without aiming first and THEN pressing the change button. However aiming button will make you peek out of cover and maybe get detected and/or mowed down instantly.
[*] So my main complaint is that all other difficulties feel a little too easy but the highest one is stupid because the AI straight up cheats and I don't think this is how difficulty should work. And yeah you can "make your own difficulty" by disabling parts of the HUD but that comes at the cost of features I maybe don't want to be fully missing such as the minimap. I just don't want the minimap to always tell me where all UNMARKED enemies are on all but the hardest and broken difficulty.
[/list]

But despite of that a very good and strong game. I got in during a sale and I am very happy with the purchase. Note that I have not played either of the DLC-s at the time of writing this review so this is purely about the base game.

I don't think I've ever played 100 hours of a game without beating the story. Sure, I could have, but there is SO much grinding to do. I both love this game and find it irritating for that reason. So, that said, there is tons to do and you should get plenty of play time. Grinding is a must. 

However, that comes with a caveat: repetitiveness. First of all, the whole game seems like a reskinned Far Cry 5. Minor tweaks, but different looks-wise. Wildlands' graphics just aren't as good. It feels much more closed in to me, and much less polished. The map is changed enough to be unrecognizable, but it has the same basic system of the bosses and underbosses in different regions of varying difficulty. Build up points and resources to get skills. Get bigger guns, get better upgrades, etc. Outposts, however, cannot be permanently conquered. 

As with Far Cry, you can go stealth or guns blazing. Some things are very easy, some are pretty difficult, but only in the sense that there are lots of enemies. There's really no puzzle or mystery aspect to anything. The story is completely ignorable. Even having watched all of the cut scenes, there's nothing pulling me into it. There's just zero depth to any of the characters or story.

Overall, yes, I'd recommend this game if you can get it cheap. But if there were grades, I'd give it a B at best. It's fundamentally solid, but there's no creativity to it.
