[h1] Introduction. [/h1]
Good day, dear users of the Steam playground. More than 90 hours later, I decided to write a review about the game itself.
I am one of those who completed Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon® Wildlands 100%, collecting intelligence from all operations. I managed to beat the game on difficulty level [b] "Ultimate" (highest difficulty level) [/b] and reached [b] 20 Tier [/b]. It took a lot of time and patience to complete all the additional tasks. I think I'm ready to tell you about it. Let's get started!

[h1] Plot. [/h1]
The game is set in [b] Bolivia [/b]. The supplies are controlled by the [b] Santa Blanca [/b] cartel, a powerful organization whose influence is destabilizing the region. The head of the organization is [spoiler] El Suenho [/spoiler] or [b] "Dreamer" [/b]. By hiring the best specialists, his organization has become the largest drug supplier in the world. [b] Santa Blanca [/b] managed to bribe the army, police and politicians. Due to the lack of protection, the Bolivian people began to lose hope for a happy future.
The US government is concerned about the growing influence of the cartel. As a result, [b] the United States Army [/b] sends an elite squad [b] "Ghosts" [/b] to uncover the connection between drug dealers and the local government and destroy the cartel.

[h1] Gameplay. [/h1]
You will take the role of one of the members of the "Ghosts" squad, and the CIA agent [spoiler] Karen Bowman [/spoiler] will be in charge of the "Regicide" operation. Your main task is to get to the "Dreamer". But this is not as easy as it seems. First, we have to disable each of the four departments of the cartel. And to get to them, you need to catch their assistants.
Think it's that simple? No matter how it is! To get to the assistants, you need to catch all the employees who play their role. Take the Production Department, for example, where each minion completes a different phase in the production of cocaine.
You will not be alone. Local rebels led by [spoiler] Amaru [/spoiler] and [spoiler] Paka Katari [/spoiler] will come to the rescue. However, their support will be extremely small and not very effective. You have to complete various secondary tasks scattered across all areas.
However, it is not the cartel people who are afraid, but the [spoiler] of the Unity soldiers [/spoiler]. These guys are much more dangerous than militants, they have good equipment and excellent equipment. These guys can screw up your operation by calling for help. Then you just have to run and not get caught in their eyes.
You can also meet heroes from other projects "Ubisoft": help [spoiler] "Rainbow-6" [/spoiler] find [spoiler] Saveiro [/spoiler], ensure [spoiler] Sam Fisher [/spoiler] security and conduct a joint operation with [spoiler] John Kozak [/spoiler] from the game Ghost Recon: Future Soldier.
You can also meet the well-known [spoiler] "Predator" [/spoiler] from a series of films.
In addition to the cooperative mode, there is PvP content, starting with the [spoiler] "Ghost War" [/spoiler] mode and ending with the [spoiler] "Battle Royale" [/spoiler]. However, it is very difficult to find people in these modes, and their development was stopped long ago. There is a chance to find a match. 

[b] Advantages: [/b]
[list]
    [*] Open world. You will see stunning and varied landscapes, from impenetrable swamps to snow-capped mountains. Most of the world is wilderness. That is, you will have to move on roads and off-road, by air and by water. Along the way, you can meet wild animals that complement the locations.
    [*] Special effects. Bright explosions, dirt on clothes and blood splatters after a shot perfectly complement the surroundings. However, that was not even what I liked. Try walking through the jungle during thunderstorms. Get a lot of positive emotions.
    [*] Personalization. We play for [spoiler] Nomad [/spoiler], but no one forbids changing his appearance or equipment. Maybe there are not hundreds of settings, but you can make your fighter. The equipment does not affect the gameplay in any way. Even the presence of a night vision device is not necessary, because you will turn it on anyway even without a special headdress. But the modifications to the weapons are beyond praise. You can customize your weapon to suit your style. If you love to actively attack bases - use a grenade launcher. Prefer to eliminate the enemy without any noise - a silencer and a telescopic sight will help you.
    [*] Partners. Yes, this game has a cooperative mode, but you shouldn't forget about artificial intelligence either. And in some cases, your artificial partners perform better assigned tasks than real players. Take for example the function [spoiler] "Synchronized shot" [/spoiler]. One press of a button and three opponents will instantly die. Your partners will never spoil a quiet operation and will always be able to "give first aid" to you.
    [*] Villains. Despite the large number of bosses that we need to get to, they are all different. Each fulfills its role and has a different character. Yes, this is an insignificant "Plus". However, when you watch (read) the intelligence data, you plunge even deeper into the universe of the game.
[/list]

[b] Disadvantages: [/b]
[list]
    [*] Pumping. The plot can be played without it. However, you will not experience all the delights of this game. Let's pretend you haven't improved anything. You will not be able to conduct more complex operations and you will not be able to call the rebels for help. And as for the number of resurrections, it generally decreases to a minimum. If you want to get absolutely all the functions, you will have to complete the tasks of the rebels. The only way they differ from each other is only in location. The tasks themselves are not boring, but the same type.
    [*]Artificial Intelligence. If the AI ​​of the partners is amazing, then the civilians suffer. They can run out under the sight or throw themselves under the wheels. To be honest, they will cause a lot of problems. Then during assignments they will interfere. Everything would be fine, but after three killed residents in a row, the mission will fail and you will have to start all over again.
    [*]Technics. It's not bad, but the physics is awful. But once you think that you are driving a toy car, not a real car. If ground transportation is even more or less, then air transportation is terrible. The physics is awful, you don't feel the same plane. However, there is one "plus": the control is very easy.
[/list]

[h1] Is Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon® Wildlands worth your attention? [/h1]
Game for an amateur. If you are not embarrassed by the constant execution of the same actions and are not afraid of difficulties due to gaming conventions - definitely take it. However, I advise you to purchase this product at a discount, which appear very often. And if you do not approve of such a gameplay, I do not recommend it.
This is not a one-time game! If you have already started playing, then I advise you to delve into the plot. Then you will understand the whole plot and the purpose of the game.

[h1] Conclusion. [/h1]
Will I keep playing? Yes! I really liked the game and I will continue to play it, starting to go through two expansions and completing the remaining achievements.
I really hope I helped someone.

Cor blimey, this Ghost Recon Wildlands game is an absolute belter, isn't it? Set in a gorgeous, somewhat-realistic version of Bolivia, it's got 21 cracking provinces to explore, each one more stunning than the last. Swamps, forests, mountains - it's like David Attenborough made a video game. And the best part? You can customize your whole squad to blend right into the scenery.

The gameplay is an absolute treat, I tell you what. This world they've built is properly reactive, with the weather, time of day, and even the enemy patrols all working together to create some opportunities. Want to infiltrate that cartel base under the cloak of darkness? Go for it, you sneaky so-and-so. Or fancy taking the guns blazing approach in broad daylight? Knock yourself out, just don't expect to survive long on the higher difficulty settings.

And the gunplay - ooh, it's a beauty. Each weapon feels distinct, with its own unique sound, recoil, and all that good stuff. Sniping from hundreds of meters away is an absolute joy, watching those hapless goons running around trying to figure out where the shot came from. Just brilliant.

The co-op is the real star of the show, though. Teaming up with your mates to cause all sorts of mayhem across this stunning open world - what could be better? It's like being in your own little A-Team, taking down the big bad cartel with a smile on your face. Sure, the odd glitch might pop up here and there, but who cares? When you're having this much fun, a few funny spawning issues are easy to overlook.

All in all, Ghost Recon Wildlands is an absolute triumph. It's got the visuals of a nature documentary, the gameplay of a hardcore tactical shooter, and the co-op madness of a classic 80s action flick. If you're after a proper, no-nonsense military experience with a side of humor, this is the game for you. Brilliant stuff, lads - top marks all round!

This is precisely the kind of game I enjoy.  I'd give it an 8/10 though, with a few points dropped for annoyances:

[h2] The good [/h2]
* Open world exploration and shooting with a huge play area
* This is a LONG game.  I've been playing for over 50 hours and I don't think I'm even a quarter of the way to main story end yet.  I imagine if I went for 100% completion I'd have to put north of 400 hours in.
* Lots of weapon & character customisation available, to fit your play style
* Lots of game/options customisation available, especially the HUD, so if you switched everything off it would be more like a simulation than a game
* "Ghost mode" (similar to what ARPG players might call "Hardcore" mode) is available (it's optional!) for ultra-difficulty.  Features limited weapon carrying, may only change loadouts when visiting a weapon case, realistic reloading (bullets still in the discarded clip are lost) and most of all PERMADEATH if you actually die
* Multiplayer is optional and not required at all; your AI teammates aren't too bad, although they sometimes take way longer to reach & revive me than I'd have liked

[h2] The not-so-good [/h2]
* Enemies respawn if you close/reload the game or if you fast travel.  It's frustrating clearing an enemy base knowing that it will be filled with enemies again next time you visit.
* The same buildings are copy-pasted throughout the game.  There's still plenty of variety but it didn't take me long to start noticing that I'd been in an identical office building before
* Whilst the main story has plenty of variety in quests, the side-quests are essentially repetitions of the same 8 missions.  3 are called "Supply raids" which are one of "Steal a plane", "Steal a chopper" or "Stop & tag a convoy truck".  The others are called "Rebel support" which are either "Catch & intimidate a minor boss", "Defend a radio vs waves of enemies", "Race from one transmitter to another", "Reach & tag a difficult-to-reach object" or "Breach a building, take out enemies inside and hack a computer before the time runs out".
* The "Watchman" mission.  Omg this can be a massive pain in the butt because it triggers automatically and can't be untracked once you have it.  It then nags you repeatedly through the game until you go and complete it.  However, that mission is incredibly difficult (designed for late-game characters), especially if you have a low-level character, it also has no checkpoints and so if you fail at any point you must restart from scratch.  If you are reading this, then I strongly recommend that you [spoiler] avoid entering the La Cruz area until your character is at least level 15 or safer level 20.  The mission triggers as soon as you set foot in La Cruz [/spoiler] .  I nearly ragequit the game because of this, but eventually I was able to cheese the mission with a combination of dropping the difficulty to minimum temporarily and also finding an optimal strategy.
* The game has a micropayments store.  The majority of what it sells is purely cosmetic or is stuff that you could get for free just by playing the game (in other words, the store just allows early unlocking).  A few game-affecting items are purchasable via the store only though.  Thankfully you can 100% ignore it though because there's plenty of weapons items and stuff available without even looking at the store-only things.
* Actually controlling your AI teammates is pretty clunky; I tend to leave them holding away from the enemy positions until I'm confident that the vast majority of bad guys are down, and we can take what's left really easily.  Otherwise, my AI teammates keep giving us away and putting us into a massive firefight.  I prefer to play much more stealthy than that.

This game is fun when you're actually playing and doing somewhat well, but the second you mess up a mission, it sends you all the way back to the beginning. The checkpoints in this game are a joke. For a game that's story is oriented around taking down a cartel, it does not feel like you are taking down a cartel. Your efforts feel truly meaningless. Once something leaves your render distance it's reset.  It's frustrating when you take out an anti-air turret and walk 300m away to have it shoot you down seconds later. I get the "replay value" argument, but this game is so enormously huge and borderline unpleasant to play, I genuinely don't see why anyone would actually want to play it through again. This has been a fantastic lock-down game:  a massive sandbox full of stuff to shoot, find & explore.  If you, like me are OCD about finding and doing everything, there is literally hundreds of hours of play-time in this game.  Unfortunately, it does have a few issues...
As has been said before, setting the game in a real-life country is problematic.  There is a lot of "hoorah", flag-waving, manly tears being wiped away over the fallen and fists shaken at corrupt officials who clearly should let someone else look after the running of their country.  Still, while ham-handed, it's pretty easy to ignore.

While comparisons can be made to the Farcry titles, this game lacks any real humour apart from the grim, cigar chomping kind.  Also unlike Farcry, the game is predominantly third person.  If, like me, you prefer first person shooters you'll spend most combats in aim-mode (which changes to a 1st person view).  If you play like this do yourself a favour and increase the "aim mouse sensitivity" in the options menu up to 80-90.  Makes for a much more responsive experience.  

As mentioned, Ubisoft continues to try to gouge players for a few extra bucks via a bunch of content that is only available via loot crates.  While I don't care about cosmetics, new weapon drops initially feel quite slim in the base game.  A shame, because new kit makes a game feel constantly fresh.  By the end of the game however you will have plenty of toys in the toybox.

Ghost Recon Wildlands is an open world sandbox game blended with the classic fast paced tactical action from the Tom Clancy Ghost Recon series. What you have here is a modern Ubisoft game - open world, lots of stuff to collect, and various missions to complete. 

Graphically Wildlands holds up really well. You'll probably need a beefy PC to run the games on Ultra settings but even at the default High settings the game is really pretty and the digitally realized country of Bolivia is a wonder to explore by foot. You'll fight in many different locales that really show off the games beautiful lighting and plant life. 

Physics leave a fair bit to be desired in this game. The guns and rockets all have range and proper bullet drop which is really nice. Catching a headshot from over 300m with a properly lined up sniper shot is always great. But these gun physics are about the only good ones here because the vehicle handling in this game is all over the place. Some cars drive like they are stuck in molasses and others can stop on a dime and perform pinpoint turns. 

Storywise the game is so so. I personally loved the story because it reminded me of a cheesy action movie but there are plenty of serious moments to be found here. The game can be really rough at some points with plenty of references and displays of all sorts of violence - mostly against the enemy forces but there are many examples of brutality towards the local population of Bolivia.  There are two endings to find in this game: One for clearing all the cartel heads and one for only clearing a portion of them.

Over all I loved Wildlands despite a few game objectives being repetitive and some items being locked behind crates. But I would recommend this game again and again.

Let me start this negative review off by stating that, if you have friends who also love a sandbox-type military game, that this might be the kind of game for you. It provides a lot of things that particular crowd will probably enjoy and can surely lead to some wonderful shenanigans in this fun sandbox they've made for those gamers.

If you don't have multiple friends interested in the game and similar schedules, the sheer repetitiveness of the missions is the game's undoing. It provides a MASSIVE map which is clearly very well made with a lot of attention to detail, but given that each location is one of just a handful of total mission types it means that for the solo player the novelty wears off quickly - in my case about 15 hours.

Speaking of the map, they deserve a lot of credit for thinking big on the map. It is huge. There are a lot of locations you can tell had a lot of time put into them, but traversing it without a helicopter is not fun. Helicopters are prevalent and plentiful and regularly armed to the teeth, so after a few hours of trying to navigate the winding mountain roads with my AI squad I stopped using cars completely. And then I stopped using the squad or my guns as everything at nearly any mission site could be killed by my helicopter.

The AI squad (for a SP experience) is somewhat competent for an AI team. It might seem immersion-breaking that they can just teleport to any vehicle you're in at will but given that they are commonly trapped in level geometry, unresponsive, or busy fighting it is probably overall much easier on the player to allow them to leave at will. Sometimes I would marvel at how they obliterated all of my enemies the moment we arrived, and others I'd come around a corner to find one of my AI teammates and the enemy standing two inches away from each other doing absolutely nothing.

The enemy AI also suffers from these bizarre spikes in competence. On some missions I was a nimble navigator operating like a Splinter Cell operative, and on other missions in the same light with almost identical situations I'd be spotted the moment I poked my head around a corner. A sicario (the basic grunt) unit with a machine pistol was as likely to miss every single shot he took from 80 meters away as he was to drill me with the full magazine and kill me on the spot. This occurred everywhere, not just in 'high difficulty' areas and was most egregious in areas with high foliage concealment where the AI could 10000% see me and I couldn't see them. This was further exacerbated by the AI blatantly pathing towards me in spite of being 'hidden' even if I was quietly ordering a mortar strike from 100m away.

Last complaint - the skill system could do with much more explanation than it currently provides in many situations. One skill increases my AI team's 'efficiency' by 8% with no explanation as to what that means. There's a skill that refills my ammo when I die... but when I die the game ends and I respawn next to an ammo box. There's a skill tree that decreases bullet damage by a flat percentage (which certainly sounds useful) but on the rare occasion I am fired upon I am regularly killed before I can even return to cover.

I know 16 hours isn't a huge amount of time with a game to provide a negative review. However, at the end of the 16th hour I couldn't find anything DIFFERENT in the game from when I started. If you're a singleplayer gamer, give this a skip. If you have a lot of buds who love to play games like this, take a flier if it's under $15.

I only played this game co-op, and even then, it was still miserable from start to finish. Not even co-op made what little good existed in this game outshine the bad. I went in hoping for something similar to the excellent tactical open world stealth gameplay in Metal Gear Solid V with the added bonus of being co-op, but it was nowhere close.

First: The enemy AI absolutely ruins any enjoyment I could have had with this game. In every other stealth game, when the AI searches for you, the AI will check your known last position, and then search the surrounding area before giving up and staying on alert. This opens up ways to approach tactically and allows for at least some margin of error when infiltrating a base, as you can kill whoever saw you and still escape or fall back, disappear, and either fall back to recover or flank from another angle to continue your assault.

In Wildlands, AIs don't search, they straight up pathfind towards your exact location. They take the shortest path between their last position and your current position while climbing over anything and everything in their way. Your exact position is immediately and telepathically known to every AI currently in the world upon detection. This means that if you alert someone on one side of the base, shoot that person, then run around to the other side of the base without being seen by anyone else, the AI will STILL go directly to your new position. Combine that with hitscan enemies that can one-or-two shot you with extreme precision, even through dense foliage, and you have a perfect recipe for frustration.

The gameplay loop itself is boring too. The mission structure is some variant of "go here, shoot this NPC, kidnap this NPC, blow up this structure, hack this" throughout the entire game with several minutes of flying a helicopter between locations in-between. Not only that, but explosive drones trivialize pretty much every: "kill this NPC" or "destroy this object" mission in the game. Just fly it in, blow it up, and you can leave before the AI somehow know to walk directly to your exact location.

Guns and gear all feel effectively the same with little punch to the weapons. A 50 cal should fire a bullet through four buildings and still have enough velocity to at least dent the side of a tank, but in this game it has practically no bullet penetration. It just feels like any old sniper rifle except it does a little more damage. That's what guns in this game feel like: It's all the same, they either shoot a little faster or do a little more damage.

Lastly, the story is incredibly boring compared to even the worst stories in previous Tom Clancy titles. Characters are all one dimensional, one-note archetypes with little to no motivation for their actions beyond either revenge on the cartel or stopping the cartel. Certain events near the end of the game are probably the most nonsensical and contrived twists I've seen in a Tom Clancy game, because it completely goes against and contradicts what shallow puddle of depth the characters had to begin with. Tom Clancy is probably rolling in his grave to think of just how poorly written everything in this game's story is.

All in all, this wasn't worth the time I invested, and while it did give my buddy and I a few solid laughs, overall I wouldn't suggest it to anyone else looking for an open world tactical stealth game. If you're searching for that type of experience, I would suggest other games such as Metal Gear Solid V and ARMA over this one.

Wildlands is a huge ambitions game with a lot of content. The whole map is absolutely massive and might be the biggest in any game out there. With that, every type of environment is covered, so you will be traversing through snowy mountains, desert hills, forests, plain fields, rivers and so on. The story revolves around a narco cartel in Bolivia. You are on a mission to take down the main boss, but first you need to defeat and capture all the underbosses that surround him. The map is divided into 21 districts and each one of those is controlled by one of those smaller bosses. You do not need to defeat them all but if you do, defeating bosses above them becomes easier. You are free to go wherever you want from the beginning but zones have different difficulties so you may need to take an incremental approach. The story is good, well told and engaging.

The gameplay though, becomes very repetitive. It revolves around getting to a location and taking out all the enemies, blowing something up or capturing a target for interrogation. There are probably over a 100 question mark locations that you can visit containing missions, collectables, skill points or weapon unlocks. It is your classic example of Ubisoft style busywork, where there is a lot of locations so that it appears like there is a lot of content to play though. It would have been nice to have better mission variety or more purpose to discovering locations instead of just go here and kill bad guys.

There is a great deal of character customization that is purely cosmetic. You have a lot of different weapons at your disposal but no real reason to swap them out as any gun can 1 shot headshot kill almost any target. So all the weapon upgrade collectables seam kind of pointless. The skill tree is okay - there are some useful upgrades and some not so much. You can upgrade capabilities of your squad, weapons, drone and equipment. 

The game is best experienced in co-op with friends as you can coordinate and take out big outposts together. You can choose to be as tactical as you want. One guy on sniper support, or drone to scout for the guys moving in. It can be a really cool experience at times. Solo mode is very playable too but you are doing all the things by yourself. Your AI squadmates do not help out that much unless it is to revive you or to perform a synced shot with you (which is a nice feature).

So overall, Wildlands is a great TPS co-op game with a strong story and world design but very repetitive mission structure. It took me about 70 hours to do and visit everything, which you are not required to do. It’s worth a play especially if you have friends to play it with. Only buy on sale of 70% off.

So while I'd argue the open world design feels a bit stale to me, it still functions enough for what this game is, Not every game can be Red Dead Redemption 2 but you might wish Ubisoft would raise the bar and create a more believable world with AI that actually simulates that it lives in the world we play in.

You might not be crazy about gunplay because there's sort of a leveling system and you just need to unlock/sink points into a trait.  I feel mixed about it, while it does provide a sense of progression, it's weird that an elite combat unit would have to learn to use C4 and mines on the job/in the AO.  Honestly the weirdest is probably unlocking team sync shot, you unlock one ghost at a time so I'd recommend it being one of your early unlocks in the game to maximize your squad. 

I enjoyed gathering intel on targets and building up to the boss encounters.  Bowman is a nice centerpiece, narrating objectives you select, and transitioning you from one goal to the next, even briefing you on the boss of each region.  You're squad provides some interesting banter/commentary on your situation, both this and a narrative character like Bowman feel missing in Breakpoint.

If you're up for more of a challenge there's a Ghost mode, which will introduce permadeath (all your progress is deleted when you die).

Ghost War is small 4v4 team deathmatch which can lead to some tense situations. Shoot too early and without taking someone down, and you may find the entire enemy squad zero in on you, too late and you may be in a compromised position (surrounded, or you're already dead).

Missions are generally left up to your discretion on how to complete them, although there are some forced stealth missions which can be very unforgiving. 

One major thing (might be an oversight but maybe not) is that clothing has 0 effect on your character and their health or stealth. One would think that if nothing else, clothing would matter for stealth, but it does not. You're just as visible in the dead of night wearing neon green as you are wearing a ghillie. This means, beyond aesthetics, there is very little reason to change your look through the game.

Overall, this is a great shooter well worth some $, though it is not perfect.

I'm ashamed to admit this is the first Tom Clancy game I have bothered to try and I must say I am thoroughly impressed.  Wildlands is an amazing game, both in terms of its open world gameplay and its amount of content.  This game caters to every play style - whether that be going into an enemy camp, guns blazing, or stealthily maneuvering yourself into that perfect sniper position and picking off enemy cartel members one by one.   A huge selection of weapons and ordinance also caters to different playstyles.  Overall an exellent and well rounded action game!

Arbitrary bullet drop across similar calibers and their respective barrel lengths, suppressors somehow lowering muzzle velocity, and the sin of assuming shotgun pellets dissipating into thin air past several yards. Avoid if you care about anything resembling an authentic ballistic model.

Also, the fair share of bugs that won't ever be fixed, just like any other Ubi title that isn't the latest entry in the series. Some immersion breaking, some forcing a game reload, some forcing you to WAIT until you get the option to reload the game, and some confiscating your ability to engage in certain mechanics should you forego any attempts to reload your save.

Gunsmith had potential(still would had it receive more post-launch support), but makes little sense often eg. gun with collapsible stock requires sourcing gear loot to enable collapsing. Loads of erroneous depictions of accessories regardless, like magazines not having a the correct capacities, attachments with sensible placements in the gunsmith, but in different locations on the gun on the character. Too many other egregious infractions for the pedantic all in all.

Singleplay romp is otherwise quite enjoyable, but level-gated upgrades and perks seem to be mostly to encourage the XP farm and grind model of gameplay loop, thus resulting in far more unnecessary but desirable engagements. Endgame grind in the form of Tier mode is quite the obvious sham in its presentation. Each advancing tier claims to increase the amount of tier xp gained(which it does), but that's ultimately offset by the next tier's xp requirements. Not really a harmful thing on its own, but it's clear it's designed to sucker the gullible few into visiting the cash shop to buy progress boosters. All that just for what, two OP guns and a bunch of cosmetic tat for hours if not days of XP grinding? Classic Ubi.

At least you can get somewhat creative with the game's arcade-like mechanics. All weapons in a given class have the same audible range regardless of their "Noise" stat bar, with separate values for suppressed and unsuppressed.  So in lieu of using noise making gadgets to cause a distraction, just discharge your weapon into the sky if you know your intended target to distract is within audible range of that weapon's class. This comes off as hilarious when both unsuppressed .30 and .50 cal discharges for sniper rifles aren't audible past 130 metres.

Difficulty is a mixed bag. Arcade mechanics mean that lying flat in low grass conceals you just as well as lying on a wide open white salt flat in black overalls. Substantial vegetation does however increase mechanical concealment. Ignore your outfit, they do not impact concealment whatsoever, despite flavor text of certain high-tech camouflage outfits indicating otherwise. Enemies also sometimes do not react to your AI team silently sniping them in view of each other using the Sync Shot mechanic while there's an alert going on, yet if you silently take down a mob while being hunted, the hostiles on the far side will automatically know their comrade was covertly neutralised, and immediately swarm that position. But the true travesty is in its Tier mode difficulty ramp. Enemies become aim-hackers due to AI not having ballistics, but are hitscan-based. Expect dual-MAC11-wielding gangsters to empty half their mags into your head from 100m like Skynet foot soldiers with homing rounds within a second, while snipers in the same difficulty frequently missing shots they should not miss at 50m. This means you will have to rely on summoning AI reinforcements to help your AI team mates during forced firefights as AI aren't subject to the same difficulty mechanics as the player.

My friend and I picked up Ghost Recon: Wildlands when it was on sale, and it quickly went from a stealthy covert ops military shooter, to "Two Idiots destabilize a multinational drug cartel". Wildlands tries to be so overly serious to the point that it's kind of hilarious at times, with the two of us playing it more like GTA than an actual serious military shooter like it wants to be. We both went in with very little expectations in the beginning, but there are genuinely some excellent moments in the game that actually made us feel we paid too little for the game when we bought it on sale.

Wildlands is an interesting game because it truly does not feel as though you're playing the main character, but that you're just assisting the protagonist. It was an interesting experience seeing how things progressed, with you sort of being bossed around and not really being paraded as a hero, but more so just someone who's the means to an end.

[code]For this review and others like it, feel free to check out and follow my personal Steam Curator page by  [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/36761101-Miphnificent]*Clicking Here*.[/url][/code]

The Good:

- The story was more interesting than I expected. There were some interesting twists and turns within the story that I did not expect, as well as some various content and such leading to the end of the game which made for an incredible feeling where we sat back and said "That was awesome". We didn't expect much regarding the story for the price point we paid, but were pleasantly surprised.

- Freedom of choice in how you tackle situations. Wildlands gives you freedom in how you decide how you're going to approach missions. Getting a little bored? Invent your own fun by doing some harebrained play that you came up with which will most likely get you killed. Don't want to stealth only through an area which has enemies? Kill them all without being seen. Even stealth segments have these capabilities, as the game allows you to employ "Stealth", rather than actual Stealth by killing everyone so nobody can notice or raise an alarm.

- Gorgeous visuals. Wildlands has sufficiently impressed me with how incredibly scenic the areas are. My favorite area in this game is a SWAMP area because of just how mystifying and magic the area seems rather than a cesspool like most games make them out to be. You've got an entire gradient of ranges to visit, from snowcapped peaks, to salt flats, to swamps, to desert. There's something out there visually for everyone.

- A wide array of weapons. A game like this is only made better by the weaponry at your disposal, and there is quite a lot to play around with. I don't think there was ever a moment in the game where I'd felt bored with the weapon I'd had, as there were so many opportunities to obtain new ones to play with.

- A plethora of vehicles, and decent driving. ALL HAIL THE ZEUS! In the beginning when we played everything seemed as if it was samey, but as we played more we began to understand that there are a LOT of different vehicles within this game, even on the civilian side of things. Certain ones are better than others with the civilian Zeus seeming like a god amongst pickups, but there's a lot of ways to get around with the driving mechanics being pretty nice. Dirtbiking straight to an objective across rocky or mountainous terrain became a quick favorite as well.

- Operation Missions. Genuinely the best point of the game from a gameplay perspective. Operations HEAVILY overshadow the main storyline and game, to the point that they were what we were primarily hunting for as we played the game. Any time one popped up we'd careen off course and go take care of it.


The Bad:

- The Ending. I'm a firm believer that the ending of a game is one of the most important parts, as it is the punctuation at the end of your journey, wrapping up whatever you have done. Wildlands' ending was about as satisfying as receiving a piece of paper for collecting all the monsters at the end of a game, with it coming down primarily to a cutscene rather than anything else after they'd built up this massive larger-than-life presence.

- The enemy AI. I do not think I died fairly a single time whilst playing this game. I'd play the game, running through and clearing entire areas before enemies could spot me, only to be seen through a wall by someone, or for a squad of enemies to randomly spawn where I'd been just 3 seconds ago right before they began firing on me. There were moments where I'd be firing at four guys and dispatching them with relative competency, and then a fifth and sixth enemy would magically pop into existence right next to one of the others. Enemies also seem to possess magic bullets which can defy the same laws your weapons have to, seemingly being able to penetrate objects that your rounds cannot.

- Difficulty balancing. There were times when the game felt almost too easy, but then there were times when the game felt incredibly unfair due to poor AI design, enemies seeing us through walls, etc. Turning up the difficulty just seemingly resulted in more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ deaths at the hands of enemies being able to magically do things which the player is told time and time again that they're unable to do. Enemies seeing you when you're a mile away and crouched and invisible, or enemies taking so many rounds that at times it felt like I was playing The Division.

- Too much filler content. There are some GENUINELY incredibly fun missions in Wildlands, but a lot of the time trying to find those or unlock them is spent slogging through the muck of the other missions which are mainly just copy and pastes of other missions. Go here, do this thing and kill this guy. Go here, interrogate this guy, etc. It wouldn't be a problem if almost 70% of the games missions were just this rehashed content.

- A lack of an ecosystem. Whilst I know this might be a weird gripe, the game world feels almost too empty, and like it's only inhabited by the enemies, civilians, and the players with the occasional llama or deer. There are so many opportunities to implement interesting wildlife, like crocodiles in the swamps which players would have to get around so they don't alert the enemies, and all sorts of various other things, and it feels like a wasted opportunity to not have them.

-
Overall Rating: 7/10

Worth $49.99? Obviously not. However, my experience sort of steers me to recommending this game at the price point of $25 or so. Wildlands often goes on sale, so my personal suggestion is picking it up when it is.

Closing Thoughts:
Ghost Recon: Wildlands feels as if it is just too much of the same at times, sprinkled with some genuinely fun moments which made me say "Wow! I wish the game was more like this all the time!", which I think says enough about the game. If Wildlands had about 50% of its main mission structure ripped out and replaced with maybe 5 more operations the game would be a much more compelling sell or purchase. Definitely recommended, but it's nothing incredible whatsoever.

Even though this did not play as a typical Ghost Recon game, I really enjoyed it. There were a ton of customization options, which made the experience feel more personal. The map is INSANELY big, with a gorgeous atmosphere that changes depending on where you are. Customization allows you to match your camouflage and gear to the appropriate environment, or wear jeans and a T-shirt as you wreak destruction throughout Bolivia. Weapon mechanics are okay, but all the pistols seem underwhelming. If all the time and energy that was put into the outfit customization, was translated to the weapons, I might have enjoyed this game a lot more. Weapon variants and options are not bad by any means, however they could be much better. Driving is a nightmare on this game, I did everything I could to avoid it. Most of the vehicle physics are disastrous, forcing me to travel mostly by air (which can be just as terrible, just faster). The story is absurdly cheesy and the missions get repetitive, especially trying to get through the entire map (not required to beat the game). However, the bonus missions connecting this beautiful world to some of the developers other games was amazing. There are interactions with Team Rainbow, Sam Fisher, and more. . . being able to fight the predator made this game amazing to me. The missions leading up to the final showdown with the legendary predator are done really well and the active camouflage blends perfectly with this games environment, making the final fight really challenging. I would have loved to see even more predator missions and content. Overall I did get through the entire game and while there was room for improvement, it was still worth the sale price. I would have a different opinion if I had paid full retail, but on sale its definitely worth the money.

UPDATE:
So, I've been playing it now, since I did pay money for this piece of garbage, and I still wouldn't recommend it.

 - The Order Wheel doesn't work for me at all when I use a controller.  It just shows two locked symbols at 9 and 3 oclock with blue and green words overlapping each other.  I've played enough to unlock all of the rebels help options and should have access to team controls, but nope.  I can use the rebel options by holding down the Tab button on the keyboard and pressing numbers 1 through 6.  So, the controller works for everything else, but not the Order Wheel, and the keyboard only works for the rebel support.  It's quite frustrating.

 - Be careful where you go, or the game will force you into missions when you would rather not attempt them at the time.  And then, if you don't do EXACTLY what it wants, it fails you, stops your gameplay, takes away any vehicle you were using, and reloads everything, putting you in a much more inconvenient location than before.  You don't have a choice in this matter.  It's garbage.

 - Your "squad" is some of the dumbest idiots yet in AI support.  One saving grace is that they can basically move right up to an enemy unit and be undetected.  Only your character can get detected by the enemies.  They also suck in lining up a sync shot, as they absolutely can't target any enemy even slightly inside a structure.  - Aiming a helicopter with weapons is atrocious.  The vehicle bobs around like it's in a hurricane.  Moving the stick just a little bit makes the reticle zip across the screen, completely messing up your aim.

Overall, I sort of enjoy the game, but mainly because I feel like I have to, since I was duped into it by the scumbags at Ubisoft, with their absolutely unhelpful uselessness.  I definitely don't recommend this trash.

 Overall the environment is fun to explore, the vast amount of different areas and landscapes you can ♥♥♥♥ around in for hours while mindlessly driving around, hiking long distances,  enjoying the view, and maybe getting run over by a train for ♥♥♥♥♥ n giggles.

Honestly, I don't know how to start off this review. 
I really dislike UBISOFT for what they've become in the last few years. 

But time to time, they keep pumping out gems like Wildlands and AC Odyssey. 
IF there is anything that I can tell about Ubisoft is that they've honestly become better at creating beautiful worlds and giving it some character.

Bolivia in this game is no exception. 
They've put their time to beautify every corner of the map, give it life.
Everywhere you go in the map, you will be awed at how full of life it is, the lightening, the NPC Crowd, the buildings, the wildlifes, the spitting llamas, you name it. Each to their own regions.

People usually overlook this fact when deciding on this game, the major faction that you fight against,
The Santa Blanca Cartel is a very intimidating faction, if you have watched NARCOS, you know how ruthless the cartels can be.  
They're your main nemesis and part of your entire journey, province by province. 

Each step you take in the province(s), you follow the back-story of the Buchons with the short videos and text lore and they do a great job of making it feel like you're cutting parts of a much bigger body AND affecting them as you play, I honestly don't know why they dropped it in Breakpoints but hey... 

Your player characters and companion are, well, what ubisoft does best.
Low-key bland and full of pride with zero to little interest wielding facts for you as the player. 
You'll get tired of them, but they can simply be ignored and aren't a important factor in this game. 

The content however, 
Is kind of short in supply.
You have 3 main types of mission, Story Mission > Side Missions > Random Convoys. 
Rest is just a collectable marathon. 

This is staple UBI, but don't let it put you down though. 
This game is a MUST PLAY, especially with a friend, on EXTREME difficulty. 

If you haven't played this game. 
DO IT! 

The boss ladder system in this game is AWESOME. 
The gameplay is harsh but AWESOME.
Everything is AWESOME.

Hey Guys,
Tom Clancy’s Ghost Recon: Wildlands is equal parts new approach to a storied franchise and familiar and well-trod open world systems. While it doesn’t break a great deal of new ground for the genre, when played with friends this cooperative open-world game can be an amazing amount of fun. Those moments are tempered by technical mishaps and inconsistencies that can be patched, but as a result, this launch ride is going to have some technical potholes that put a damper on an otherwise excellent experience.

This game has a similar vibe to Just Cause 2, but with a bunch of character customisation and solid weapon customisation. The world is huge and feels alive, with plenty of civilian NPCs milling around.

The gameplay isn't particularly complex and can get samey after a while, but feels solid. The variety of weapons gives you a few ways to tackle the various missions, from up close to half a kilometre away.

For the best experience, play with friends. The AI teammates are only really useful for the "sync shot" feature, but can be turned off in the options which is cool. 

The game has a lot of settings you can mess with, creating your own experience. You can play casually, with a minimap that gives indication of where unseen enemies are, or you can turn all the HUD off and have a very tense, difficult and realistic experience.

I keep coming back to this game, and probably will as long as the servers are up.

- The game crashes now and then
- Difficulty: While most missions are doable, some stealth missions are overly hard and tedious. If there were more breakpoints or a save-function, these would be more fun. However they have several stages, little mistakes in stage 2 or 3 force you to start all over again in phase 1 which already took half an hour. So you end up doing the same boring thing over and over.
- Weapon upgrades: There's a huge number of upgrades and different weapons you can find on the map. Yet for some strange reason some weapons are already OP and don't allow to apply any upgrades. So I am basically going with some of my OP starter rifles, no progress here. Everything I found so far - almost all areas cleared now - seems to be worse than these and upgrades are useless, not even applicable.
- Vehicle drop algorithm: A nice idea to call a vehicle wherever you are, however, most of the time these are dropped a) 300m away while you are immobilized and under fire, dragging a bad guy and need to escape fast, b) on the other side of rivers, streets, or forests you just crossed, c) (the classic) inside a heavily armed camp, unreachable without clearing it first. Other times you fail missions, because npcs you work with refuse to climb into your car, most of these fixed themselves though, when starting over the mission.

Overall this is still a great game with very decent graphics and a cool atmosphere, highly recommended!

[h1]7/10[/h1][b]Standard Ubisoft Filler-Fest, Now With Added Jingoism![/b][hr][/hr]I think by now most people go into these open-world Ubisoft games knowing they'll really enjoy the first area and then start to notice it repeating by the third, right? I don't have to go over that again, we all know the deal.

With that in mind, it's quite a fun game. Kinda. There's tedium in travelling here to there, listening to military jargon over walkie-talkies and watching terribly written cartel goons trying to sound edgy, despite being written by a flannel-wearing, craft-beer-touting Frenchman. It's jingoistic as hell, so much so that Bolivia demanded reparations because some French hipsters over in Paris pretended an entire continent has more guns per square foot than potable water. There's also tedium in the entire gameplay loop by the end, because it's just so egregiously padded out. It's so full of filler, in fact, that you don't even have to visit half the game: they give you an out by letting you play the final mission at something like 60% completion if you go to the right districts in the right order. When you're relieved you can end it early, but are still willing to finish it, you know you're playing a Ubisoft 7/10.

It's a game where you go from here to there and click on heads in the right order, after sending up a drone and putting AR arrows above people's heads in order to figure out what that right order is. That's it, really. The ballistics are satisfying and the environments look good, and vary wildly from place to place. Even on the hardest difficulty, however, it's a mindless droning kind of experience. Despite promises of realism and immersion, it's a game where difficulties just bump up numbers: the patrolling AI is psychic on all difficulties, and just gain laser aim to compliment it in higher modes. Despite being touted as one of those operator AF kinda games, one gun over the other just trades off stats, and it's a huge pain in the ass travelling from here to there to pick up a scope that only works with half the guns that share rails with the other half so that doesn't even make sense and I'm rambling. It's a rambly kinda game. Get it cheap and get it out of the way.

To be honest, I have a love-hate relationship with this game. I'm giving it a thumbs up because for the most part it's a really fun stealth shooter that gives you a large open world, a slough of bad guys to shoot and a lot of tools to get the job done. I've poured a lot of hours into it and even then I'm only halfway through the game because I'm taking my time picking up guns, gun parts, and upgrading my skills. It's also a big plus for me when you provide a great amount of customization for your character and your NPC squadmates to make them look awesome.  But as much as I love the feel of being a cool, customizable commando squad leader, this game has its moments that have made me rage quit on a couple of occasions. 

The story follows a team of commandos taking down a drug cartel that's taken over Bolivia. That's about it for narrative. You have a bunch of mini-bosses to take down on your way to the main antagonist, and they do come with their own cutscenes and backstory if you're interested, but I figure most of these guys are either going to die or going to jail so I don't really care.

Gameplay is what you'd normally expect from stealth shooters; you sneak around, take out bad guys if you can, and if you are detected it's run and gun time. There's a bigger emphasis on stealth here though, especially in the first part of the game when you're weak and don't have as many tools at your disposal. Even when you've fully upgraded your health, it's still really easy for a simple grunt to take you down if they flank you, so stealth is typically your best approach to any situation if you can help it. The enemies are a little more sensitive in this game as well, able to detect you at farther distances and able to hear silenced weapons if you're shooting them too close to patrolling guards. This means you really have to plan out your approach and scout out enemy positions with a camera drone or binoculars before you move in, because being detected in the middle of an enemy base that has a army of guards, mounted gun emplacements, mortars, and alarms that call helicopters can lead to a very swift death for you and your squad. In fact, there are some moments where it's ridiculous how quickly these guys can detect you at a distance. More on that later. 

Your NPC squad is a bit of a mixed bag. They can be really handy a lot of situations, being able to fire at targets from passenger seats in vehicles, being able to revive you when you are downed, and able to simultaneously snipe marked enemies with flawless accuracy. They're also able to help you with recon by marking enemies for you. Often, they see enemies through buildings and landscape like they have X-ray vision, which is a bit of an immersion-breaking bug, but it is helpful so I'm not going to complain too much. On the other hand, there's moments when they feel completely brain-dead. They'll normally hang back when you're infiltrating an enemy base, which is good because if you tell them to follow you they'll throw caution out the window and end up getting detected, forcing you to fight for your life. They also get stuck on the landscape or objects in the area on occasion, though I mostly noticed this in underground areas which you don't encounter very often. 

However, my biggest gripe with this game comes from the Unidad. THE FRICKING UNIDAD. I'm not gonna lie, they're one of the main reasons why I'm writing this review. I cannot stress enough how much I hate these guys with a passion. Basically, they're Bolivia's military police that are low-key allied with the cartel, and they're supposedly dangerous and elite soldiers. Why, you may ask? Because they have high quality gear? Because they have military training? No, it's because they crap their pants and call for reinforcements at the first sign of danger, no matter what the situation is! 

"Oh, we just caught four lone guys in the middle of our base full of trained soldiers, machine guns, mortars, APCS and helicopters, BETTER CALL REINFORCEMENTS." 

Like, I get it, they're an enemy that's meant to make the game challenging and make you think twice before taking the direct attack approach. Still, I can't help but wish that these guys got a little bit of a nerf, because as soon as they start calling for reinforcements it is nonstop soldiers, armored cars and helicopters. Like, at the very least, give me a little more of a cushion between waves of reinforcements so I can consider my options. To make things worse, they always show up at the worst times possible. If you're trying to infiltrate a cartel base on the side of the road, then you'd better get the heck away from that road because I promise you a Unidad patrol car will drive up behind you, spot you, and start ripping into you with a mini gun while calling their entire army to back them up. I've lost count of how many times a stealth mission went south because a lone Unidad car just so happened to pass by me while I was scoping a base out. 

Some of the most aggravating missions in the game revolve around fighting these guys; I wouldn't call these moments hard, I'd call them outrageously unfair. Like a mission where you have to sneak onto a base without killing anyone, defend a computer download while all the soldiers you could have taken out beforehand start swarming the area like crazed serial killers, and then make a mad dash out of the base while being chased by endless armored cars and helicopters. Or a mission where you have to kill an Unidad commander while his base is attacked by cartel gangsters. The cartel gunmen last like thirty seconds before they get smoked, and then the base is on high alert the rest of the mission. That means the guards on the ground can spot you and alert everyone much faster, and snipers in the guard towers can see you a mile away like they're the freaking eye of Sauron. And if that wasn't enough, there's a helicopter just camping above the base, and it can see almost everything too, though it wasn't as bad as the snipers. I was on normal difficulty for this mission, so I bumped it down to easy, but even then it felt like it barely made a difference on the difficulty. Maybe I'm just stupid and there was a better way to do these mission, I don't know. But as an average player, I'm having a hard time believing anyone play tested those missions and deemed the difficulty fair. IT WAS THAT RIDICULOUS! 

Overall, I do really enjoy this game and I love the stealth/action vibe it gives, even if it does have some frustrating aspects here and there and the Unidad is annoying beyond belief. If you want a game that offers fun stealth gameplay, action packed hit and run warfare, and a fair amount of character and loadout customization, this game might scratch that itch. However, if you want a game with a compelling story, gameplay that isn't repetitive, or to feel like a demigod destroying everything in your path, this might not be what you're looking for.

Wildlands is a game that you'll either love or hate. For me, I personally loved it. If you aren't 100% sure about buying this game (on sale or not) watch some videos of its gameplay on youtube. Everything I put is obviously from my experience, and I just think its time to review this game.

First is the graphics. I play this game running an i7-9700k, GTX 1070, and 64GB of ram. Overall, I can hit 50-60 fps 1080p on almost all settings maxed. I don't think I ever really got a frame drop, Maybe like once from blowing up a few to many things at once but other then that the game runs very nicely. And so, with this game being system-heavy, the visuals follow suit. For me, it is absolutely beautiful. The water, sky, grass, vehicles, people, mountains, all of it looks great on Ultra/high settings. And the vast variety of landscapes like snow, swamps, salt lakes, Rocky mountains, Desert, etc. It is overall just breathtaking and you will find yourself just roaming around because of how pretty it is.

Second, the main campaign. Wildlands has a plethora of bosses controlling regions, in which it lets you choose which ones to go after and when. As you dig your way in, you'll find harder bosses with different difficulties of levels. and eventualy El Sueno, the big bad boss. I found almost all the characters in the game intriguing, good and bad guys alike. They put a lot of backstory into there characters and I think it really plays out well because you end up really getting to know them, whether you are going to kill them, hunt them, kidnap them or whatever. It really feels real. The cutscenes held character, and the differing missions surrounding bosses were enjoyable. It feels and plays like a natural and unrestricted experience.

Third, the side missions. This is where I find a lot of hate, even something I noticed right at its release. They are the same thing over and over to get resources for upgrades, throughout the entire game. But, oddly enough, I didn't mind them. I think, at least for me, is because the changing location always allowed for different circumstances. I like it because of the fact its all somewhere different even if the mission is the same. Hijacking a truck, for example, could be way different in an urban city vs. the mountains with thin roads and little traffic. The good news is, whether you like them or not, they are in no way required. It is very much possible to finish the game with the starter gear and weapons.

Fourth, the driving. Vehicles come in variety, with different purposes and characteristics. Say, perhaps, you take a van and stow your newly aquired short-term prisoner in the back. Take a sports car, and there is only room for one passenger, so you have speed but no friends to come along. On the PC specifically, it works well in one case and horrible in another. If you're trying to be slow and seaky, or perhaps just obeying the rules of the road, goodluck. Just to keep my speed down I have to tap the key at a consistent rate to stay on par with traffic. However, once you're accustomed to the driving, you'll find it quite useful. The high speed chases are much easier, as just holding the key keeps you at max speeds, drifting comes naturally, and split-second maneuvers are not just a thing of legend. Although this was my experience, and I noticed A LOT, or more so the majority of people hated the driving system.

Fifth, customizability. (Did I spell that right?) Weapons, well most of them, have several interchangeable parts that you can unlock to increase performance or change from that scope you hate. There's lots of paint jobs, even part by part. I loved playing around with different weapons, It really lets you play around with your own playstyle, whether you like stealth, loud or both you can really play around with what you want and how you want it.  Your character can be changed to your heart's desire, You have the disposal of ghillie suits, Costumes, Masks, Basically anything you can think of. Which is one thing I think ubisoft does really well is the customizablilty in a lot of there games.

Seventh, my verdict. I have endured easy success, endless failure (that one city mission in Narco Road MY OH MY), but overall I found it to be worth my time. I honestly think its a little underrate, I really found myself invested in the story and really enjoyed the experience. Get this game on sale, and I'm sure you'll get something out of it.

There's no other way to put it. This game and the followup Breakpoint are bad Ghost Recon games.

It's one similar mission after the other with repetitive objectives. There's one immensely irritating mission that flaunts every little issue with the game's inherent design and the painfully poor friendly AI (The El Pulpo mission for everyone who's played the game). 

All in all, it has its moments of being fun. I haven't done any of the PVP, but there's surely reviews abundant about that floating around. And if you're a total gear-eccentric, there's a lot of fun stuff to deck your operator out in, thought you're going to have to purchase some DLC to get 'kit' that isn't just a 5.11 drop. 

As an old game, it's worth getting on sale for just a few hours of messing around WITH friends. Otherwise, save your money, and definitely avoid Breakpoint like the plague.

I put almost 400 hours into the game, from the bug-ridden launch through 100% completion in every DLC. Wildlands is one of the most enjoyable co-op, tactical shooters I've played. Its a nice balance of arcade-y input and tactical action that lets a four player team take it super serious (mandatory at higher difficulties) or go in guns blazing. The transition from a perfectly executed tactical stealth op to a scrambling gun fight when someone drops the ball is seemless and constantly entertaining. 

In particular, Wildlands has the gold standard for drop in / drop out co-op multiplayer. You can play the game 100% co-op from the beginning. If a player jumps in to join you on a mission / zone they haven't reached yet, the game has no problem allowing them to participate and even gives them credit for any missions that are completed and unlocks that are found in their own save game. Players can easily go back and replay old missions to help out a friend who hasn't completed as much of the game. Players are also free to roam anywhere in the open world, which allows the team to divide and conquer or spread out for multiple angles of approach on an objective (ground, air, sniper / LMG overwatch, etc.). More co-op games could learn from what Wildlands does so well in this space.

I would personally consider Wildlands a game with few flaws, but they exist and are worth being aware of. The Teammate AI is a little lack luster, this is a game that was built from the ground up assuming you would play with other people and I strongly recommend playing it that way. The story is a pretty by the numbers, spec-ops military story; partly par for the course for a Tom Clancy military story line but the simplistic story is also what enables the seamless drop in / drop out multiplayer to work so well. There's not a lot of shocking twists and turns or personal character growth throughout the story, but its also not really the point of the "fun" in the game (for the record, the "fun" is infiltrating an enemy base to grab intel and then shooting your way out when the plan invariably goes belly up!). Compared to historic Ghost Recon games, this outing has definitely tilted more arcade-y and less tactical. If you're looking for old school Ghost Recon, this isn't it, but I feel the modern upgrades are what made this title so successful.

Long and short, I recommend Ghost Recon Wildlands for anyone who enjoys tactical shooters with their friends. Roaming the Bolivian countryside getting up to hijinks and taking down cartel strongholds with three friends is some of the best times I've had gaming in the last few years.

FUN FOR WHAT IT IS, BUT...
This game was fun for approximately 30 hours.  I played the majority with one friend in multiplayer.  The graphics are amazing; especially at night!  You can see all the lights, in all the cities for miles, along with the lights from cars moving around the mountains.  It was nice that there was no tether so you could move as far away from other players as you want.  The game provides a decent open world where you can pick what order you want to do things and attack each mission/challenge as you please.  There were levels of realism to things that we enjoyed.  There were a LOT of options for customizing your character's appearance which was nice.  Unfortunately...

The guns available were fine but it didn't seem that one weapon was much different from another.  We spent the majority of the game playing with the same weapons and never traded them out for something else.  It didn't feel like we needed to collect all the weapons and parts on the map as a result.  

While we enjoyed a lot of things about the game, once we reached the 4 skull difficulty levels, we became frustrated by how the game chose to increase the challenge.  We  liked the added siren warning system, choppers in the air, and Unidad presence (bad guys with armor), we were very irritated with how the game would spawn random bad guys, sometimes right beside you, even while you were hiding and out of sight.  Somehow, the AI always knew where you were at, even when hiding or moving through heavy ground cover.  There is almost zero ability to be strategic because even though you could place proximity mines around a building you were camped, the AI would spawn directly beside you.  Strategy is further complicated, when one player is detected, the other player is detected as well, even if they are on the other side of the compound and not near you.

The rebels were ANNOY!  They randomly show up and mess up your strategy because they automatically start attacking the bad guys and draw attention to your presence.  Whatever you do, don't let them out of their cages because the game will start spawning more bad guys randomly around you, even in places you have already cleared.

The vehicles were not great.  They were hard to control and easily damaged.  We had the most fun on the dirty bikes which were great at getting around off road.

In the end, we enjoyed the game for what it was, but didn't complete it.  We started to feel like we were just struck in a loop of doing the same thing over and over in a different location.  We wanted this to be a more tactical shooter game but strategy became almost impossible for the above reasons.

This game has a bit of a learning curve, but after a few hours of gameplay you will start to get the hang of it.  The single player campaign has a loose structure, but is quite entertaining.  If you like stealth shooters this is one of the best I've played.  I haven't played the online yet so I can't comment on that.

Although not quite as interactive as some, Wildlands boasts arguably one of the best open worlds ever created. It is a jaw-droppingly huge and incredible world to explore. Although it is scaled down and only a rough impression of the real-world Bolivia, it still feels like the full entirety of an actual country (albeit minus any large metropolitan areas, unfortunately). Still, as the title of the game suggests, the focus is on the wilderness, and Wildlands' map does not disappoint. Amazon rainforest, paradise lake resorts, cocaine farms hidden in the depths of the jungle, high-altitude woodland, snow-capped mountains, arid, rocky foothills, and even the famously desolate expanse of Bolivia's salt flats.

The best way to play this game is with a strict no-fast-travel rule - including fast travel at all is frankly a crime in a world this fun to traverse. When you take fast travel away, you actually have to hike across these expansive wildernesses, talk to locals for intel, put around in "borrowed" old cars on lengthy road trips, dodge military patrols and checkpoints, and generally inhabit the backwoods of a fictionalized country.

Speaking of fiction, the story content is relatively good. It's much more reminiscent of classic Tom Clancy stories of civil unrest, powerful terrorist organizations, and outnumbered and under-resourced special forces, as opposed to the tediously bland techno-vomit of newer, posthumously ghostwritten "Tom Clancy" dreck (prime example: Breakpoint). This is also where the gameplay excels, because where it lacks in open world depth, it makes up for in dozens of engaging, elaborately-produced mini-campaigns in each region of the map as you target the various bad guy lieutenants in order to expose and go after their bosses in turn.

One mission has you abduct, extract, and interrogate some flunkie for information, and the co-op possibilities really shine here: My friends and I nabbed the target at gunpoint and took out his guards while one of us pulled up in an escape vehicle. We stuffed the target into the trunk while the bad guys closed in, so we peeled off into the desert. Eventually we shook the pursuit and found ourselves alone, at night, in the middle of afore-mentioned desolate salt flats. So, naturally, we did the only Correct & Proper thing: dragged the guy out of the trunk and put him in front of the blinding headlights of our car in the middle of nowhere and interrogated him there. One we were finished with him, we knocked him out and left him for dead, driving off to find civilization again and our next objective...

The story missions really carry a lot of the gameplay, especially in co-op. Unfortunately, as mentioned, the gameplay outside of those missions can get a little thin. Combat encounters tend to be pretty formulaic, the difficulty settings suck, and once you've been at it for awhile you can start to see the simplistically-exploitable rules of what is a sadly rather shallow simulation.

Still, that one flaw is the only thing really dragging this game down. I wish it had some of the more evolved features of Breakpoint, because aside from that Wildlands is a far superior game - damn near a work of art on account of what is by far my favorite open world I've ever played Make Believe Soldier in.

Long Story: Ghost Recon Wildlands is something of a strange game when it comes to the Tom Clancy name. It's not a tactical shooter and it's not an in-depth military game, instead, it's a game that tries to be this hybrid open-world shooter without ever perfecting the formula. You're dumped into the surprisingly immersive war-torn Bolivia, chalkful of people to shoot, places to explore, and more. Something Ubisoft is very capable of doing, the game worlds are usually their strong suit. However, their faults lie in some important parts elsewhere in the game. The big issue that primarily plagues Wildlands is that while it's not exceptionally bad at anything, it's not exceptionally great either. It's just an open-world military shooter. The game does become exponentially better when playing with friends though. The game SLIGHTLY reminds me of ARMA in that I can play with some friends and infiltrate a base together and get immense satisfaction successfully clearing a base using tactics with each other. That's what I think this game was designed with in mind. That being said, I do have some personal complaints. First being that the customization is fairly lackluster, half the customization options make you look as if you're dressing up for an airsoft match which isn't very good (this problem is mitigated by the much more tactical-looking special outfits but those offer no customization, detracting from player agency). Second is the AI, it's either dumb as rocks and couldn't spot you in an open-field or it's spot you from 3 miles away in a jungle and snipe you with a pistol, there is no in-between. I wish the AI was just a bit better to go up against. At the end of the day, Wildlands is a pretty good game and there's not really a whole lot out there to offer what it does on the scale that it does. It's better with friends but servicable as a single-player title. I can however promise that it is so much better than the trainwreck that is GR: Breakpoint.

Ubisoft basically only makes one "open world" game these days.  If you've played any of the later Far Cry games, Watchdogs, etc. you already know what you're getting with this title.

All of these games offer a couple of hours of refreshing, novel content before they start to feel like a mindless slog.   The fictionalized version of Bolivia in this game is a beautiful landscape of arid hills and shimmering lakes, but it feels hollow - like a theme park version of a real country populated by soulless animatronics.  It's  "Westworld" version of South America for you - the player - to live out your action movie super commando fantasy.

NPC cartel soldiers and rebel guerrillas alike just roam around the many (many... many...) roads brainlessly until you decide to take some action.  The game dialog suggests you're dropping into the middle of a shadow war between the Bolivian army, the Santa Blanca cartel and the rebel faction but in practice there's no sense of a bigger stage.   All of the action takes place within 50 yards of your location at that precise moment and as soon as you leave that location everything is reset.   Military outposts you wipe out are spontaneously re-garrisoned, lavish casinos you destroy are rebuilt and filled again with wealthy party goers. 

The title of the game and the designation of your squad, "Ghosts", seems to suggest that you're there to act invisibly; to get in and get out without anyone ever knowing about your presence.   To infiltrate using guile and stealth and accomplish your objectives without leaving so much as a ripple...  Yet there's no disincentive to roll up to each and every mission marker in a fully loaded attack helicopter and just lay waste to everyone.   Need to plant listening devices in a lieutenant's personal estate?   Murder everyone, stroll in and place your bugs, and then stroll out.  Mission accomplished!   No one raises an eyebrow at the pile of bodies left behind, and indeed the bodies all vanish after 30 seconds anyway.

As always, you can rely on Ubisoft to make a competently mediocre game.  It's an experience which captures all of the elements of what technically makes up a video game, while managing to avoid any of the soul or engagement that makes a video game actually fun and memorable.

The game offers a bonanza of different weapons and weapon attachments, but who cares?  All you do is headshot everyone from the bushes and it hardly matters what gun you use or what the "handling" stat is for it.  I don't even know what the Handling stat does, because the game never bothers explaining it.  I guess the developers realized it didn't actually matter too.

The premise of the game is that your squad is assigned to travel from province to province within Bolivia and systematically dismantle the Santa Blanca narco organization (sorry - "narco TERRORISTS"), but after the third such province I just didn't care any more.  Each region offers the same basic structure - 6 Story Missions to find out where the head honcho for that region is hiding out, followed by a final mission where you go kill or capture them.  Along the way you can help out the rebels with some pointless fetch quests which unlock better versions of the pointless "Rebel Support" call outs, but who cares?  Kill the 'buchon', blah blah blah some vapid dialog from your CIA handler about how much of an impact what you did will have (Spoiler alert: it has zero impact and everything in the region stays exactly the same), and then you steal yet another helicopter to fly over to yet another region to do it all over again.

I'm not even sure why the late Tom Clancy's name is still attached to any of these games.  Sure, back in the 80's and 90's he wrote some popular military thrillers but how is any of this connected to his work?  Did he write a book called "Ghost Recon Wildlands" or does any Ubisoft game where an M4 carbine appears qualify as existing under the "Tom Clancy Military Action" umbrella?

tldr; by this point I should no better than to keep paying actual money for Ubisoft games, and so should you.  Let's all do our patriotic duty and demand better games than this.
